Because that replacement happily creates hyphens at the ends when the input starts or finishes with punctuation, the trim has to come after it, not before — running them the other way round leaves `"what-"` from `"What?!"`.

tests.name: a title with nothing usable is empty
does not double up existing hyphens

hints: Three transformations in order: lowercase, replace separator runs with a hyphen, then remove hyphens at the ends.
A character class with a `+` quantifier replaces a whole run at once — that is what stops `"a   b"` becoming `"a---b"`.
Anchors let you strip the ends: `^-+` and `-+$`, or one alternation with the global flag.

challenge:ch-str-palindrome.solutionExplanation: Separating normalisation from comparison is what keeps this simple: after the `replace`, the palindrome question is asked of a string with no special cases left in it. The two-pointer walk compares from both ends inward and stops as soon as a pair disagrees, so a non-palindrome like `"abca"` is rejected on the first comparison rather than after building a whole reversed copy. Reversing via `[...clean].reverse().join("")` is equally correct and shorter; it just allocates a second string where this does not.

tests.name: a classic phrase palindrome
tests.body: expect(isPalindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama")).toBe(true);

hints: Normalise first, compare second. Once the string is stripped down to lowercase letters and digits, the check itself is one comparison.
A string has no `reverse` method, but an array does — and a string can become an array and back again.
You can also compare from both ends inward with two indices, which avoids building a second string at all.

challenge:ch-str-word-wrap.solutionExplanation: The three branches are the whole algorithm: an empty line always accepts the next word, a non-empty line accepts it only if the word *and its joining space* still fit, and otherwise the line is flushed. Putting the empty-line case first is what handles an unbreakably long word — it goes onto its own line without a fit check, exactly as the specification requires. The `+ 1` in the fit test is the space that will be added, and forgetting it produces lines one character too long. The final flush after the loop is what saves the last line, which no word ever pushes.

tests.name: wraps at a word boundary
tests.body: expect(wrapText("the quick brown fox", 10)).toEqual(["the quick", "brown fox"]);

tests.name: a short text stays on one line
never exceeds the width when it can avoid it
tests.body: for (const line of wrapText("aa bb cc dd ee ff", 5)) expect(line.length <= 5).toBe(true);

tests.name: an over-long word gets its own line
an empty string produces no lines
a whitespace-only string produces no lines
fills a line exactly to the width
breaks one character past the width
produces no empty lines
tests.body: for (const line of wrapText("  a  b  ", 1)) expect(line.length > 0).toBe(true);

tests.name: every word survives in order
tests.body: expect(wrapText("one two three four five", 9).join(" ")).toBe("one two three four five");

hints: Split into words first, then decide line by line. Trying to scan character by character makes the "never break a word" rule much harder.
Keep a current line. For each word, ask whether adding it (plus the joining space) would exceed the width; if so, finish the current line and start a new one.
The over-long-word case falls out naturally if you always place a word on an empty line regardless of whether it fits.

challenge:ch-str-run-length.solutionExplanation: Encoding measures each run with an inner loop and then jumps the outer index past it, so every character is visited once. Decoding is where the interesting bug lives: reading exactly one digit after each letter works perfectly on `"a3b2c1"` and silently corrupts `"a12"` into eleven characters instead of twelve. The `\d+` in the pattern is what makes multi-digit counts work, and `matchAll` hands back the character and the digits as separate capture groups so no manual index tracking is needed.

tests.name: always writes a count, even for one
handles a run longer than nine
round-trips a long generated string
decoding does not stop at the first digit

hints: For encoding, walk the string tracking the current character and how many of it you have seen in a row. Flush the run when the character changes — and again after the loop.
For decoding, the character is always one character but the count is one *or more* digits. Keep reading digits while the next character is a digit.
A regex with a global flag and a capture group for the digits does the decoding scan for you: a letter followed by one-or-more digits.

challenge:ch-str-mask-card.solutionExplanation: The two-pass structure exists because "keep the last four digits" cannot be answered until you know how many digits there are — and separators must not be counted, which is what `replace(/\D/g, "")` strips. The single walk then rebuilds the string in place, so every space and hyphen lands at its original index and the output length matches the input length. Masking by character position instead of digit position is the tempting shortcut, and `"12 34"` is the case that exposes it.

tests.name: masks all but the last four
masks exactly one digit when there are five
separators do not count toward the four
the last four visible characters are the original digits

hints: The "last four" is counted in digits, not in characters — a separator sitting near the end must not use up part of that budget.
Count the digits first. Then walk the string once, masking a digit only while you have not yet reached the final four.
Walking backwards is an alternative: count digits from the right and start masking once you pass four.

challenge:ch-str-query-string.solutionExplanation: Splitting each pair with `indexOf("=")` rather than `split("=")` is what preserves an equals sign inside a value — `"eq=a=b"` must yield `"a=b"`, not `"a"`. The `+`-to-space replacement has to happen *before* `decodeURIComponent`, since that function leaves `+` untouched by design. The three-branch accumulation is the repeated-key rule stated directly, and `Object.hasOwn` is used rather than `key in result` so an inherited name like `"toString"` is not mistaken for a value already collected.

tests.name: collects a repeated key into an array
a single occurrence is not an array
a bare key has an empty value
an empty query gives an empty object
a lone question mark gives an empty object
keeps an equals sign inside a value

hints: Split on `&` to get the pairs, then split each pair on `=` — but only on the *first* `=`, or a value containing one will be truncated.
`decodeURIComponent` does not turn `+` into a space. Replace `+` yourself before decoding, or the plus survives literally.
For repeated keys, check whether the key is already present: absent means store the value, present-and-not-an-array means wrap both into one, already-an-array means push.

challenge:ch-str-template.solutionExplanation: A function replacer is what makes "leave it alone if the key is missing" expressible at all — returning `whole`, the full matched text, puts the placeholder back byte for byte. The presence check uses `Object.hasOwn` for two reasons: a value of `0` or `""` is present and must be substituted, so a truthiness test would be wrong, and an inherited name like `toString` is not a real value, so `key in values` would be wrong too. Converting through `String(value)` rather than concatenation keeps the `null` case explicit instead of letting it stringify to `"null"`.

tests.name: leaves an unknown key in place
renders a present null as empty
leaves text with no placeholders alone
does not treat single braces as placeholders

hints: `String.prototype.replace` accepts a function as its second argument. It is called for each match and its return value becomes the replacement.
The replacer receives the whole match first, then each capture group — so you can return the whole match unchanged when the key is missing.
Check for the key with `Object.hasOwn`, not by testing whether the value is falsy: a present value of `0` or `""` must still be substituted.

challenge:ch-str-escape-html.solutionExplanation: A single pass with a lookup sidesteps the ordering trap entirely: each character is examined once and replaced once, so no replacement can ever see the output of another. That is why `escapeHtml("<")` correctly yields `&lt;` — the literal text the user typed, rendered visibly, rather than a working tag. Chained `replace` calls can be made correct by escaping `&` first, but the ordering constraint is invisible in the code and easy to break later. Note the scope of this function: it makes text safe as *element content and attribute values*, which is not the same as making it safe inside a `<script>` block, a URL, or a CSS context — each of those needs its own escaping.

tests.name: does not double-escape its own output
escapes the ampersand before the others
leaves no raw angle bracket behind
tests.body: const out = escapeHtml(""); expect(out.includes("<")).toBe(false); expect(out.includes(">")).toBe(false);

hints: A single pass with a lookup object is both simpler and safer than five chained `replace` calls.
If you do chain replacements, `&` must be first — escaping it last would turn the `&` in `<` into `&lt;`.
A character class matching all five characters, with the global flag, lets one `replace` handle every case.

challenge:ch-rx-extract-links.solutionExplanation: Two decisions carry this pattern. Using negated character classes rather than `.*` keeps each match tight: `.` is greedy and would match past the first `]`, so `"[a](1) and [b](2)"` would come back as a single link with the text `a](1) and [b`. Excluding `\n` in the same classes is what enforces the no-line-break rule, since `.` already excludes newlines but the negated classes do not. The negative lookbehind `(?<!!)` asserts that the position before the `[` is not a `!` without consuming a character — that last part matters, because a version that consumed the preceding character would fail on a link at the very start of the string, and would also let two adjacent constructs interfere.

tests.name: extracts a link from surrounding prose
keeps a link next to an image
no links gives an empty array
an empty string gives an empty array
does not span a line break
ignores parentheses with no bracket part
handles a url with a query string
an image between two links does not merge them

hints: Two capture groups: one for the text between the brackets, one for the URL between the parentheses.
Use `[^\]\n]*` and `[^)\n]*` rather than `.*` — a greedy `.*` would run past the first closing bracket and swallow several links at once.
To skip images, require that the character before the `[` is not a `!`. A negative lookbehind `(?<!!)` does it, or you can capture the preceding character and check it.

challenge:ch-rx-escape-and-highlight.solutionExplanation: Escaping is not optional politeness here — without it, a query of `"("` throws a `SyntaxError` and crashes the search box, and a query of `".*"` matches the entire string. That is the regex equivalent of an injection bug: user data being interpreted as code. The `$&` in the replacement means "the matched text", which is the shortest way to write "put a backslash before whatever this was". In `highlight`, using a replacer function rather than a fixed string is what preserves casing: `match` holds the text as it appeared in the original, so a search for `"cat"` in `"CAT"` wraps `CAT` and not `cat`. Note what this deliberately does not do — it inserts raw `<mark>` tags, so `text` must already be trusted or separately escaped before it reaches the page.

tests.name: treats a star as literal without throwing
does not throw on unbalanced brackets
handles a plus in the query
a query matching everything does not run away
handles a query longer than the text

hints: Escaping means putting a backslash in front of every character that has a special meaning in a pattern: `. * + ? ^ $ { } ( ) | [ ] \`.
One `replace` with a character class covers them all, using `$&` or a function to reference the matched character.

For `highlight`, build the pattern from the escaped query with the `g` and `i` flags, and use a replacer function so the *matched text* is what goes inside the tags — that is what preserves the original casing.

challenge:ch-rx-csv-line.solutionExplanation: This is a small state machine, and it is a state machine because CSV is not a regular language once quoting is involved — the meaning of a comma depends on context, which a single pattern cannot express cleanly. The `inQuotes` flag is that context. Looking one character ahead at `line[i + 1]` distinguishes an escaped quote from a closing one, and advancing `i` past the second quote is what stops it being reinterpreted. The final `fields.push(field)` outside the loop is essential and easy to forget: no comma follows the last field, so nothing inside the loop ever emits it — which is also why an empty line correctly yields one empty field rather than none.

tests.name: an empty line is one empty field
a quoted field may contain a comma
a quoted field may contain spaces
several quoted fields in a row
a quoted field holding only a quote
handles many fields
tests.body: const line = Array.from({ length: 200 }, (_, i) => "f" + i).join(","); expect(parseCsvLine(line).length).toBe(200);

hints: Walk the line character by character with a flag for whether you are currently inside a quoted field.
A comma only separates fields when you are *not* inside quotes. That single condition is what makes quoted commas work.
Inside quotes, a `"` followed by another `"` is a literal quote — consume both and append one. A lone `"` ends the quoted section.

challenge:ch-date-days-between.solutionExplanation: Normalising both dates to UTC midnight *before* subtracting is what makes the division exact. The naive version — subtracting the raw timestamps and dividing — is off by a fraction of a day whenever the two dates straddle a daylight-saving transition in the local zone, because a local day can be 23 or 25 hours long; rounding papers over it most of the time and then produces an off-by-one at the worst moment. UTC has no such transitions, so once both values are at UTC midnight the difference is genuinely a whole number of days. `Date.UTC` returns a timestamp rather than a `Date`, which conveniently means nothing is allocated and neither input is touched.

tests.name: the same day at different times is zero
a non-leap year has no 29 February
a full non-leap year is 365 days
a full leap year is 366 days
does not modify the inputs
tests.body: const a = new Date(Date.UTC(2024, 2, 1)); const t = a.getTime(); daysBetween(a, new Date(Date.UTC(2024, 2, 5))); expect(a.getTime()).toBe(t);

hints: Reduce each date to a UTC midnight timestamp first: `Date.UTC(d.getUTCFullYear(), d.getUTCMonth(), d.getUTCDate())`.
Once both are at UTC midnight, the difference really is an exact multiple of 86,400,000, because UTC has no daylight saving.
Do not mutate the inputs with `setHours` — build new timestamps instead.

challenge:ch-date-business-days.solutionExplanation: Stepping one day at a time and only decrementing on a working day is what makes weekends and holidays compose without any arithmetic tricks — three consecutive holidays simply take three extra steps, with no special case. `setUTCDate` handles month and year rollover for you: setting the date to 32 in March lands correctly on 1 April, which is why the month-boundary test needs no code of its own. Copying the input first is not politeness but necessity, since `setUTCDate` mutates in place and a caller's date silently shifting is a genuinely nasty bug. The zero case returns before the loop precisely so that it can return a weekend date unchanged, as specified. Using the UTC getters throughout keeps the result independent of the machine running it.

tests.name: skips a whole weekend when adding several
zero on a weekend returns that weekend date
a holiday on a weekend changes nothing
does not modify the input
tests.body: const d = new Date(Date.UTC(2024, 2, 1)); const t = d.getTime(); addBusinessDays(d, 5); expect(d.getTime()).toBe(t);

tests.name: never lands on a weekend for a positive count
tests.body: for (let n = 1; n <= 20; n += 1) { const out = addBusinessDays(new Date(Date.UTC(2024, 2, 1)), n); expect(out.getUTCDay()).not.toBe(0); expect(out.getUTCDay()).not.toBe(6); }

tests.name: ten business days from a Monday is two weeks later

hints: Work with a copy: `new Date(date.getTime())`. Everything after that uses the UTC getters and setters.
Step one day at a time in the right direction, and only decrement the remaining count when the day you land on is a working day.
A `Set` of the holiday strings makes the check constant-time, and `toISOString().slice(0, 10)` gives you the same `YYYY-MM-DD` shape to compare against.

challenge:ch-date-relative-time.solutionExplanation: Ordering the unit table from largest to smallest means the first unit that fits is the right one, so "90 minutes" becomes "1 hour ago" rather than "90 minutes ago" without any extra comparison. Separating magnitude from direction early — the absolute value chooses the unit, the sign chooses the phrasing — halves the number of branches. Taking `now` as a parameter is what makes every one of these tests deterministic; a version calling `Date.now()` internally could only be tested against itself or with a mocked clock. In production `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat` does this properly, with correct pluralisation in every language, and is what you should reach for — the month and year approximations here are exactly the kind of thing a real internationalisation library handles for you.

tests.name: a few seconds ago is just now
a few seconds ahead is just now
the same instant is just now
a single day in the future is singular
rounds down to the largest whole unit
the boundary at ten seconds is not just now

hints: Work with the absolute difference to choose the unit, and use the sign only to pick between `"... ago"` and `"in ..."`.
A table of `[unitName, milliseconds]` from largest to smallest lets one loop find the right unit — take the first whose size fits.
Pluralise from the count, not the unit: append an `s` unless the count is exactly 1.

challenge:ch-num-money.solutionExplanation: Parsing through string manipulation rather than `parseFloat(text) * 100` is the whole point: that multiplication is not reliable, since `"0.07"` becomes 7.000000000000001 and `"1.15"` becomes 114.99999999999999, so rounding is required and the rounding direction becomes a source of half-cent errors. Splitting on the decimal point and padding never involves a fractional value at all. Once everything is integer cents, addition is exact — the thousand-times-one-penny test would drift with floats and lands on exactly `"10.00"` here. The sign is handled explicitly at both ends because `Math.floor(-5 / 100)` is `-1`, not `0`, which would render `-0.05` as `"-1.95"`; working with the absolute value and prefixing the sign avoids reasoning about how floor behaves on negatives.

tests.name: sums exactly where floats would not
the float version really is wrong
an empty list sums to zero
a negative total under a unit formats correctly

hints: Split the string on the decimal point instead, and pad the fractional part to two digits. That is pure string work with no float involved.
Formatting back is the same operation reversed: divide by 100 with integer division and remainder, then pad the remainder to two digits — and be careful with the sign.

challenge:ch-num-precision.solutionExplanation: The `a === b` shortcut does more work than it looks: it settles two identical infinities, and it makes `0` and `-0` equal, since `===` considers them so. Everything non-finite that survives that check — a `NaN`, or two opposite infinities — is then rejected by the finiteness guard, which also stops `Infinity - Infinity` producing a `NaN` that would silently fail the final comparison anyway. Scaling the tolerance by the larger magnitude is what makes one function work across the whole range: an absolute tolerance of 1e-9 would call 1e12 and 1e12+1 different (they are indistinguishable at that precision) and would call 1e-12 and 2e-12 equal (they differ by a factor of two). The one case relative tolerance cannot handle is comparison against exact zero, where no non-zero value is ever within a relative distance — which is why `nearlyEqual(0, 0.001)` is correctly false, and why code comparing against zero needs an absolute threshold chosen for its domain.

tests.name: strict equality really does fail there
zero is not nearly equal to a small number
a large relative difference is caught at a large scale
a large relative difference is caught at a small scale
infinity is not nearly equal to a finite number

hints: Handle the exact cases first: if `a === b`, they are equal (this also covers both infinities and both zeros).
`NaN` fails every comparison, so a `Number.isNaN` check on either value returning false handles it — and a non-finite value that was not caught by `a === b` cannot be nearly equal to anything.
The relative test is `Math.abs(a - b) <= tolerance * Math.max(Math.abs(a), Math.abs(b))`.

exercise:ex-m23-04-c.solutionExplanation: The original `try` block only ever scheduled a timer and then finished, popping its frame — by the time the callback ran, the event loop pushed it onto an **empty stack** with no relationship to that `catch`. Moving the handler inside the callback puts it on the same stack as the throw, so it works. The second test confirms the timing: nothing is caught synchronously, because the failure has not happened yet when `guarded` returns.

tests.name: catches the error
tests.body: const log = []; guarded(log); const __end = Date.now() + 2000; while (!(log.length >= 1) && Date.now() < __end) await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 1)); expect(log).toEqual(["caught"]);

tests.name: does not catch synchronously
tests.body: const log = []; guarded(log); expect(log).toEqual([]); await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 30));

tests.name: does not throw out of guarded
tests.body: const log = []; expect(() => guarded(log)).not.toThrow(); await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 30));

tests.name: catches on repeated calls
tests.body: const log = []; guarded(log); guarded(log); const __end = Date.now() + 2000; while (!(log.length >= 2) && Date.now() < __end) await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 1)); expect(log).toEqual(["caught", "caught"]);

hints: The try/catch must share the callback's stack.
Move the try/catch inside the timer callback.

exercise:ex-m23-04-d.solution: Error handling must be repeated at every level, with no single shared failure path
exercise:ex-m23-04-d.solutionExplanation: Indentation is uncomfortable; the repeated error handling is what causes real defects. Every level needs its own `if (error)` block, and missing one silently swallows that failure — with no way to say "if anything in this sequence fails, do X" in a single place. Performance and memory are not meaningfully different, and callbacks are not outdated: every event listener is one. The difficulty is specific to sequencing several **dependent** async operations with error handling, which is exactly what Promises were designed to fix.
hints: Which problem causes actual bugs rather than discomfort?

exercise:ex-m23-05-b.solutionExplanation: Synchronous code always runs first, so `"sync"` leads despite being written last. Then the event loop **drains the entire microtask queue** before taking another task — and promise callbacks are microtasks while timer callbacks are tasks. So `"promise"` runs before `"timer"`, even though the timer was scheduled first with a zero delay. Two different queues, with microtasks having priority.
hints: Which queue drains first after the synchronous code finishes?

exercise:ex-m23-05-d.solution: It makes the eventual result a value that can be returned, stored and chained
exercise:ex-m23-05-d.solutionExplanation: A callback-based function returns `undefined` — the result exists only inside a function you handed away, which is why dependent steps must nest and error handling cannot be shared. A Promise is an **object returned immediately** representing the eventual result, so it can be returned from a function and chained. Everything else — flat chaining, a single `.catch`, `Promise.all` — follows from that one property. Nothing gets faster, nothing runs in parallel, and the event loop is still exactly what delivers the callbacks.
hints: What could a callback-based function return to its caller?

exercise:ex-m24-02-a.solutionExplanation: The braces make it a block body, so `v.toUpperCase()` is evaluated and thrown away — the callback returns `undefined`, and the promise `.then` produced fulfils with that. The second callback receives `undefined`. Nothing throws, which is what makes this bug quiet: the symptom appears one link **later** than the mistake. Removing the braces or adding `return` fixes it.
hints: Does the first callback return anything?

exercise:ex-m24-02-c.solutionExplanation: The original started `loadOrders` and dropped it, so the first `.then` fulfilled with `undefined` immediately and the next callback tried to read `.length` from that. Returning the promise makes the chain **wait** and unwrap the array. Switching to concise arrow bodies removes the braces entirely, which makes the whole class of mistake impossible to reintroduce — a good default for single-expression callbacks.

tests.name: returns a Promise
tests.body: const p = orderCount(1); expect(p instanceof Promise).toBe(true); await p;

tests.name: does not reject
tests.body: let rejected = false; await orderCount(3).catch(() => { rejected = true; }); expect(rejected).toBe(false);

hints: The first `.then` starts `loadOrders` but never returns it.
Add `return`, or use a concise arrow body.

exercise:ex-m24-03-c.solutionExplanation: `.finally` runs on both paths and — crucially — **passes the original value or rejection straight through**, which is what makes the first and fourth tests pass simultaneously. Its callback receives no argument and its return value is ignored, so it cannot accidentally change the result. The hidden test confirms `loading` is set **before** the async work begins, since the flag is only useful while the task is actually running.

tests.name: passes the value through
tests.body: const s = {}; expect(await withSpinner(() => Promise.resolve("v"), s)).toBe("v");

tests.name: clears loading after success
tests.body: const s = {}; await withSpinner(() => Promise.resolve("v"), s); expect(s.loading).toBe(false);

tests.name: clears loading after failure
tests.body: const s = {}; await withSpinner(() => Promise.reject(new Error("x")), s).catch(() => {}); expect(s.loading).toBe(false);

tests.name: still rejects with the original reason
tests.body: const s = {}; let msg = null; await withSpinner(() => Promise.reject(new Error("original")), s).catch((e) => { msg = e.message; }); expect(msg).toBe("original");

tests.name: sets loading true while running
tests.body: const s = {}; const p = withSpinner(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r(1), 10)), s); expect(s.loading).toBe(true); await p;

hints: Set `state.loading = true` before starting.
Use `.finally(() => { state.loading = false; })`.
Return the resulting promise so the caller still sees the value or rejection.

exercise:ex-m24-03-d.solution: Rethrow the error, so the chain stays rejected and a caller can still handle it
exercise:ex-m24-03-d.solutionExplanation: A `.catch` that returns normally — including returning nothing — **recovers** the chain, so every following `.then` runs as though nothing failed and the caller receives a fulfilled promise. If you cannot genuinely recover, that is a false success: the promise equivalent of Module 22's swallowed error. Rethrowing keeps the failure travelling so the real handler upstream can act on it, while still letting you log it on the way past.
hints: What does a .catch that returns normally do to the chain?

exercise:ex-m24-04-c.solutionExplanation: `allSettled` is the only combinator that never rejects, which is exactly the requirement — `all` would have rejected on the first failure and discarded the successes. Filtering on `status` then mapping to `value` extracts just the usable results. The hidden test confirms order follows the **input**, not completion: the slow widget still comes first, because `allSettled` preserves input order just as `all` does.

tests.name: returns all values when all succeed
skips the failures
tests.body: expect(await loadAllWidgets([() => Promise.resolve("a"), () => Promise.reject(new Error("x")), () => Promise.resolve("c")])).toEqual(["a", "c"]);

tests.name: returns an empty array when all fail
tests.body: expect(await loadAllWidgets([() => Promise.reject(new Error("x")), () => Promise.reject(new Error("y"))])).toEqual([]);

tests.name: never rejects
tests.body: let rejected = false; await loadAllWidgets([() => Promise.reject(new Error("x"))]).catch(() => { rejected = true; }); expect(rejected).toBe(false);

tests.name: preserves the order of successes
tests.body: expect(await loadAllWidgets([() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r("slow"), 15)), () => Promise.resolve("fast")])).toEqual(["slow", "fast"]);

hints: `Promise.allSettled` never rejects.
Filter results by `status === "fulfilled"`, then map to `value`.

exercise:ex-m24-04-d.solutionExplanation: `Promise.any` fulfils with the first **fulfilment**, ignoring rejections, and only rejects — with an `AggregateError` listing every reason — when all inputs fail. That is precisely the mirror-server requirement. `race` would reject as soon as the *fastest* mirror failed, even with two healthy ones remaining. `all` requires every mirror to succeed, defeating the point of redundancy. `allSettled` would wait for all three rather than returning as soon as one succeeded.
hints: You want the first success, not the first response of any kind.

exercise:ex-m24-05-b.solutionExplanation: Each `.then` queues **only its own callback**; the next link is not queued until the previous one has actually run. So initially only `A1` and `B1` are pending, in that order. Running `A1` queues `A2`, running `B1` queues `B2` — both landing behind the already-pending work — producing strict alternation. Chains interleave rather than running to completion one at a time.
hints: When is the second link of a chain queued?

exercise:ex-m24-05-d.solution: The drain never ends, so timers, rendering and events never get a turn — the page freezes
exercise:ex-m24-05-d.solutionExplanation: The event loop drains the microtask queue until it is **empty**, and microtasks added during the drain join that same drain. Scheduling one unconditionally from within a microtask means the queue never empties, so the loop never proceeds to tasks or rendering — freezing the page exactly as a synchronous infinite loop would, and without any stack overflow to signal it. `setTimeout` genuinely yields because it queues a **task**, which the loop only reaches after the microtask queue is clear.
hints: When does the event loop stop draining the microtask queue?

exercise:ex-m25-02-c.solutionExplanation: The `cause` option from Module 22 preserves the original error — including its **type**, which the fourth test verifies by checking `instanceof TypeError`. Throwing rather than returning keeps the chain rejected, so the caller cannot mistake a failure for success; the fifth test guards that specifically. `return await` is again required inside the `try`, since without it a rejection would bypass the `catch` and the wrapping would never happen.

tests.name: rejects with the wrapper message
tests.body: let m = null; await loadProfile(() => Promise.reject(new Error("db down"))).catch((e) => { m = e.message; }); expect(m).toBe("profile unavailable");

tests.name: preserves the original as cause
tests.body: let c = null; await loadProfile(() => Promise.reject(new Error("db down"))).catch((e) => { c = e.cause; }); expect(c.message).toBe("db down");

tests.name: preserves the original error type
tests.body: let c = null; await loadProfile(() => Promise.reject(new TypeError("bad"))).catch((e) => { c = e.cause; }); expect(c instanceof TypeError).toBe(true);

tests.name: still rejects rather than returning
tests.body: let rejected = false; await loadProfile(() => Promise.reject(new Error("x"))).catch(() => { rejected = true; }); expect(rejected).toBe(true);

tests.name: wraps a synchronous throw too
tests.body: let m = null; await loadProfile(() => { throw new Error("sync"); }).catch((e) => { m = e.cause.message; }); expect(m).toBe("sync");

hints: `return await loader();` inside the try.
`throw new Error("profile unavailable", { cause: error });`

exercise:ex-m25-02-d.solution: Without await the promise is returned unwaited, so a rejection escapes the try and the catch never runs
exercise:ex-m25-02-d.solutionExplanation: `return load()` hands the promise back immediately and the function exits the `try` block before the promise settles — so a later rejection has no handler in scope and reaches the caller unwrapped. `return await load()` keeps the function **suspended inside the try**, so a rejection throws there and the `catch` genuinely applies. Note this only matters inside `try`/`catch` (or `try`/`finally`): elsewhere the two forms are equivalent for the caller, and the plain form is marginally more direct.
hints: Is the function still inside the try block when the promise settles?

exercise:ex-m25-03-c.solutionExplanation: `allSettled` is the only combinator that never rejects, satisfying the fourth test — `Promise.all` would have thrown on the first failure and discarded the successes alongside it. Mapping the loaders to promises **before** awaiting is what makes it concurrent, which the hidden test measures. Filtering on `status` then mapping to `value` extracts just the usable results, and order still follows the input rather than completion.

tests.name: returns all values when all succeed
skips failures
tests.body: expect(await loadWidgets([() => Promise.resolve("a"), () => Promise.reject(new Error("x")), () => Promise.resolve("c")])).toEqual(["a", "c"]);

tests.name: never rejects
tests.body: let rejected = false; await loadWidgets([() => Promise.reject(new Error("x"))]).catch(() => { rejected = true; }); expect(rejected).toBe(false);

tests.name: overlaps rather than serialising
tests.body: const ev = []; const mk = (n) => () => { ev.push(n + "+"); return new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => { ev.push(n + "-"); r(n); }, 10)); }; await loadWidgets([mk("a"), mk("b"), mk("c")]); expect(ev.slice(0, 3)).toEqual(["a+", "b+", "c+"]);

hints: `loaders.map((load) => load())` starts them all.
`await Promise.allSettled(...)` never rejects.
Filter on `status === "fulfilled"`, then map to `value`.

exercise:ex-m25-03-d.solution: If b rejects while still suspended on await a, that rejection is momentarily unhandled
exercise:ex-m25-03-d.solutionExplanation: The concurrency is genuine — both operations start immediately, so the timing matches `Promise.all`. The problem is **handler timing**: no handler is attached to `b` until execution reaches `await b`, so a rejection arriving before then is briefly unhandled, which some environments report as a warning. `Promise.all` attaches handlers to every promise the moment it is called, avoiding the window entirely. Prefer it unless you specifically need to do other work between starting and awaiting.
hints: When does a handler get attached to the second promise?

exercise:ex-m25-04-a.solutionExplanation: `forEach` discards its callback's return value, so the async callbacks are started but never awaited. Each suspends at `await null` before reaching its `push`, so nothing has been pushed when `out.length` is read — giving `0`. The pushes happen later as microtasks. This is exactly why `forEach` must never be used when you need to wait for asynchronous work.
hints: Does forEach wait for the promise its callback returns?

exercise:ex-m25-04-c.solutionExplanation: `map` **collects** the promises — unlike `forEach`, which discards them — so `Promise.all` can wait for every one. The second test is the important contrast with sequential processing: despite wildly different durations, results still follow **input** order rather than completion order, because `Promise.all` preserves position. The third measures genuine concurrency, and the fifth confirms the all-or-nothing rejection inherited from `Promise.all`.

tests.name: preserves order despite differing durations
tests.body: expect(await processAll([15, 2, 8], (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r(ms), ms)))).toEqual([15, 2, 8]);

tests.name: overlaps rather than serialising
tests.body: const ev = []; await processAll(["a", "b", "c"], (n) => { ev.push(n + "+"); return new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => { ev.push(n + "-"); r(n); }, 10)); }); expect(ev.slice(0, 3)).toEqual(["a+", "b+", "c+"]);

tests.name: rejects if any handler fails
tests.body: let rejected = false; await processAll([1, 2], async (n) => { if (n === 2) throw new Error("x"); return n; }).catch(() => { rejected = true; }); expect(rejected).toBe(true);

tests.name: starts every item before any finishes
tests.body: const started = []; await processAll([1, 2, 3], (n) => { started.push(n); return Promise.resolve(n); }); expect(started).toEqual([1, 2, 3]);

hints: `items.map((item) => handler(item))` starts them all.
`await Promise.all(...)` collects the results.

exercise:ex-m26-02-a.solutionExplanation: JSON has no `undefined` value, and in an **object** a property holding it is dropped entirely — leaving an empty object rather than a null-valued key. This matters when sending data: a field you expected to clear on the server may simply never arrive. Inside an **array** the same value becomes `null` instead, since removing it would shift the indices.
hints: Can JSON represent undefined at all?

exercise:ex-m26-02-c.solutionExplanation: The reviver runs for **every** key/value pair at every depth, which is why the nested and array tests pass with no extra recursion — `JSON.parse` walks the structure for you. Checking `typeof value === "string"` first is essential, since `test` would coerce numbers and objects to strings and produce false matches. Returning `value` unchanged in the else branch is what preserves everything that is not a date; a reviver returning `undefined` would delete the property entirely.
hints: `JSON.parse(text, reviver)` calls the reviver for every key/value pair.
Test `typeof value === "string"` and match against an ISO pattern.
Return `value` unchanged when it does not match.

exercise:ex-m26-03-c.solutionExplanation: The order matters: `204` **is** a success, so `response.ok` is already `true` for it and the not-ok check must come first for genuine failures. Returning `null` before reaching `.json()` avoids the parse error an empty body would cause — a very common bug against `DELETE` endpoints, which conventionally return `204`. The hidden test distinguishes an explicit `null` from an accidental `undefined` falling off the end of the function.

tests.name: parses a normal success
tests.body: const f = () => Promise.resolve(new Response(JSON.stringify({ a: 1 }), { status: 200 })); expect(await request(f, "/x")).toEqual({ a: 1 });

tests.name: returns null for 204
tests.body: const f = () => Promise.resolve(new Response(null, { status: 204 })); expect(await request(f, "/x")).toBe(null);

tests.name: does not throw on 204
tests.body: const f = () => Promise.resolve(new Response(null, { status: 204 })); let threw = false; await request(f, "/x").catch(() => { threw = true; }); expect(threw).toBe(false);

tests.name: throws on 404
tests.body: const f = () => Promise.resolve(new Response("x", { status: 404 })); let m = null; await request(f, "/x").catch((e) => { m = e.message; }); expect(m).toBe("HTTP 404");

tests.name: treats 204 as ok
tests.body: const f = () => Promise.resolve(new Response(null, { status: 204 })); expect(await request(f, "/x")).not.toBe(undefined);

hints: Check `!response.ok` first, then the 204 case.
`204` is a success, so `ok` is already true for it.

exercise:ex-m26-03-d.solution: A response body is a stream and can only be read once — reading it twice throws
exercise:ex-m26-03-d.solutionExplanation: The body arrives as a stream, so consuming it marks `bodyUsed` as `true` and any further read throws a `TypeError`. This bites specifically when someone adds a debug log of the body and the real parse then fails — making the logging itself look like the cause. Call `response.clone()` **before** the first read if you need the body twice, or log the already-parsed value instead.
hints: What does `response.bodyUsed` become after the first read?

exercise:ex-m26-04-c.solutionExplanation: Testing `data !== undefined` rather than `if (data)` is what makes the hidden test pass: `0` and `false` are legitimate bodies, and a truthiness check would silently drop them — the same falsy-value trap seen throughout the curriculum. The `= {}` default on the options parameter lets `api(f, "/x")` be called with two arguments, per Module 14. Centralising the `ok` check, `204` handling and header logic means no call site can forget them, which is precisely how the mistakes in this lesson happen.

tests.name: defaults to GET with no body
tests.body: let opts = null; const f = (u, o) => { opts = o; return Promise.resolve(new Response("{}", { status: 200 })); }; await api(f, "/x"); expect(opts.method).toBe("GET"); expect(opts.body).toBe(undefined);

tests.name: attaches a body when data is given
tests.body: let opts = null; const f = (u, o) => { opts = o; return Promise.resolve(new Response("{}", { status: 200 })); }; await api(f, "/x", { method: "POST", data: { a: 1 } }); expect(opts.body).toBe('{"a":1}');

tests.name: sets Content-Type only with a body
tests.body: let opts = null; const f = (u, o) => { opts = o; return Promise.resolve(new Response("{}", { status: 200 })); }; await api(f, "/x"); expect(opts.headers["Content-Type"]).toBe(undefined);

tests.name: returns null for 204
tests.body: const f = () => Promise.resolve(new Response(null, { status: 204 })); expect(await api(f, "/x", { method: "DELETE" })).toBe(null);

tests.name: throws on failure
tests.body: const f = () => Promise.resolve(new Response("x", { status: 500 })); let m = null; await api(f, "/x").catch((e) => { m = e.message; }); expect(m).toBe("HTTP 500");

tests.name: sends a falsy body when data is 0
tests.body: let opts = null; const f = (u, o) => { opts = o; return Promise.resolve(new Response("{}", { status: 200 })); }; await api(f, "/x", { method: "POST", data: 0 }); expect(opts.body).toBe("0");

hints: Build the options object, then add body/headers conditionally.
Test `data !== undefined`, not `if (data)`.
Check `!response.ok` first, then the 204 case.

exercise:ex-m26-04-d.solution: The string "[object Object]", because the body is coerced to text
exercise:ex-m26-04-d.solutionExplanation: A request body must be text (or a Blob/FormData) — `fetch` does **not** serialise objects for you. Passing one coerces it via `String()`, producing the useless `"[object Object]"` that the server cannot parse, hence the `400`. You must call `JSON.stringify(user)` yourself. Confusingly, omitting the `Content-Type: application/json` header produces the *same* `400` from a completely different cause, so check the Network panel's request payload to tell them apart.
hints: What does an object become when converted to a string?

exercise:ex-m26-05-c.solutionExplanation: Creating a **new** `AbortController` after each abort is essential — a signal's aborted state is permanent, so reusing one would make every request after the first fail instantly, which the hidden test guards against. The fourth test reproduces the real race: the slow first search is superseded by a fast second one, and aborting guarantees the stale result can never overwrite the current one. `return await` inside the `try` is required so the rejection is caught here rather than escaping, per Module 25.

tests.name: returns a search function
tests.body: const s = makeSearcher(() => Promise.resolve("x")); expect(typeof s).toBe("function");

tests.name: returns the result of a single search
tests.body: const s = makeSearcher((q) => Promise.resolve("r:" + q)); expect(await s("a")).toBe("r:a");

tests.name: passes a signal to the search function
tests.body: let sig = null; const s = makeSearcher((q, signal) => { sig = signal; return Promise.resolve(q); }); await s("a"); expect(sig).not.toBe(null); expect(typeof sig.aborted).toBe("boolean");

tests.name: the superseded search resolves to null
tests.body: const mk = (q, signal) => new Promise((res, rej) => { const t = setTimeout(() => res("r:" + q), q === "slow" ? 30 : 5); signal.addEventListener("abort", () => { clearTimeout(t); const e = new Error("a"); e.name = "AbortError"; rej(e); }); }); const s = makeSearcher(mk); const first = s("slow"); const second = s("fast"); expect(await first).toBe(null); expect(await second).toBe("r:fast");

tests.name: uses a fresh controller each time
tests.body: const mk = (q, signal) => new Promise((res, rej) => { const t = setTimeout(() => res(q), 5); signal.addEventListener("abort", () => { clearTimeout(t); const e = new Error("a"); e.name = "AbortError"; rej(e); }); }); const s = makeSearcher(mk); await s("a"); expect(await s("b")).toBe("b");

hints: Store the controller in a variable the returned function closes over.
Abort the old one, then create a **new** one — a controller cannot be reset.
Catch AbortError and return null; rethrow anything else.

exercise:ex-m26-05-d.solution: Yes — debouncing reduces how many requests are sent, but two that do get sent can still return out of order
exercise:ex-m26-05-d.solutionExplanation: They solve **different** problems. Debouncing waits for a pause before sending, cutting the number of requests — but if the user pauses, types more, and pauses again, two requests are genuinely in flight, and nothing stops the earlier one arriving last and overwriting the newer results. Aborting the previous request guarantees a superseded response can never be applied. Bandwidth is a side benefit, not the reason. Production search boxes typically use both.
hints: Does debouncing guarantee only one request is ever in flight?

exercise:ex-m26-06-c.solution: A publishable key that is origin-restricted and can only perform limited, low-risk operations
exercise:ex-m26-06-c.solutionExplanation: A publishable key is **designed** to be public: it is scoped to low-risk operations and typically restricted by origin and rate limit, so exposure causes limited damage. The other three all ship a secret to the browser, where anyone can read it. Build-time environment variables are **inlined into the bundle** — that is exactly what `VITE_*` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` prefixes warn about. Minification is not encryption, and base64 is an encoding anyone can reverse in a second.
hints: Which one is designed to be public?

exercise:ex-m26-06-d.solution: It returns an opaque response with status 0 and an unreadable body, so the failure becomes silent instead of visible
exercise:ex-m26-06-d.solutionExplanation: `no-cors` does not grant permission; it **opts out of needing it** by requesting an opaque response. The error disappears, which feels like progress, but `status` is `0`, `ok` is `false`, and the body cannot be read at all — so an API request now fails **silently** rather than loudly. A visible error you can diagnose is strictly better than a silent one. The mode exists for cases like caching an image where the body was never needed.
hints: What can you actually read from an opaque response?

exercise:ex-m27-02-b.solution: A cookie — it is sent to the server automatically on every request
exercise:ex-m27-02-b.solutionExplanation: The requirement is that the **server** knows the value while rendering, and a cookie is attached to every matching request automatically — which is exactly what cookies are for. `localStorage` is purely client-side; the server never sees it unless JavaScript explicitly sends it, which is impossible for the initial page request before any JavaScript has run. `sessionStorage` has the same limitation plus per-tab isolation, and a variable does not survive navigation at all.
hints: Which one does the server actually see?

exercise:ex-m27-02-d.solution: A cross-origin fetch does not send cookies unless credentials: "include" is set — and the server must allow credentials with an explicit origin
exercise:ex-m27-02-d.solutionExplanation: A subdomain is a **different origin** (Module 26), so this is a cross-origin request — and `fetch` omits cookies on those by default. The session cookie is never attached, so the API sees an unauthenticated request even though the cookie exists in the browser. The fix has two halves that must both be present: the client passes `credentials: "include"`, and the server responds with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` plus an **explicit** `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` — a wildcard `*` is rejected when credentials are involved. Testing the API directly works because that is a same-origin request.
hints: Are those two URLs the same origin?
Does fetch send cookies cross-origin by default?

exercise:ex-m27-03-b.solutionExplanation: Guarding each parameter keeps default state out of the URL, so the first test produces a bare path rather than a string of redundant parameters. `append` rather than `set` is what allows repeated `tag` values — `set` would keep only the last. `?? []` makes a missing `tags` property harmless, which the hidden test checks. `searchParams` encodes the space as `+` automatically, so the query is safe without manual work.
hints: `url.searchParams.set` for single values, `append` for repeated ones.
Guard each addition with a condition.
`state.tags ?? []` handles a missing array.

exercise:ex-m27-03-d.solution: history.pushState, then render the new results yourself
exercise:ex-m27-03-d.solutionExplanation: `pushState` changes the URL and adds a history entry **without** reloading, so JavaScript state and scroll position survive and back works naturally — you simply render the new results yourself. Both `location.href` and `location.reload()` discard the entire page and start fresh, losing exactly what the requirement asked to preserve. `location.replace` also reloads **and** removes the history entry, so back would skip the previous filter entirely.
hints: Which options reload the page?

exercise:ex-m27-04-c.solution: The observer keeps a reference to the target, so the element and everything it references stay alive — a memory leak
exercise:ex-m27-04-c.solutionExplanation: An observer holds a reference to each observed target, so removing the element from the DOM is not enough to release it — the observer keeps it, along with any closures and data it references, reachable indefinitely. Repeated across many component mounts this accumulates into a real leak. Call `disconnect()` in whatever teardown path exists, or `unobserve(target)` when a single element no longer needs watching, as lazy-loading does per image.
hints: What does the observer hold on to?

exercise:ex-m27-04-d.solution: Detecting changes made by a third-party widget you cannot modify
exercise:ex-m27-04-d.solutionExplanation: When **your** code changes the DOM you already know it happened, so reacting at the point of change is simpler, synchronous and cheaper than observing. `MutationObserver` earns its place only for changes you do not control — a third-party widget, a browser extension, or legacy code you cannot edit. Clicks are handled by event listeners, and observers watch the DOM rather than variables. Observing a large subtree under constant churn does real work on every batch, so it is a last resort.
hints: Do you already know when your own code changes the DOM?

exercise:ex-m27-05-c.solution: Parsing a large file without freezing the interface
exercise:ex-m27-05-c.solutionExplanation: A worker runs on a separate thread, so heavy computation there leaves the main thread free to render and respond — exactly the blocking problem from Module 23. The other three all require the **DOM**, which a worker cannot touch: there is no `document` or `window` inside one. The usual pattern is to compute in the worker and `postMessage` the result back so the main thread does the rendering.
hints: What does a worker have no access to?

exercise:ex-m27-05-d.solution: It asks whether the capability is actually available now — which also covers absence for reasons unrelated to browser version, such as an insecure origin
exercise:ex-m27-05-d.solutionExplanation: Feature detection answers the only question that matters: can I use this right now? That covers cases version-sniffing cannot — `navigator.clipboard` is undefined on an insecure origin even in the newest browser, so a version check would wrongly conclude it is available. User-agent strings are also routinely spoofed and change over time, and a version check silently breaks on browsers that gained the feature later.
hints: Can a modern browser still lack navigator.clipboard?

exercise:ex-m28-02-b.solution: The module fails to load — the requested export does not exist
exercise:ex-m28-02-b.solutionExplanation: Named imports are **not** destructuring: they bind to a specific export name, and that name is resolved against the module's real export list before any code runs. A name that does not exist is an error at load time, so the typo is reported immediately with a clear message. This is a genuine advantage over a default export, where a misspelled local name is simply accepted and the problem surfaces much later.
hints: Is a named import really destructuring?

exercise:ex-m28-02-d.solution: It succeeds — the binding is fixed but the object it points to is not, so every importer now sees debug: true
exercise:ex-m28-02-d.solutionExplanation: The read-only rule applies to the **binding**: `config = somethingElse` would throw, because the declaring module owns that name. Mutating the object it references is allowed, exactly as with `const` in Module 01 — and since every importer shares the same object, the change is visible everywhere with nothing recording where it came from. That is shared global state through the back door. Export a function that performs the change, or freeze the object.
hints: What exactly is read-only — the binding, or the object?

exercise:ex-m28-03-c.solution: A ReferenceError — b.js reads the binding before a.js has initialised it
exercise:ex-m28-03-c.solutionExplanation: The cycle itself is handled: both modules are linked during instantiation without error. The failure is at **evaluation** — `a.js` starts, pauses to evaluate `b.js`, and `b.js` reads a binding whose initialising statement in `a.js` has not run yet. That is the temporal dead zone from Module 10 crossing file boundaries. There is no infinite loop, because the registry records a module as in-progress. Note the same cycle would appear to work if `b.js` only used the value inside a function called later, which is why cycles break unpredictably after refactors.
hints: When is the binding actually initialised?

exercise:ex-m28-03-d.solution: Extract formatName into its own module that both import
exercise:ex-m28-03-d.solutionExplanation: Moving the shared helper into a third module removes the cycle from the graph entirely: both files now depend on it, and neither depends on the other. That is a real fix, and it usually reveals that the helper belonged in its own module anyway. Delaying the import — by moving it into a function or using `import()` — only hides the timing problem, leaving a cycle that can fail again after any refactor. Merging the files would work but produces one large module that conflates two concerns, trading a structural problem for a worse one.
hints: Which option removes the cycle rather than delaying it?

exercise:ex-m28-04-c.solution: A 400KB chart library used only on a report page a few users open
exercise:ex-m28-04-c.solutionExplanation: Splitting pays off when a chunk is **large** and used by **few** users or **late** in the session — 400KB removed from the initial download for most visitors is a substantial win, and the extra round trip is negligible against the size saved. Splitting a 2KB module used everywhere is a net loss: you trade a trivial size saving for an extra request on the critical path. The entry point and shared constants are needed immediately by definition, so deferring them only delays startup.
hints: Large, and needed by few — or small, and needed by all?

exercise:ex-m28-04-d.solution: No — modules are cached by specifier, so the second call reuses the first result
exercise:ex-m28-04-d.solutionExplanation: The once-only rule applies to dynamic imports too: the module registry caches by specifier, so the second `import()` returns the same module without downloading or evaluating again. Even a call made while the first is still in flight joins the existing request rather than starting another. That is what makes hover-preloading effectively free — the download usually completes before the click, so the click resolves instantly. Just add `.catch(() => {})` to the speculative call so a failed preload does not become an unhandled rejection.
hints: How many times is a module evaluated?

exercise:ex-m28-05-c.solutionExplanation: The split is the lesson: `chooseAction` is a decision expressed as input to output, so all four rule tests need nothing but a plain object — no mocking, no setup. `runAction` is the thin shell that performs the effect, and because the effects are **passed in** rather than imported it is testable with two ordinary functions. Looking up exactly one effect by the chosen key is what makes the hidden test pass: only the decided branch ever runs. Checking `typeof effect === "function"` before calling is what turns a missing effect into `null` instead of a `TypeError`.

tests.name: leaves a light free user alone
leaves a normal paid user alone
returns null when the effect is absent
does not call other effects
tests.body: let warned = false; runAction({ plan: "free", usage: 90 }, { upgrade: () => "x", warn: () => { warned = true; } }); expect(warned).toBe(false);

hints: Handle the free case first, then the paid case, then fall through to "none".
`effects[key]` may be undefined — check before calling.
`chooseAction` must not call anything from `effects`.

exercise:ex-m28-05-d.solution: It has grown two responsibilities that change for different reasons
exercise:ex-m28-05-d.solutionExplanation: The useful test is **reasons to change**, not size: a long module with one clear job is fine, while a short one holding unrelated helpers is not. Line and export counts are symptoms that sometimes correlate and often mislead. Splitting because a file *might* grow is speculative and produces a maze of one-function files where following a flow means opening six of them — split when the second responsibility is actually there.
hints: What is the actual test for a module boundary?

exercise:ex-m29-01-b.solutionExplanation: `b.get()` has `b` to the left of the dot, so implicit binding makes `this` be `b` and `this.v` is `2`. It does not matter that the function was written inside `a` — a function does not belong to an object, it is just a value stored on a property, and both objects hold the identical function. This is exactly the "method borrowing" that makes the definition-site intuition fail.
hints: What is immediately to the left of the dot?

exercise:ex-m29-01-d.solution: `undefined` in strict mode and `globalThis` in sloppy mode — so strict mode turns a silent global-variable bug into an immediate TypeError
exercise:ex-m29-01-d.solutionExplanation: Default binding differs by mode, and the difference is a safety feature. In sloppy mode `this` is the global object, so `this.total = 0` in a mislaid method silently creates a global that breaks something unrelated later. In strict mode `this` is `undefined`, so the same line throws at the point of the mistake. Since ES modules and class bodies are always strict, assume `undefined` in any modern code.
hints: What happens to `this.total = 0` in each mode?

exercise:ex-m29-02-c.solution: `bind` returns a new function each call, so the two are different objects and removal matches nothing
exercise:ex-m29-02-c.solutionExplanation: `bind` does not modify the original function — it returns a **new** one, so calling it twice produces two unrelated function objects. `removeEventListener` matches listeners by identity, so it finds nothing to remove and the handler keeps firing, which is also a memory leak while the element lives. The fix is to bind once and keep the reference — typically in a constructor or factory — then pass that same reference to both add and remove.
hints: What does bind return?

exercise:ex-m29-02-d.solution: Bind once, store the result, and use that reference for both add and remove
exercise:ex-m29-02-d.solutionExplanation: Removal matches listeners by identity, so the reference passed to `removeEventListener` must be the exact function that was added. Binding once and storing it satisfies both requirements: the receiver is fixed, and the identity is stable. Passing `obj.method` directly loses the receiver — the listener would run with the element as `this`. Binding inline, or wrapping in a fresh arrow, creates a different function at each call site, so the removal silently matches nothing.
hints: Removal matches by identity.

exercise:ex-m29-03-c.solutionExplanation: Spreading `fixed` before `rest` reproduces exactly what `bind` does with its extra arguments — pre-filling from the left only. Rest parameters make the edge cases free: no fixed arguments spreads an empty array, and a fixed `0` is passed through unchanged, which the hidden test checks (a truthiness filter would have dropped it). Because the result is an ordinary function, the fifth test works: partially applying a partially applied function simply stacks another layer.

tests.name: prepends one argument
tests.body: const add = (a, b) => a + b; expect(partial(add, 10)(5)).toBe(15);

tests.name: works with no fixed arguments
tests.body: const add = (a, b) => a + b; expect(partial(add)(2, 3)).toBe(5);

tests.name: is reusable
tests.body: const add = (a, b) => a + b; const add10 = partial(add, 10); expect([add10(1), add10(2)]).toEqual([11, 12]);

tests.name: returns a function, not a result
preserves a falsy fixed argument
tests.body: const add = (a, b) => a + b; expect(partial(add, 0)(5)).toBe(5);

hints: Return a function taking `...rest`.
Call `fn(...fixed, ...rest)`.
Rest and spread handle the empty cases for free.

exercise:ex-m29-03-d.solution: a — the first bind is permanent, and call cannot override it
exercise:ex-m29-03-d.solutionExplanation: Binding is permanent: the function `bind` returns ignores any receiver supplied later, so `call(b)` passes arguments but leaves `this` as `a`. Writing your own `bind` makes the reason obvious — the wrapper calls the original with the captured receiver and never consults its own `this`, so there is nothing for `call` to affect. The same is true of a second `bind`: `f.bind(a).bind(b)` still uses `a`.
hints: Can a bound function be rebound?

exercise:ex-m29-04-c.solution: An object method that needs to read the object via `this`
exercise:ex-m29-04-c.solutionExplanation: An object literal creates **no scope**, so an arrow written as a method looks past the object to whatever surrounds it — usually module top level, where `this` is `undefined`. The failure is silent rather than loud, which makes it the most common arrow mistake. Every other option is fine: a callback inside a method is exactly what arrows are for, since it inherits the method's receiver, and a helper using no `this` is unaffected either way.
hints: Does an object literal create a scope?

exercise:ex-m29-04-d.solution: Ordinary — an arrow cannot be constructed and has no prototype property
exercise:ex-m29-04-d.solutionExplanation: Calling `new` on an arrow throws `TypeError: ... is not a constructor`. Arrows have no `[[Construct]]` behaviour and no `prototype` property, so there is nothing for `new` to create an object from or link to — which follows from having no own `this` to bind the new object to. `bind` does not help, since binding an arrow cannot give it a receiver. Use an ordinary function, or a `class`.
hints: What happens when you call `new` on an arrow?

exercise:ex-m29-05-a.solution: The method is shared on the prototype and takes `this` from the call site; the field is a per-instance arrow permanently bound to that instance
exercise:ex-m29-05-a.solutionExplanation: A prototype method is **one** function every instance shares, and like any ordinary function it takes `this` from the call site — so detaching it and calling it plainly throws, since class bodies are always strict. A class field creates a **new** arrow per instance, captured in the constructor's scope, so it can never lose the instance and is safe to pass directly as a handler. The cost is memory: one function per instance rather than one in total, which matters only at large instance counts.
hints: What happens to each when detached?

exercise:ex-m29-05-c.solutionExplanation: Closing over `toggle` rather than reading `this` is what makes the fourth and fifth tests pass: destructuring cannot detach a variable the arrow captured, and supplying a foreign receiver changes nothing because the arrow never consults one. Assigning the handler as a plain property after building the object gives it a **stable identity**, which the sixth test requires and which a getter would have broken by returning a new function on each read — the same identity problem as re-binding in lesson 2. Each call to `createToggle` builds a separate object, so the toggles are independent.

tests.name: ignores a foreign receiver
tests.body: const t = createToggle(false); expect(t.handler.call({ on: true })).toBe(true);

tests.name: keeps toggles independent
tests.body: const a = createToggle(false); const b = createToggle(false); a.handler(); expect(b.on).toBe(false);

hints: Build the object first, then attach an arrow that closes over it.
The arrow must update the object's `on` so the third test passes.
A getter would create a new function each read — use a plain property.

exercise:ex-m30-01-c.solutionExplanation: `Object.keys` lists **own** enumerable properties only — it does not walk the prototype chain. Adding a property to the prototype makes it *readable* through `c` by delegation, but it never becomes an own property of `c`, so `Object.keys(c)` stays empty. This is the practical consequence of "lookup, not copying", and it is why iterating an object's keys and reading its properties can disagree — lesson 2 covers the tools that distinguish the two cases.
hints: Does Object.keys walk the chain?

exercise:ex-m30-01-d.solution: Engines optimise for a stable object shape, and code whose inherited behaviour changes partway through is hard to reason about
exercise:ex-m30-01-d.solutionExplanation: It is a real, specified function that works — the objection is not correctness. Engines optimise property access by assuming an object's shape, prototype included, stays fixed after creation; changing it forces those optimisations to be discarded for that object. The stronger reason is comprehension: an object that inherits one set of behaviour and then another is genuinely hard to follow. Set the prototype at creation instead, with `Object.create`, a constructor, or a class.
hints: What do engines assume about an object after it is created?

exercise:ex-m30-02-c.solutionExplanation: The assignment created an **own** property on `o` that shadowed the inherited one; it never modified `proto`. `delete` removes only own properties, so it lifted the shadow and left the prototype untouched — reading `o.v` now walks the chain and finds `1` again. `delete` cannot remove an inherited property at all, so repeating it would change nothing. This "shadow, then reveal" behaviour follows directly from the rule that reads walk the chain while writes create own properties.
hints: What exactly did the assignment create, and what did delete remove?

exercise:ex-m30-02-d.solutionExplanation: Assigning `item.tags = []` creates an **own** property that shadows whatever the prototype holds, so pushing into it can never reach the shared object — which is what the fifth and sixth tests check. Writing a fresh `[]` on every call is essential: reusing one array outside the function would recreate the original bug in a new form, as the hidden test confirms. This is the general rule the lesson establishes — **behaviour** on the prototype, **mutable state** on the instance — and it is exactly what a constructor or class field does.

tests.name: instances do not share tags
tests.body: const p = { tags: [] }; const a = createItem(p); const b = createItem(p); a.tags.push("x"); expect(b.tags).toEqual([]);

tests.name: each instance gets a distinct array
tests.body: const p = {}; const a = createItem(p); const b = createItem(p); expect(a.tags === b.tags).toBe(false);

hints: `Object.create(proto)` sets up delegation.
Then assign a **new** array as an own property.
A fresh `[]` per call is what keeps instances independent.

exercise:ex-m30-03-c.solutionExplanation: `Object.create(Constructor.prototype)` is steps 1 and 2 in one call, and it is exactly why the fourth test passes: prototype methods are reachable because the link was made before the constructor ran. `apply` supplies both the receiver and the spread arguments. The final check implements step 4 faithfully — and the explicit `!== null` guard is what makes the hidden test pass, since `typeof null === "object"` (Module 02's historical bug) would otherwise wrongly treat `null` as an overriding object. A returned function would also override, since functions are objects.

tests.name: passes several arguments
tests.body: function P(a, b) { this.sum = a + b; } expect(construct(P, [2, 3]).sum).toBe(5);

tests.name: inherits prototype methods
tests.body: function P(n) { this.n = n; } P.prototype.get = function () { return this.n; }; expect(construct(P, [7]).get()).toBe(7);

tests.name: honours a returned object
tests.body: function P() { this.tag = "instance"; return { tag: "override" }; } expect(construct(P, []).tag).toBe("override");

tests.name: ignores a returned null
tests.body: function P() { this.tag = "instance"; return null; } expect(construct(P, []).tag).toBe("instance");

hints: `Object.create(Constructor.prototype)` covers steps 1 and 2.
`Constructor.apply(instance, args)` covers step 3 and gives you the return value.
`typeof null === "object"`, so guard against it explicitly.

exercise:ex-m30-03-d.solution: Whether Ctor.prototype appears anywhere in obj's prototype chain
exercise:ex-m30-03-d.solutionExplanation: It is a chain-membership test, not a parentage test — which is why `Object.create(User.prototype) instanceof User` is `true` despite `new` never running, and why an object genuinely built by `User` becomes `false` if `User.prototype` is later reassigned. It also explains `user instanceof Object` being `true`, since `Object.prototype` is in the chain. The consequence worth remembering is **cross-realm failure**: an array from an iframe has that realm's `Array.prototype`, so `instanceof Array` is `false` — use `Array.isArray`.
hints: Can an object never touched by `new` still pass?

exercise:ex-m30-04-b.solutionExplanation: `Object.create(Parent.prototype)` is what makes the fourth test pass — the old `new Parent()` idiom would have run the constructor and put its properties on the shared prototype. Restoring `constructor` matters because replacing `Child.prototype` discarded the automatic one, so `instance.constructor` would otherwise report the parent. The hidden test is the reason for `defineProperty` rather than a plain assignment: a normal assignment creates an **enumerable** property, so `constructor` would show up in `Object.keys` and `for...in`, unlike every real built-in. Module 36 covers those descriptor flags in full.

tests.name: links the prototypes
tests.body: function P() {} function C() {} inherit(C, P); expect(Object.getPrototypeOf(C.prototype)).toBe(P.prototype);

tests.name: inherits parent methods
tests.body: function P() {} P.prototype.hi = function () { return "hi"; }; function C() {} inherit(C, P); expect(new C().hi()).toBe("hi");

tests.name: restores constructor
tests.body: function P() {} function C() {} inherit(C, P); expect(new C().constructor).toBe(C);

tests.name: does not run the parent constructor
tests.body: let ran = 0; function P() { ran += 1; } function C() {} inherit(C, P); expect(ran).toBe(0);

tests.name: instances pass both instanceof checks
tests.body: function P() {} function C() {} inherit(C, P); const c = new C(); expect([c instanceof C, c instanceof P]).toEqual([true, true]);

tests.name: child methods added after still work
tests.body: function P() {} function C() {} inherit(C, P); C.prototype.own = function () { return 1; }; expect(new C().own()).toBe(1);

tests.name: constructor is not enumerable
tests.body: function P() {} function C() {} inherit(C, P); expect(Object.keys(C.prototype)).toEqual([]);

hints: `Object.create(Parent.prototype)` links without calling anything.
Assign that to `Child.prototype`.
A plain assignment makes `constructor` enumerable — use `Object.defineProperty` to match built-in behaviour.

exercise:ex-m30-04-d.solution: It is impossible — built-in prototypes are frozen
exercise:ex-m30-04-d.solutionExplanation: Built-in prototypes are **not** frozen — the extension in this lesson ran perfectly and had to be deleted afterwards. That is exactly why the guidance is framed as "discouraged" rather than "impossible": it works, which is what makes it tempting. The other three are all genuine: name collisions between libraries, `for...in` pollution from the enumerable assignment, and future standards colliding with your name — as actually happened when `Array.prototype.flat` was standardised.
hints: Did the lesson's example run successfully?

exercise:ex-m31-01-c.solution: A ReferenceError — the binding exists but is in the temporal dead zone
exercise:ex-m31-01-c.solutionExplanation: Classes **are** hoisted, but into the temporal dead zone, exactly like `let` and `const` from Module 10 — which is why the error says "Cannot access before initialization" rather than "is not defined". So the common shorthand "classes are not hoisted" is technically wrong; the accurate statement is that they cannot be *used* before their definition is evaluated. A function declaration differs precisely here: it is fully initialised at scope entry and can be called early.
hints: Compare with `let`, not with `function`.

exercise:ex-m31-01-d.solution: Calling a class without new always throws, and class methods are non-enumerable
exercise:ex-m31-01-d.solutionExplanation: Both are real, checkable differences: a constructor function called plainly silently created globals in sloppy mode, and its methods assigned with `=` are enumerable so they appear in `for...in`. The other options describe the myth this lesson exists to correct — classes are prototype machinery. Instances still have a chain, methods are still shared rather than copied, and `typeof MyClass === "function"`.
hints: Two of the differences are enforcement and enumerability.

exercise:ex-m31-02-b.solutionExplanation: Validating **before** mutating is what makes the sixth test pass — throwing after a partial update would leave the object in a state that never should have existed, the invariant-preservation point from Module 22. The `#balance` field gives real encapsulation, which the last two tests confirm: it is absent from `Object.keys` and from `JSON.stringify`, unlike a `_balance` convention. The getter with no matching setter makes `balance` read-only from outside, so every change must go through the validating methods — that is the entire value of the pattern.

tests.name: deposits
tests.body: const a = new Account(); a.deposit(50); expect(a.balance).toBe(50);

tests.name: withdraws
tests.body: const a = new Account(); a.deposit(50); a.withdraw(20); expect(a.balance).toBe(30);

tests.name: rejects an overdraft
tests.body: const a = new Account(); a.deposit(10); expect(() => a.withdraw(11)).toThrow();

tests.name: leaves the balance unchanged after a failed withdrawal
tests.body: const a = new Account(); a.deposit(10); try { a.withdraw(99); } catch {} expect(a.balance).toBe(10);

tests.name: the balance is not an own property
tests.body: const a = new Account(); a.deposit(5); expect(Object.keys(a)).toEqual([]);

tests.name: is not serialised
tests.body: const a = new Account(); a.deposit(5); expect(JSON.stringify(a)).toBe("{}");

hints: Declare `#balance = 0;` at the top of the class body.
Validate before mutating, so a rejected operation changes nothing.
`get balance() { return this.#balance; }` exposes it read-only.

exercise:ex-m31-02-d.solution: render() as a prototype method; onClick as a field holding an arrow
exercise:ex-m31-02-d.solutionExplanation: `render()` is called normally, so the call site supplies the receiver and a shared prototype method is right — one function, non-enumerable, overridable by a subclass. `onClick` is handed to `addEventListener`, which calls it with the **element** as `this`, so a prototype method would lose the instance; an arrow field is created per instance and permanently bound, making it safe to pass. Making everything a field costs one function per instance and, more importantly, makes them enumerable own properties that appear in `Object.keys` and JSON.
hints: Which one gets called without a receiver?

exercise:ex-m31-03-c.solutionExplanation: Passing the message to `super` lets `Error` handle `message` and the stack trace properly — reconstructing them by hand loses the stack. Setting `name` explicitly is required because `Error` does not derive it from the class, so it would otherwise read `"Error"`. Because `extends` put both `HttpError.prototype` and `Error.prototype` in the chain, both `instanceof` checks pass, which is what lets calling code catch broadly and then narrow by type — the pattern from Module 22, now with the mechanism visible.

tests.name: a client error is not a server error
can be caught as an Error
tests.body: let caught = null; try { throw new HttpError(503, "down"); } catch (e) { caught = e; } expect(caught.status).toBe(503);

hints: `super(message)` lets Error set message and stack.
Assign `this.name` yourself — Error does not derive it.
`get isServerError() { return this.status >= 500; }`

exercise:ex-m31-03-d.solution: undefined — subclass field initialisers run only after super() returns
exercise:ex-m31-03-d.solutionExplanation: The order is: `super()` runs the base constructor to completion, **then** the derived class's field initialisers run, **then** the rest of the derived constructor body. So a base constructor calling an overridden method reaches the subclass implementation — that part is normal polymorphism — but any subclass field it reads is still `undefined`. This is why calling overridable methods from a constructor is a well-known hazard: assign after `super()` in the derived constructor, or pass the value into the base constructor instead.
hints: When exactly do a derived class's fields initialise?
