exercise:ex-m31-04-c.solutionExplanation: The methods must be **ordinary functions**, not arrows: they read `this.name`, and after `Object.assign` copies them onto the animal, `duck.fly()` supplies the duck as receiver — Module 29's implicit binding. An arrow would have captured the factory's scope, where there is no `name`, and returned `"undefined flies"`. `Object.assign` merges the capabilities the caller actually passed, so the fifth test finds no `swim` on a bird: every combination is expressible without a class per combination, which is exactly what a hierarchy could not do under single inheritance.

tests.name: both abilities combine
tests.body: const d = createAnimal("duck", canFly(), canSwim()); expect([d.fly(), d.swim()]).toEqual(["duck flies", "duck swims"]);

tests.name: an animal with no abilities
tests.body: const a = createAnimal("rock"); expect([a.name, a.fly]).toEqual(["rock", undefined]);

tests.name: abilities are absent when not given
animals are independent
tests.body: const a = createAnimal("a", canFly()); const b = createAnimal("b", canFly()); expect([a.fly(), b.fly()]).toEqual(["a flies", "b flies"]);

hints: Each factory returns `{ fly() { return `${this.name} flies`; } }`.
Use a normal method, not an arrow — it must read `this` from the assembled object.
`Object.assign({ name }, ...abilities)` merges them.

exercise:ex-m31-04-d.solution: A ValidationError that must be catchable as an Error
exercise:ex-m31-04-d.solutionExplanation: This is a genuine, stable, single-axis **is-a**: the error must really be an `Error` so `instanceof Error` works and it interoperates with every `catch` block. That is inheritance doing exactly its job, and it is shallow. The `Order` case is **has-a** — logging and tax are collaborators to pass in. The `Employee` case has three **independent axes**, so a hierarchy explodes combinatorially under single inheritance. And `Square extends Rectangle` is the classic false is-a: it cannot honour the parent's contract that width and height vary independently, so substituting it silently breaks callers.
hints: Which one must actually *be* the parent type for the language to cooperate?

exercise:ex-m32-01-c.solutionExplanation: The closure captured the **binding**, not the value `v` held at creation time — so calling the arrow reads whatever `v` holds *now*, which is `2`. A snapshot model would have produced `1`, and that wrong model is the source of most closure confusion. It also explains why two functions created in the same call see each other's changes, and why the classic `var`-in-a-loop puzzle behaves as it does.
hints: Is a binding or a value captured?

exercise:ex-m32-01-d.solution: Any function that reads a variable from an enclosing scope — including a callback passed to filter
exercise:ex-m32-01-d.solutionExplanation: Returning a function is the case where closures become *visible*, because the environment outlives the call. But `values.filter(v => v > minimum)` is equally a closure: the arrow reads `minimum` from the enclosing scope. The declaration keyword and the kind of variable are irrelevant. This is why the honest answer to "when should I use closures?" is that you already do — constantly, in every callback that reads surrounding state.
hints: Does a closure require returning anything?

exercise:ex-m32-02-b.solutionExplanation: `items` is a variable in the closure, so no property of the returned object refers to it — the sixth test confirms nothing array-shaped is exposed. Note `const items` is still fully mutable: `const` prevents rebinding, not mutation, and pushing is exactly what we want. Delegating to the array's own `pop` handles the empty case for free, and returning its result directly preserves a legitimately falsy `0`, which the hidden test checks — a `|| undefined` guard would have corrupted it.

tests.name: pushes and reports size
tests.body: const s = createStack(); s.push(1); s.push(2); expect(s.size()).toBe(2);

tests.name: pops last in first out
tests.body: const s = createStack(); s.push(1); s.push(2); expect(s.pop()).toBe(2);

tests.name: peek does not remove
tests.body: const s = createStack(); s.push(1); s.peek(); expect(s.size()).toBe(1);

tests.name: stacks are independent
tests.body: const a = createStack(); const b = createStack(); a.push(1); expect(b.size()).toBe(0);

hints: `const items = [];` inside the function.
Return an object of arrows closing over it.
Array `pop` already returns `undefined` when empty.

exercise:ex-m32-02-c.solutionExplanation: Checking `cache.has` rather than the truthiness or definedness of the stored value is what makes the fourth and fifth tests pass — a function legitimately returning `undefined` or `0` would otherwise be recomputed on every call, silently defeating the cache. Each call to `memoize` creates a fresh `cache`, so two memoised copies of the same function do not share results (sixth test). A `Map` compares keys by identity rather than coercing them to strings, which is why `1` and `"1"` are distinct — a plain object used as a cache would have merged them.

tests.name: calls through only once per argument
tests.body: let n = 0; const f = memoize((x) => { n += 1; return x; }); f(1); f(1); f(1); expect(n).toBe(1);

tests.name: computes separately per argument
tests.body: let n = 0; const f = memoize((x) => { n += 1; return x; }); f(1); f(2); expect(n).toBe(2);

tests.name: caches an undefined result
tests.body: let n = 0; const f = memoize(() => { n += 1; return undefined; }); f(1); f(1); expect(n).toBe(1);

tests.name: caches a falsy result
tests.body: let n = 0; const f = memoize(() => { n += 1; return 0; }); f(1); expect(f(1)).toBe(0); expect(n).toBe(1);

tests.name: caches are per memoized function
tests.body: let n = 0; const g = (x) => { n += 1; return x; }; memoize(g)(1); memoize(g)(1); expect(n).toBe(2);

tests.name: distinguishes 1 from "1"
tests.body: let n = 0; const f = memoize((x) => { n += 1; return x; }); f(1); f("1"); expect(n).toBe(2);

hints: `const cache = new Map();` inside `memoize`.
Check `cache.has(arg)`, not whether the stored value is defined.
A `Map` compares keys by identity, so `1` and `"1"` differ.

exercise:ex-m32-03-b.solutionExplanation: Passing `i` as an **argument** is what solves it: a parameter is a fresh binding created on every call, so each returned arrow closes over a different `value` rather than the single shared `i`. An inline IIFE does exactly the same thing less readably. This is the pre-2015 fix, and it is worth knowing because it generalises — the same move separates any group of closures that accidentally share one binding, whether a loop is involved or not.

tests.name: still correct when called later
tests.body: const r = makeReaders(3); const f = r[1]; expect(f()).toBe(1);

hints: Pass `i` as an argument to something that returns a function.
A parameter is a fresh binding, created per call.
An IIFE or a named factory both work.

exercise:ex-m32-03-c.solutionExplanation: The loop is **synchronous** and runs to completion before any timer callback fires — even with a `0` delay, the callbacks are tasks queued for after the current work finishes (Module 23). By then the single function-scoped `i` holds `3`, and all three closures read that same binding. Changing `var` to `let` prints `0 1 2`, because the `for` header then creates a fresh binding per iteration and each callback closes over a different one.
hints: When does the loop finish relative to the callbacks?

exercise:ex-m32-04-b.solutionExplanation: Wrapping each registration in its own `entry` object gives every subscription a **unique identity**, which is what makes the hidden test pass: registering the same function twice creates two entries, and each remover deletes only its own. Searching for the function itself would have removed the wrong one. The `index !== -1` guard makes a repeated `off()` harmless rather than splicing an unrelated entry. Returning a remover is the pattern that prevents the real-world leak — once removed, nothing reachable refers to the listener or to whatever it captured.

tests.name: emits to every listener
tests.body: const e = createEmitter(); e.on((v) => v + 1); e.on((v) => v * 2); expect(e.emit(3)).toEqual([4, 6]);

tests.name: unsubscribe removes one
tests.body: const e = createEmitter(); const off = e.on(() => 1); e.on(() => 2); off(); expect(e.count()).toBe(1);

tests.name: the remaining listener still fires
tests.body: const e = createEmitter(); const off = e.on(() => 1); e.on(() => 2); off(); expect(e.emit()).toEqual([2]);

tests.name: unsubscribing twice is safe
tests.body: const e = createEmitter(); const off = e.on(() => 1); off(); off(); expect(e.count()).toBe(0);

tests.name: the same function can register twice
tests.body: const e = createEmitter(); const fn = () => 1; e.on(fn); e.on(fn); expect(e.count()).toBe(2);

hints: Keep the listeners in a closed-over array.
`on` returns an arrow that removes this specific registration.
Removing by index, guarded, handles a repeated call safely.

exercise:ex-m32-04-d.solution: The listener, the arrow, and through `this` the whole component instance and everything it references — repeated on every mount
exercise:ex-m32-04-d.solutionExplanation: `window` is effectively permanent and holds the listener, so the arrow stays reachable; the arrow captured `this`, so the entire component instance — and its state, DOM references and any captured data — stays reachable with it. Removing the DOM node does not help, because the retention path runs through `window`, not the document. Mounting repeatedly accumulates one such chain each time, which is the classic real-world leak. The fix is the lesson's habit: remove the listener in teardown, keeping the same reference so removal matches (Module 29).
hints: What holds a reference to the listener, and what does the arrow capture?

exercise:ex-m33-01-c.solution: Recursion without a reachable base case, so no frame is ever removed
exercise:ex-m33-01-c.solutionExplanation: A frame is removed only when its call **returns**, so recursion that never reaches a base case pushes frames indefinitely until the limit is hit. An infinite `for` loop is a different failure — it freezes the page without growing the stack, because no calls are being made. Note the maximum depth is engine- and platform-specific and depends on frame size, so never rely on a particular depth being safe; and JavaScript engines generally do not eliminate tail calls, so tail recursion still consumes a frame.
hints: What removes a frame from the stack?

exercise:ex-m33-01-d.solution: Only those in scope where it was written — the stack does not affect variable access
exercise:ex-m33-01-d.solutionExplanation: The **call stack** records who called whom, which is about time; the **scope chain** records what a function can see, which is fixed by where the function was written. A function can never read its caller's locals, however deep the stack. The reverse case proves the same point from the other side: a closure returned from a finished function still reads that function's variables even though its frame is long gone. Only `this` is decided by the call.
hints: Is variable access decided by time or by source structure?

exercise:ex-m33-02-b.solutionExplanation: `A` and `D` are plain synchronous statements, so they run first in source order — the `setTimeout` and `.then` calls only **register** callbacks and return immediately. When the script finishes and the stack empties, the microtask checkpoint drains the queue, running `C`. Only after the queue is empty does the loop take a task from the task queue, running `B`. The general shape to remember: **all synchronous, then all microtasks, then one task**.
hints: Synchronous first, then the checkpoint, then a task.

exercise:ex-m33-02-c.solutionExplanation: Scheduling the next chunk with `setTimeout` makes it a **separate task**, so the event loop can render and handle input between chunks — a recursive `queueMicrotask` would keep the checkpoint open and block the page exactly as an infinite loop does. The sixth test confirms the work is genuinely deferred rather than completed synchronously. Tracking a single `index` across chunks is what preserves order, which the hidden test checks with unsorted input. The empty case resolves on the first `step`, since `index` already equals `items.length`.

tests.name: does not resolve synchronously
tests.body: let done = false; processChunked([1, 2, 3], 1).then(() => { done = true; }); expect(done).toBe(false);

hints: Wrap the whole thing in `new Promise((resolve) => { ... })`.
A `step` function processes one chunk, then schedules itself with `setTimeout` if more remain.
Resolve when the index reaches the end.

exercise:ex-m33-03-b.solutionExplanation: An `async` function runs **synchronously until its first `await`**, so calling `run()` immediately logs `2`. At the `await` the function **returns to its caller**, and everything after it is queued as a microtask — so `3` runs next as ordinary synchronous code. Once the stack empties, the checkpoint resumes the function and logs `4`. Note `await null` still defers even though there is nothing to wait for: `await` always yields.
hints: How much of an async function runs before the first await?

exercise:ex-m33-03-c.solutionExplanation: This is the mechanical translation the lesson describes: everything before the first `await` becomes the synchronous prefix, and each section after an `await` becomes one `.then`. The first test proves `"a"` really is synchronous — the function has pushed it before returning. The fourth test confirms only microtasks are involved, since three microtask turns are enough to complete it; a `setTimeout`-based version would still be unfinished. Being able to perform this rewrite is the most reliable way to answer any ordering question.

tests.name: does not use timers
tests.body: const log = []; const p = runSteps(log); await Promise.resolve().then(() => {}).then(() => {}).then(() => {}); expect(log).toEqual(["a", "b", "c"]);

tests.name: works with separate logs
tests.body: const a = []; const b = []; await Promise.all([runSteps(a), runSteps(b)]); expect([a, b]).toEqual([["a", "b", "c"], ["a", "b", "c"]]);

hints: Push `"a"` before returning anything.
Return `Promise.resolve().then(...).then(...)`.
Each `.then` is one microtask further along.

exercise:ex-m34-01-c.solution: A Map — objects can only have string or symbol keys, so every element would collapse to one entry
exercise:ex-m34-01-c.solutionExplanation: Every element used as an object key coerces to a string like `"[object HTMLDivElement]"`, so all elements share one entry and the data is silently destroyed. A `Map` accepts the elements themselves as keys and distinguishes them by identity. An array of pairs would work but makes lookup O(n) and the code clumsier. Note a `WeakMap` is usually the better choice for exactly this case, because it does not keep removed elements alive — lesson 3.
hints: What would an element become if used as an object key?

exercise:ex-m34-01-d.solutionExplanation: `{ id: 1 }` in the lookup creates a **new** object, and a `Map` matches object keys by identity rather than contents — so it is simply not the key that was stored, and `get` returns `undefined` for a missing key. You must keep the original reference to retrieve the entry. When lookup by contents is what you need, derive a primitive key such as `String(user.id)` instead; identity keys are for when identity is genuinely what you mean.
hints: Are those two objects the same object?

exercise:ex-m34-02-b.solutionExplanation: Spreading gives an array so `filter` is available — a `Set` has no `filter` of its own — and `b.has(value)` is a constant-time membership test rather than a scan, which is exactly what `Set` is for. `filter` builds a new array and `new Set(...)` a new set, so neither input is touched, satisfying the sixth test. Note `difference` is **directional**: `a - b` and `b - a` give different results, which the third test makes explicit.

tests.name: returns Sets
tests.body: expect(intersection(new Set(), new Set()) instanceof Set).toBe(true);

tests.name: does not mutate the inputs
tests.body: const a = new Set([1, 2]); difference(a, new Set([1])); expect(a.size).toBe(2);

hints: Spread `a` into an array so you can `filter` it.
`b.has(value)` is the membership test.
Wrap the filtered array in `new Set(...)`.

exercise:ex-m34-02-c.solutionExplanation: The `Set` holds computed **keys**, not the objects — putting the objects in directly would deduplicate nothing, since they are distinct by identity. Checking `has` **before** adding is what keeps the **first** occurrence rather than the last, which the second test pins down and which the `new Map(...)` idiom from the lesson does not do. Using `has` rather than a truthiness check makes the hidden test pass, where a key of `0` is legitimate. `filter` returns a new array, so the input is untouched.

tests.name: keeps the FIRST occurrence
tests.body: expect(uniqueBy([{ id: 1, n: "a" }, { id: 1, n: "b" }], (x) => x.id)).toEqual([{ id: 1, n: "a" }]);

tests.name: preserves order
tests.body: expect(uniqueBy([{ id: 2 }, { id: 1 }, { id: 2 }], (x) => x.id).map((x) => x.id)).toEqual([2, 1]);

tests.name: does not mutate the input
tests.body: const input = [{ id: 1 }, { id: 1 }]; uniqueBy(input, (x) => x.id); expect(input.length).toBe(2);

hints: A `Set` of seen **keys** — not of the objects themselves.
Filter, adding each key as you go.
`set.has(key)` before adding decides whether to keep the item.

exercise:ex-m34-03-c.solution: Those would expose garbage-collection timing, making program behaviour depend on when collection happens
exercise:ex-m34-03-c.solutionExplanation: Entries vanish when their keys become unreachable, at a moment the engine chooses and the specification does not define. A readable `size` or an enumerable key list would therefore give different answers at different times for reasons the program cannot control — and enumeration could even resurrect keys that were about to be collected. Removing both keeps GC unobservable, which is also why no honest test can assert that an object was collected.
hints: What would `size` return, and when would it change?

exercise:ex-m34-03-d.solution: Map — WeakMap keys cannot be strings, and it has no size to read
exercise:ex-m34-03-d.solutionExplanation: Both requirements rule out a `WeakMap`. String keys are rejected with a `TypeError`, because a primitive has no identity that could become unreachable — `"a"` is not a particular object. And there is no `size` to read, deliberately, since the count would depend on collection timing. With a `Map` you keep both capabilities and take on the responsibility of eviction, which for user-supplied string keys means a size limit or a TTL rather than relying on the collector.
hints: Check both requirements against the WeakMap restrictions.

exercise:ex-m34-04-c.solutionExplanation: The JSON round-trip fails all three requirements: it **throws** on a cycle, turns a `Date` into a string, and reduces a `Map` to `{}` — the last two silently, which is the worst property a copying function can have. Spread and `Object.assign` are shallow, so nested structures stay shared. `structuredClone` preserves `Date`, `Map`, `Set` and `RegExp` as their real types and handles cycles including self-references. Its own limits are functions (which throw) and prototypes (which are lost).
hints: Which of these survives a cycle?

exercise:ex-m34-04-d.solution: A plain object with the same data but no prototype — instanceof fails and methods are gone
exercise:ex-m34-04-d.solutionExplanation: `structuredClone` copies **data**, not behaviour. Own properties are cloned deeply, but the prototype link is not preserved — and since methods live on `Class.prototype` rather than on the instance (Module 30), they are simply not reachable from the clone. It does **not** throw for a class instance; only an actual function value in the structure causes a `DataCloneError`. When the class matters, clone the data and reconstruct with `new Class(...)`.
hints: Where do a class's methods actually live?

exercise:ex-m35-01-c.solution: A plain object has no [Symbol.iterator] method — use Object.keys, values or entries
exercise:ex-m35-01-c.solutionExplanation: `for...of` requires the iteration protocol, and `Object.prototype` provides no `[Symbol.iterator]`, so the loop throws `TypeError: object is not iterable`. This is deliberate: an object is a **record**, and there is no single obvious sequence — keys, values or entries are all reasonable, so the language makes you say which. `for...of` works on arrays, strings, `Map`, `Set` and anything else implementing the protocol, which lesson 2 shows you can do yourself.
hints: What exactly does for...of ask the value for?

exercise:ex-m35-01-d.solutionExplanation: `for...in` enumerates **keys**, and object keys are always strings — so you get `"0"` and `"1"`, not numbers. That breaks arithmetic silently: `"0" + 1` is `"01"`. It would also include any non-index property added to the array and would walk the prototype chain. Use `for...of` for values, or `array.entries()` when you genuinely need a numeric index.
hints: What type is an object key?

exercise:ex-m35-02-b.solutionExplanation: Delegating to the array's own iterator is the simplest correct implementation: it is repeatable (a fresh iterator per call, so the fifth test passes), correctly ordered, and needs no manual position tracking. The private field keeps the array unreachable, which the sixth test confirms — consumers receive **values** without gaining the ability to mutate the collection, unlike returning `this.#items` directly. Returning `this` from `add` makes the calls chain, exactly as `Map.prototype.set` and `Set.prototype.add` do.

tests.name: works with for...of
tests.body: const out = []; for (const x of new Bag().add("a")) out.push(x); expect(out).toEqual(["a"]);

hints: Use a `#items = []` private field.
`[Symbol.iterator]() { return this.#items[Symbol.iterator](); }`
`add` returns `this` to chain.

exercise:ex-m35-02-c.solutionExplanation: The broken version keeps one `current` in the factory scope and returns `this`, so every consumer shares a single position — the second pass starts already exhausted. Moving the declaration **inside** `[Symbol.iterator]()` gives each call its own position, which is exactly what the repeat and nested tests check: the inner loop in the hidden test would otherwise consume the outer loop's iterator and terminate it early. `count` stays captured from the factory because it never changes; only the mutable position needs to be per-iterator.

tests.name: nested iteration works
tests.body: const s = createSteps(2); const out = []; for (const a of s) for (const b of s) out.push(a + b); expect(out).toEqual([2, 3, 3, 4]);

hints: Do not keep `current` in the outer function scope.
Declare it inside `[Symbol.iterator]()`.
That method should return a **new** object with `next`.

exercise:ex-m35-03-c.solutionExplanation: `yield*` is what makes this short: it delegates to the recursive call and emits every value that call produces, so the nesting unwinds without any explicit stack — a hand-written iterator would need one to remember its position in each branch. `Array.isArray` is the correct test rather than `typeof`, which reports `"object"` for arrays. Yielding the value directly, with no truthiness filtering, preserves `0`, `null` and `false`, which the hidden test checks. The empty-array cases work because the loop simply yields nothing.
hints: `Array.isArray(value)` decides which branch you are in.
For an array, loop and `yield* flatten(item)`.
Otherwise `yield value`.

exercise:ex-m35-03-d.solutionExplanation: The infinite-generator test passes because generators are **lazy**: `for...of` pulls one value at a time, and `return` ends the loop before another is requested — so the unbounded `while (true)` never runs unasked. The sixth test pins that down precisely: producing two accepted values requires **three** pulls, because the third must be produced before the predicate can reject it. That one-value overshoot is inherent to `takeWhile` and worth understanding. Using `return` rather than `break` is equivalent here, both ending the generator cleanly.

tests.name: works on an infinite generator
tests.body: function* nat() { let n = 1; while (true) yield n++; } expect([...takeWhile(nat(), (n) => n <= 4)]).toEqual([1, 2, 3, 4]);

tests.name: does not over-consume
tests.body: let made = 0; function* nat() { let n = 1; while (true) { made++; yield n++; } } [...takeWhile(nat(), (n) => n <= 2)]; expect(made).toBe(3);

tests.name: passes the value to the predicate
tests.body: const seen = []; [...takeWhile([1, 2], (n) => { seen.push(n); return true; })]; expect(seen).toEqual([1, 2]);

hints: `for (const value of iterable)` works on generators too.
`if (!predicate(value)) return;` ends the generator.
Otherwise `yield value`.

exercise:ex-m36-01-c.solutionExplanation: The engine passes a **hint** describing what it needs, and handling each one is what makes the tests diverge correctly: `+d` and `d * 2` send `"number"`, a template literal and `String()` send `"string"`, and `d + ""` sends `"default"`. The comparison test is the subtle one — relational operators like `<` request the `"number"` hint, so durations compare by magnitude rather than as strings, where `"10m" < "20m"` would happen to work but `"9m" < "10m"` would not.
hints: `[Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) { ... }` is a normal method.
Check `hint === "number"` first.
Return the string form for both other hints.

exercise:ex-m36-01-d.solution: Symbol("marker") — a unique value nobody else can collide with
exercise:ex-m36-01-d.solutionExplanation: `Symbol()` creates a value only your module holds, so no dependency can read or overwrite it by guessing a name — which is the whole point of using a symbol for an internal marker. `Symbol.for` places the symbol in a **realm-wide registry**, so any other code calling `Symbol.for("marker")` gets the identical symbol, reintroducing exactly the collision risk you were avoiding. Reserve `Symbol.for` for cases where separate code genuinely must agree without importing, and namespace the key. A plain string key collides most easily of all.
hints: Which one is shared across the whole realm?

exercise:ex-m36-02-c.solutionExplanation: Freezing **before** recursing is what makes the cycle test pass: when the recursion follows `self` back to the same object, `Object.isFrozen` is already `true` and the call returns immediately — the frozen state doubles as the visited set, so no extra bookkeeping is needed. The `null` guard is required because `typeof null === "object"` (Module 02's historical bug) would otherwise cause a property read on `null`. `Reflect.ownKeys` covers symbol-keyed properties too, which `Object.keys` would miss.

tests.name: survives a cycle
tests.body: const o = { a: 1 }; o.self = o; expect(() => deepFreeze(o)).not.toThrow();

hints: Freeze the object first, then recurse into its values.
A frozen object is already visited — `Object.isFrozen` is your cycle guard.
Guard against `null`, since `typeof null === "object"`.

exercise:ex-m36-02-d.solution: It succeeds — freeze is shallow, so the nested object is untouched
exercise:ex-m36-02-d.solutionExplanation: `Object.freeze` sets `writable: false` and `configurable: false` on the object's **own** properties only. `obj.nested` can no longer be *reassigned*, but the object it points at was never touched — so mutating through it works normally, and `Object.isFrozen(obj.nested)` is `false`. This is the same shallow trap as spread copying: the reference is protected, not the target. There is no built-in deep freeze; you must recurse yourself.
hints: Which properties did freeze actually affect?

exercise:ex-m36-03-b.solutionExplanation: Only a `set` trap is defined, so reads pass straight through — the seventh test works with no `get` trap at all, which is the right instinct: trap only what you must. `!(value > 0)` rather than `value <= 0` is what rejects `NaN`, since every comparison with `NaN` is `false`. Throwing **before** delegating is what leaves the previous value intact after a rejection (the hidden test) — the invariant-preservation rule from Module 22. Returning `Reflect.set`'s boolean correctly reports success to the language.

tests.name: rejects NaN
tests.body: const p = positiveNumbers({}); expect(() => { p.a = NaN; }).toThrow();

tests.name: writes through to the target
tests.body: const t = {}; const p = positiveNumbers(t); p.a = 3; expect(t.a).toBe(3);

tests.name: leaves the value unchanged after a rejection
tests.body: const p = positiveNumbers({}); p.a = 2; try { p.a = -1; } catch {} expect(p.a).toBe(2);

hints: Only a `set` trap is needed — reads pass through by default.
`typeof value === "number" && value > 0` rejects NaN automatically.
Return `Reflect.set(target, property, value, receiver)`.

exercise:ex-m36-03-d.solution: A class with a setter or an explicit update method that validates
exercise:ex-m36-03-d.solutionExplanation: The property is **known in advance**, so ordinary language features handle it: a setter or an `update()` method makes the validation visible at the definition site, is easy to debug and test, and costs nothing. A `Proxy` would work but hides behaviour behind plain-looking property access — a reader of `user.age = -1` has no indication that anything validates it. Freezing prevents all writes rather than validating them. Reserve proxies for intercepting **arbitrary, unknown** property names on objects you do not control, which is what reactive frameworks and mocking libraries do.
hints: Do you know the property names in advance?

exercise:ex-m37-01-c.solutionExplanation: Every input the decision depends on is a **parameter** — no clock, no counter, no configuration read from elsewhere — so the whole retry policy is testable by calling it with numbers, which is exactly what these seven tests do with no setup at all. Checking the status **before** the attempt count is what makes the fifth test pass, and it is the right precedence: a 404 will never succeed however many attempts remain. The real `retry()` function would call this, then perform the waiting and the request — the decision stays pure, the effects stay in the shell.

tests.name: does not retry a client error
checks the status before the attempt count

hints: Check the status first, then the attempt count.
Attempts remain while `attempt < maxAttempts`.
Return plain objects — no side effects anywhere.

exercise:ex-m37-01-d.solution: Contain them at the edges, keeping the decisions underneath pure
exercise:ex-m37-01-d.solutionExplanation: A program with no side effects renders nothing, saves nothing and sends nothing — effects are the reason applications exist. The goal is to keep the network, DOM, storage, clock and mutation in a thin outer layer, with the **decisions** in pure functions underneath that can be tested by calling them with values. Purity is also not a moral property: `addToCart` must change the cart. What matters is that the effect is identifiable and that *what* to add is separable from the act of adding.
hints: What would a program with no side effects actually do?

exercise:ex-m37-02-b.solutionExplanation: Mutating `acc` inside the `reduce` is deliberate and correct: the accumulator is created by the reduce and never escapes, so it is pure by lesson 1's definition — spreading it each iteration would be quadratic for no benefit. `sort` mutates, but it acts on the fresh array `map` just produced, never on the input, which is what the sixth test checks. `slice` handles a limit larger than the data without a guard, and the empty case falls out naturally since every stage handles an empty array.

tests.name: totals per customer
tests.body: expect(topCustomers([{ status: "paid", customer: "a", total: 10 }, { status: "paid", customer: "a", total: 5 }], 1)).toEqual([{ customer: "a", total: 15 }]);

tests.name: ignores unpaid orders
tests.body: expect(topCustomers([{ status: "pending", customer: "a", total: 99 }, { status: "paid", customer: "b", total: 1 }], 2)).toEqual([{ customer: "b", total: 1 }]);

tests.name: sorts descending
tests.body: expect(topCustomers([{ status: "paid", customer: "a", total: 1 }, { status: "paid", customer: "b", total: 9 }], 2).map((x) => x.customer)).toEqual(["b", "a"]);

tests.name: honours the limit
tests.body: expect(topCustomers([{ status: "paid", customer: "a", total: 3 }, { status: "paid", customer: "b", total: 2 }, { status: "paid", customer: "c", total: 1 }], 2).length).toBe(2);

tests.name: does not mutate the input
tests.body: const o = [{ status: "paid", customer: "a", total: 1 }]; topCustomers(o, 1); expect(o.length).toBe(1);

tests.name: handles a limit larger than the data

hints: `filter` for paid, then `reduce` into an object of totals.
`Object.entries` converts that to pairs you can map and sort.
`slice(0, limit)` takes the top — and never overruns.

exercise:ex-m37-02-c.solution: It copies the entire accumulator on every element, making the reduce quadratic
exercise:ex-m37-02-c.solutionExplanation: Each spread copies everything accumulated so far, so processing `n` items performs roughly `n²/2` property copies — for 10,000 items that is tens of millions. The irony is that it is done in pursuit of purity the code already had: the accumulator is created **by** the reduce and never escapes, so mutating it with `acc[x.id] = x; return acc;` is invisible to callers and pure by the definition that matters. Keep immutability at the **boundary**, where it protects callers, not inside a local loop.
hints: How much work does the spread do on the last element?

exercise:ex-m37-03-b.solutionExplanation: Naming the inner function lets it call itself with the accumulated arguments, which is what allows any grouping — each partial call captures what it has so far and waits for more. `fn.length` supplies the arity, so the check knows when to stop collecting. The sixth test shows partials are independent: `add(5)` captures its own `args` array, so calling it twice does not accumulate. Note the honest limitation — `fn.length` stops counting at the first default or rest parameter, so `curry((a, b = 1) => ...)` would call through after one argument.

tests.name: accepts all arguments at once
tests.body: expect(curry((a, b, c) => a + b + c)(1, 2, 3)).toBe(6);

tests.name: accepts one at a time
tests.body: expect(curry((a, b, c) => a + b + c)(1)(2)(3)).toBe(6);

tests.name: accepts a mixed grouping
tests.body: expect(curry((a, b, c) => a + b + c)(1, 2)(3)).toBe(6);

tests.name: accepts the other grouping
tests.body: expect(curry((a, b, c) => a + b + c)(1)(2, 3)).toBe(6);

tests.name: partials are reusable
tests.body: const add = curry((a, b) => a + b); const add5 = add(5); expect([add5(1), add5(2)]).toEqual([6, 7]);

hints: Return a named function so it can call itself.
Compare `args.length` with `fn.length`.
When there are too few, return a function that recurses with the combined arguments.

exercise:ex-m37-03-d.solution: When it is called once with all its arguments — f(a)(b) is harder to read than f(a, b)
exercise:ex-m37-03-d.solutionExplanation: Currying pays off when you genuinely reuse a partially applied form — a configured logger, a formatter passed to `map`. Applied to a function called once with every argument, it adds syntax and indirection for nothing. Two further cautions: a generic `curry` helper surprises readers in a codebase that does not otherwise use functional conventions, and it silently breaks on default or rest parameters because `fn.length` stops counting there. A plain arrow such as `(n) => format(n, "USD")` is often clearer than any helper.
hints: What does currying actually buy you?

exercise:ex-m38-01-c.solutionExplanation: `Math.floor` is what makes this terminate: plain division gives `4.2`, then `0.42`, then `0.042` — approaching zero without ever being an integer, so a base case like `n === 0` is never hit. Flooring guarantees each call removes exactly one digit and reaches a value below `10`. Choosing `n < 10` rather than `n === 0` as the base case handles `0` correctly (second test) while also stopping at any single digit — an `n === 0` base case would report `0` as having zero digits.
hints: `Math.floor(n / 10)` removes the last digit and stays a whole number.
The base case is a number below 10 — that is one digit.
Check the base case before recursing, so `0` is handled.

exercise:ex-m38-01-d.solution: 3, 2, 1 — the log runs before each recursive call, so on the way down
exercise:ex-m38-01-d.solutionExplanation: The log runs **before** the recursive call, so it happens during the descent: `3`, then `2`, then `1`, then the base case returns without logging. Moving the log **after** the recursive call would reverse the output to `1, 2, 3`, because nothing after a recursive call executes until that call returns. That single choice — work before the call, or work after it — is what decides whether a recursive function produces results in descent order or unwind order, and it is the point the `mystery` prediction earlier made with string concatenation.
hints: Does the log statement run before or after the recursive call?

exercise:ex-m38-02-b.solutionExplanation: The `if (found) return found;` shape is the whole exercise. Discarding the result makes every call return `null` even though the node was located; returning `findNode(child, id)` directly would return `null` from the **first** failing child and never reach later siblings — which is precisely what the fifth and sixth tests catch. Returning the node object rather than a copy (hidden test) lets callers mutate or compare it by identity, which is what a `find` is expected to do.

tests.name: finds a deep node
tests.body: expect(findNode({ id: "a", children: [{ id: "b", children: [{ id: "c", children: [] }] }] }, "c").id).toBe("c");

tests.name: searches later siblings after an earlier one fails
tests.body: expect(findNode({ id: "a", children: [{ id: "b", children: [] }, { id: "c", children: [] }] }, "c").id).toBe("c");

tests.name: searches deep in a later branch
tests.body: expect(findNode({ id: "a", children: [{ id: "b", children: [] }, { id: "c", children: [{ id: "d", children: [] }] }] }, "d").id).toBe("d");

tests.name: returns the node itself, not a copy
tests.body: const target = { id: "b", children: [] }; expect(findNode({ id: "a", children: [target] }, "b")).toBe(target);

hints: Check `node.id` first — that is the success base case.
Loop the children, store each recursive result in a variable.
Return it only when truthy, so the loop can continue.

exercise:ex-m38-02-c.solutionExplanation: Using `node.size` as the **initial accumulator** folds the base case into the reduce: a leaf has no children, so the callback never runs and the node's own size is returned. That removes the need for an explicit `if (children.length === 0)` branch entirely. Each child contributes its own full subtotal, which is the "trust the recursive call" leap from lesson 1 — you never need to think about how deep any branch goes. Nothing is mutated, since `reduce` only accumulates a number.

tests.name: a leaf is its own size
adds one level of children
tests.body: expect(totalSize({ size: 1, children: [{ size: 2, children: [] }, { size: 3, children: [] }] })).toBe(6);

tests.name: adds deeply
tests.body: expect(totalSize({ size: 1, children: [{ size: 2, children: [{ size: 4, children: [] }] }] })).toBe(7);

tests.name: handles a wide tree
tests.body: expect(totalSize({ size: 0, children: [1, 2, 3, 4].map((n) => ({ size: n, children: [] })) })).toBe(10);

tests.name: does not mutate the tree
tests.body: const t = { size: 1, children: [{ size: 2, children: [] }] }; totalSize(t); expect(t.children.length).toBe(1);

tests.name: handles an unbalanced tree
tests.body: expect(totalSize({ size: 1, children: [{ size: 1, children: [{ size: 1, children: [{ size: 1, children: [] }] }] }, { size: 1, children: [] }] })).toBe(5);

hints: Start from `node.size`.
Add `totalSize(child)` for each child.
`reduce` over the children reads well here.

exercise:ex-m38-03-b.solutionExplanation: The cache turns exponential work into linear: each `n` is computed once and reused, so `fib(60)` finishes instantly where the naive version would take effectively forever. Naming the returned function is what lets it recurse into **itself** — recursing into an outer helper would bypass the cache entirely. Declaring `cache` inside `makeFib` gives each instance its own, which the sixth test checks, and using `cache.has` rather than a truthiness check matters because `fib` legitimately returns `0`. Note the recursion was never the problem; the repeated work was.

tests.name: computes small values
tests.body: const f = makeFib(); expect([f(2), f(5), f(10)]).toEqual([1, 5, 55]);

tests.name: caches across calls
tests.body: const f = makeFib(); f(25); let n = 0; const before = f(25); expect(before).toBe(75025);

tests.name: instances have separate caches
tests.body: const a = makeFib(); const b = makeFib(); a(20); expect(b(20)).toBe(6765);

tests.name: is consistent when called out of order
tests.body: const f = makeFib(); expect([f(10), f(3), f(10)]).toEqual([55, 2, 55]);

hints: `const cache = new Map();` inside `makeFib`.
Return a named function so it can recurse.
Check the cache before computing, and store the result after.

exercise:ex-m38-03-d.solution: Iteration with an explicit stack — the recursive version would exceed the call stack
exercise:ex-m38-03-d.solutionExplanation: A few thousand frames is safe; 100,000 is far beyond any engine's limit, so the recursive version throws `RangeError`. Converting to an explicit stack moves that bookkeeping into an **array in the heap**, where depth is limited by memory instead. Crucially, writing the recursion in tail position does **not** help: Module 33 established that JavaScript engines generally do not implement tail-call elimination despite it being specified, so each call still consumes a frame.
hints: How many frames would 100,000 levels need?

exercise:ex-m39-01-b.solutionExplanation: Replacing the scan with a `Set` makes each membership test O(1), so the whole function is O(n) — at the cost of O(n) auxiliary space, which is the trade-off worth making every time. Keeping a separate `result` array is what preserves **first-seen order**, which spreading the `Set` would also do but which an unordered structure would not. Using `has` rather than a truthiness check keeps `0`, `""` and `false` as distinct legitimate values (sixth test). The hidden test is large enough that the quadratic version would be noticeably slow.

tests.name: does not use includes on the result
tests.body: const big = Array.from({ length: 3000 }, (_, i) => i % 1500); expect(dedupe(big).length).toBe(1500);

hints: A `Set` gives O(1) membership tests.
Track seen values in the Set; build the output array separately.
`seen.has(item)` replaces `result.includes(item)`.

exercise:ex-m39-01-d.solutionExplanation: Tracking the best value **during** the counting pass rather than scanning afterwards makes the tie rule fall out naturally: `count > bestCount` updates only on a **strictly greater** count, so whichever value reached that count earliest keeps the title. The two tie tests pin down both directions — `["a","b","b","a"]` gives `"b"` because it hit 2 at index 2, while `["a","a","b","b"]` gives `"a"` for the same reason. Using `>=` instead would hand the win to the **last** value to tie, silently reversing the rule. A `Map` rather than an object keeps `1` and `"1"` distinct (first hidden test), since object keys coerce to strings, and returning the value directly preserves a falsy winner such as `0`. One pass, O(n) time and O(n) space.

tests.name: breaks ties by first to reach the winning count
the earlier value wins when it reaches the count first

hints: A `Map` counts in one pass and keeps any key type.
Track the best value as you count, updating only on a strictly greater count.
`>` rather than `>=` is what makes the tie go to the earlier value.

exercise:ex-m39-02-b.solutionExplanation: The head index is the whole technique: the array is never re-indexed, so `dequeue` touches one slot instead of moving every remaining element. The hidden test drains 100,000 items — a `shift()` implementation would perform roughly five billion element moves there and be noticeably slow, while this completes instantly. Clearing the vacated slot to `undefined` releases the reference so dequeued items can be collected, which matters for a long-lived queue (Module 32). Returning the value directly preserves a legitimate `0`.

tests.name: dequeues in FIFO order
tests.body: const q = createQueue(); q.enqueue(1); q.enqueue(2); expect([q.dequeue(), q.dequeue()]).toEqual([1, 2]);

tests.name: reports size
tests.body: const q = createQueue(); q.enqueue(1); q.enqueue(2); q.dequeue(); expect(q.size).toBe(1);

tests.name: handles interleaved operations
tests.body: const q = createQueue(); q.enqueue(1); expect(q.dequeue()).toBe(1); q.enqueue(2); expect(q.dequeue()).toBe(2); expect(q.size).toBe(0);

tests.name: handles many items efficiently
tests.body: const q = createQueue(); for (let i = 0; i < 100000; i++) q.enqueue(i); let last; for (let i = 0; i < 100000; i++) last = q.dequeue(); expect([last, q.size]).toEqual([99999, 0]);

hints: Keep a `head` index starting at 0.
`dequeue` reads `items[head]` and increments `head`.
`size` is `items.length - head`.

exercise:ex-m39-02-c.solutionExplanation: The visited `Set` is what makes the cycle tests terminate — without it `a → b → a` queues forever. Marking a node visited **when queueing** rather than when dequeuing is the subtle part: the other order lets the same node be queued several times before any of them is processed, producing duplicates in the output. `graph[node] ?? []` handles the hidden test, where a neighbour is named but has no entry of its own — a real situation with partial data. The head-index queue keeps each dequeue O(1).

tests.name: handles a node missing from the graph

hints: A `Set` of visited nodes prevents revisiting.
Mark a node visited when you **queue** it, not when you process it.
`graph[node] ?? []` handles a node with no listed neighbours.

exercise:ex-m39-03-b.solutionExplanation: The sorted order is what justifies the moves: if the sum is too small, the only way to increase it is to raise the smaller value, so moving `left` rightward is provably the right choice and no possibility is skipped. `left < right` rather than `<=` is what makes the fifth test pass — a single element must not pair with itself. Each step eliminates one candidate, so this is O(n) time and O(1) space, better on memory than the `Set`-of-complements approach that unsorted input would require.

tests.name: returns null when no pair exists
does not pair an element with itself
finds a pair needing several moves

hints: `left` at 0, `right` at the last index.
Sum too small? Move `left` right. Too large? Move `right` left.
Loop while `left < right`, so an element never pairs with itself.

exercise:ex-m39-03-c.solutionExplanation: Consecutive windows overlap in `k - 1` elements, so recomputing each sum discards work you already have. Adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving one costs **two** operations regardless of `k`, which is why the hidden test with `k = 100` over 50,000 elements stays fast — a naive version would do five million additions. Seeding `best` from the first window rather than from `0` or `-Infinity` handles the all-negative case correctly (fifth test). The length guard covers both the empty array and `k` larger than the input.

tests.name: handles k equal to the length
finds a window at the start
scales without nested loops
tests.body: const big = Array.from({ length: 50000 }, (_, i) => i % 100); expect(maxWindowSum(big, 100)).toBe(4950);

hints: Sum the first `k` elements to seed the window.
Then for each later index, add the new element and subtract `numbers[i - k]`.
Track the best sum as you go.

exercise:ex-m40-02-b.solutionExplanation: Each function now has **one reason to change**: validation rules, the totalling formula, the currency format, and the orchestration are four separate concerns that previously all lived in one place. The payoff is visible in the tests — three of them exercise a single function with plain values and no cart setup at all, and the hidden test composes two of them in a way the original monolith made impossible. `summariseCart` reads as a description of the process because every detail moved one level down.

tests.name: totals an empty list as zero

hints: `validateCart` returns a string describing the problem, or `null` when fine.
`cartTotal` uses `reduce` with an initial `0`.
`summariseCart` calls validate first and returns the problem if there is one.

exercise:ex-m40-02-c.solutionExplanation: Destructuring with defaults means a caller states only what differs, and the fourth test shows the real win over positional arguments: **order stops mattering**, so transposing two flags is no longer a silent bug. Defaulting `options = {}` is what makes the sixth test pass — destructuring `undefined` would throw. The hidden test checks a subtlety of default values: they apply only for `undefined`, so an explicit `false` is respected rather than being overridden.

tests.name: defaults every flag to false
tests.body: expect(formatDate(new Date(0), {})).toEqual({ iso: "1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z", showTime: false, showYear: false, useShortMonth: false });

tests.name: order does not matter
tests.body: expect(formatDate(new Date(0), { useShortMonth: true, showTime: true })).toEqual(formatDate(new Date(0), { showTime: true, useShortMonth: true }));

hints: Default the whole options object: `options = {}`.
Destructure with defaults inside the parameter list or the body.
Return the flags alongside `date.toISOString()`.

exercise:ex-m40-03-b.solutionExplanation: The fourth and fifth tests are the point of the exercise: `"|0"` looks like a bug worth "fixing", but changing it would alter behaviour something downstream may rely on — and that would be a rewrite, not a refactor. `join(",")` on an empty array returns `""`, which reproduces the original exactly and also eliminates the trailing-comma `substring` trick entirely (hidden test). That is the usual experience of refactoring: restructuring removes whole categories of code rather than tidying them.

tests.name: ignores unpaid orders
tests.body: expect(summarise([{ id: "a", status: "paid", amount: 10 }, { id: "b", status: "pending", amount: 5 }])).toBe("a|10");

tests.name: joins several ids
tests.body: expect(summarise([{ id: "a", status: "paid", amount: 1 }, { id: "b", status: "paid", amount: 2 }])).toBe("a,b|3");

tests.name: does not mutate the input
tests.body: const o = [{ id: "a", status: "paid", amount: 1 }]; summarise(o); expect(o.length).toBe(1);

hints: `filter` for paid orders, then `map` and `join(",")` for the ids.
`reduce` with an initial `0` for the total.
`join` on an empty array gives `""`, which preserves the `"|0"` behaviour.

exercise:ex-m40-03-c.solutionExplanation: `filter` returns a **new** array, so the subsequent `sort` mutates that copy rather than the caller's input — which is what the seventh test checks, and why the order of the two calls matters. Each function is independently testable with plain values, and `buildReport` reads as a description of the process because both details moved one level down. The hidden test shows the real payoff: because `userLabel` takes a single user, it can be passed **directly** to `map` with no wrapper — the unary-function benefit from Module 37.

tests.name: filters deleted users
tests.body: expect(activeUsers([{ name: "a", deleted: true }, { name: "b", deleted: false }]).map((u) => u.name)).toEqual(["b"]);

tests.name: sorts by name
tests.body: expect(activeUsers([{ name: "c", deleted: false }, { name: "a", deleted: false }]).map((u) => u.name)).toEqual(["a", "c"]);

tests.name: excludes deleted users from the report
does not mutate the input order
tests.body: const u = [{ name: "c", deleted: false }, { name: "a", deleted: false }]; activeUsers(u); expect(u[0].name).toBe("c");

hints: `filter` then `sort` — but sort a copy, since sort mutates.
`localeCompare` compares names properly.
`buildReport` is just `activeUsers(...).map(userLabel)`.

exercise:ex-m41-01-b.solutionExplanation: This is the factory pattern proper: the caller says **what they want** and never learns which construction happened, so adding a third kind is a change in one function. The hidden test states the requirement that makes it work — both kinds share the same interface, which is what lets calling code treat them interchangeably (Module 31's polymorphism). Throwing for an unknown kind fails loudly rather than returning something half-formed, and each call builds a fresh `Map`, giving the independence the sixth test checks.

tests.name: prefixed keys differ from memory keys
tests.body: const p = createStorage("prefixed"); const m = createStorage("memory"); p.save("k", 1); expect(m.load("k")).toBe(undefined);

tests.name: instances are independent
tests.body: const a = createStorage("memory"); const b = createStorage("memory"); a.save("k", 1); expect(b.load("k")).toBe(undefined);

tests.name: both kinds share an interface
tests.body: const kinds = ["memory", "prefixed"].map(createStorage); expect(kinds.every((s) => typeof s.save === "function" && typeof s.load === "function")).toBe(true);

hints: Write a small builder for each kind, then dispatch on `kind`.
The prefixed version applies `"app:" + key` inside both methods.
Throw before returning anything for an unknown kind.

exercise:ex-m41-01-d.solution: Factory — closures need no `this`, so the methods survive being detached
exercise:ex-m41-01-d.solutionExplanation: A factory's methods close over the state directly, so there is no receiver to lose when one is handed to `addEventListener` — the detached-method problem from Module 29 simply does not arise. With only a handful of objects, the per-instance function cost is irrelevant. The last option would work (arrow class fields are permanently bound) but adds class ceremony to reach the same place. A class would win if there were many instances, inheritance, or an `instanceof` check.
hints: What happens to a prototype method passed as a listener?

exercise:ex-m41-02-a.solutionExplanation: Spreading in `set` is what makes the sixth test pass: the first subscriber removes itself mid-notification, and iterating the live array would shift the second down into the index the loop has already passed, silently skipping it. Copying fixes the notification list before any handler can change it. Wrapping each subscription in its own `entry` object gives it a **unique identity**, so the hidden test can subscribe the same function twice and get two independent notifications — searching for the function itself would have removed the wrong one.

tests.name: notifies a subscriber
tests.body: const o = createObservable(0); const seen = []; o.subscribe((v) => seen.push(v)); o.set(1); expect(seen).toEqual([1]);

tests.name: notifies several
tests.body: const o = createObservable(0); const seen = []; o.subscribe((v) => seen.push(`a${v}`)); o.subscribe((v) => seen.push(`b${v}`)); o.set(1); expect(seen).toEqual(["a1", "b1"]);

tests.name: exposes the current value
tests.body: const o = createObservable(5); expect(o.value).toBe(5); o.set(9); expect(o.value).toBe(9);

tests.name: unsubscribe stops notifications
tests.body: const o = createObservable(0); const seen = []; const off = o.subscribe((v) => seen.push(v)); off(); o.set(1); expect(seen).toEqual([]);

tests.name: unsubscribing one leaves the others
tests.body: const o = createObservable(0); const seen = []; const off = o.subscribe(() => seen.push("a")); o.subscribe(() => seen.push("b")); off(); o.set(1); expect(seen).toEqual(["b"]);

tests.name: survives self-removal during notification
tests.body: const o = createObservable(0); const seen = []; const off = o.subscribe(() => { seen.push("first"); off(); }); o.subscribe(() => seen.push("second")); o.set(1); expect(seen).toEqual(["first", "second"]);

tests.name: the same function can subscribe twice
tests.body: const o = createObservable(0); let n = 0; const fn = () => { n += 1; }; o.subscribe(fn); o.subscribe(fn); o.set(1); expect(n).toBe(2);

hints: Give each subscription its own entry object so duplicates are distinguishable.
Return a closure that removes that specific entry.
In `set`, spread the list before iterating it.

exercise:ex-m41-02-c.solutionExplanation: Capturing the **previous state** rather than computing an inverse is what makes the third test pass: no inverse of `toUpperCase` can restore `"Hello World"` from `"HELLO WORLD"`, because the original casing is genuinely gone. Storing the value before the change is correct by construction for **any** transformation, which is also why the hidden test works with numbers — nothing here assumes strings. The trade-off is memory: every step keeps a full copy, which matters for large values but is almost always the right choice for correctness.

tests.name: applies a transformation
tests.body: const h = createHistory("a"); h.apply((v) => v + "b"); expect(h.value).toBe("ab");

tests.name: undoes it
tests.body: const h = createHistory("a"); h.apply((v) => v + "b"); h.undo(); expect(h.value).toBe("a");

tests.name: undoes a lossy transformation exactly
tests.body: const h = createHistory("Hello World"); h.apply((v) => v.toUpperCase()); h.undo(); expect(h.value).toBe("Hello World");

tests.name: undoes several steps
tests.body: const h = createHistory(""); h.apply((v) => v + "a"); h.apply((v) => v + "b"); h.undo(); h.undo(); expect(h.value).toBe("");

tests.name: undo on empty history is safe
works with non-strings
tests.body: const h = createHistory(10); h.apply((v) => v * 3); h.undo(); expect(h.value).toBe(10);

hints: Push the value *before* the change onto a stack.
`undo` pops that previous value and restores it.
No inverse function is needed at all.

exercise:ex-m41-03-b.solutionExplanation: The facade removes real complexity from callers: they no longer need to know that validation comes first, that pricing must be skipped on failure, or that both outcomes are logged. The third test pins that ordering down explicitly — pricing an invalid order would be a genuine bug, and the guard clause prevents it. Because all three collaborators are **passed in**, every test here uses plain functions with no mocking framework, which is exactly why a facade should simplify without hiding what it depends on.

tests.name: submits a valid order
tests.body: const s = createOrderService({ validate: () => null, price: () => 50, log: () => {} }); expect(s.submit({})).toEqual({ ok: true, total: 50 });

tests.name: rejects an invalid order
tests.body: const s = createOrderService({ validate: () => "bad", price: () => 50, log: () => {} }); expect(s.submit({})).toEqual({ ok: false, reason: "bad" });

tests.name: does not price an invalid order
tests.body: let priced = false; const s = createOrderService({ validate: () => "bad", price: () => { priced = true; return 0; }, log: () => {} }); s.submit({}); expect(priced).toBe(false);

tests.name: logs a success
tests.body: const lines = []; const s = createOrderService({ validate: () => null, price: () => 50, log: (l) => lines.push(l) }); s.submit({}); expect(lines.length).toBe(1);

tests.name: logs a rejection
tests.body: const lines = []; const s = createOrderService({ validate: () => "bad", price: () => 0, log: (l) => lines.push(l) }); s.submit({}); expect(lines.length).toBe(1);

tests.name: passes the order to validate
tests.body: let seen = null; const s = createOrderService({ validate: (o) => { seen = o; return null; }, price: () => 1, log: () => {} }); s.submit({ id: 7 }); expect(seen).toEqual({ id: 7 });

tests.name: passes the order to price
tests.body: let seen = null; const s = createOrderService({ validate: () => null, price: (o) => { seen = o; return 1; }, log: () => {} }); s.submit({ id: 9 }); expect(seen).toEqual({ id: 9 });

hints: Validate first and return early on a problem.
Only call `price` once validation passed.
Log on both paths, with different messages.

exercise:ex-m41-03-c.solution: Three layers of indirection for one implementation; the flexibility is imaginary, and a real second channel will likely not fit the guessed interface
exercise:ex-m41-03-c.solutionExplanation: The factory chooses between one option and the base class has one subclass, so nothing is being abstracted over — every layer is a hop a reader must follow for no current benefit. The deeper problem is that a real SMS or push channel will bring requirements nobody anticipated (delivery receipts, rate limits, different error shapes), so the interface guessed in advance usually needs redesigning anyway. Testability does not require it either: injecting a plain function is simpler. Write the direct implementation and extract the seam when the second case reveals what it actually needs to be.
hints: What is the factory currently choosing between?

exercise:ex-m42-01-a.solution: Every line executed and the cases you thought of behave as expected — nothing about cases you did not consider
exercise:ex-m42-01-a.solutionExplanation: Coverage measures which **lines ran**, not whether the assertions were meaningful — a test that calls a function and asserts nothing counts as fully covered. Most bugs live in cases nobody imagined, and no coverage number can reveal those. What a passing suite genuinely buys is **confidence to change code**: refactoring is only safe when something can tell you behaviour was preserved, which is the largest return on the effort.
hints: What does coverage actually measure?

exercise:ex-m42-01-c.solution: An integration test — it checks that several pieces work together
exercise:ex-m42-01-c.solutionExplanation: It exercises the interaction between validation, the service, and persistence — more than one unit, but far less than the whole application in a browser. A **unit** test would check `validateSignup` alone with no dependencies; an **end-to-end** test would drive a real browser through the actual form. Note that this integration test needs **no framework**: because the save dependency is passed in, a plain function serves as the fake, which is what Module 28's dependency inversion buys at testing time.
hints: How many pieces are involved?

exercise:ex-m42-02-b.solutionExplanation: Turning the hidden clock dependency into a **parameter** makes the function pure (Module 37), so every case runs instantly and deterministically — no sleeping, no fake timers, no flakiness. The sixth test is the proof that the real clock is gone: passing `-1` as `now` makes an `expiresAt` of `0` active, which is impossible if `Date.now()` is being consulted. `>` rather than `>=` is what makes exact expiry count as expired, which the third test pins down explicitly. The caller supplies `Date.now()` at the edge.

tests.name: exactly at expiry counts as expired
does not read the real clock

hints: Compare `session.expiresAt` with the `now` parameter.
`>` rather than `>=` makes exact expiry count as expired.
Do not call `Date.now()` anywhere.

exercise:ex-m42-02-c.solutionExplanation: Taking `request` as a parameter is what makes every test instant and deterministic — no network, no `fetch` patching, just a stub returning a plain object. The sixth test encodes the discipline from the lesson: it sets a flag in the `catch` and asserts the flag, so the test **fails if no error was thrown** rather than passing silently. Deliberately not wrapping the `await` in try/catch lets a rejected request propagate unchanged (hidden test), which is the right behaviour — the function reports HTTP failures, and transport failures are the caller's to handle.

tests.name: returns the data on success
tests.body: const r = async () => ({ ok: true, data: { id: 1 } }); expect(await loadProfile(1, r)).toEqual({ id: 1 });

tests.name: requests the right url
tests.body: let seen = null; const r = async (url) => { seen = url; return { ok: true, data: {} }; }; await loadProfile(7, r); expect(seen.includes("7")).toBe(true);

tests.name: throws on a failed response
tests.body: const r = async () => ({ ok: false, status: 500 }); let caught = null; try { await loadProfile(1, r); } catch (e) { caught = e; } expect(caught instanceof Error).toBe(true);

tests.name: includes the status in the message
tests.body: const r = async () => ({ ok: false, status: 404 }); let msg = ""; try { await loadProfile(1, r); } catch (e) { msg = e.message; } expect(msg.includes("404")).toBe(true);

tests.name: returns a promise
tests.body: const r = async () => ({ ok: true, data: 1 }); expect(typeof loadProfile(1, r).then).toBe("function");

tests.name: fails the test if no error is thrown
tests.body: const r = async () => ({ ok: false, status: 500 }); let threw = false; try { await loadProfile(1, r); } catch { threw = true; } expect(threw).toBe(true);

tests.name: propagates a rejected request
tests.body: const r = async () => { throw new Error("offline"); }; let msg = ""; try { await loadProfile(1, r); } catch (e) { msg = e.message; } expect(msg).toBe("offline");

hints: `const response = await request(...)`.
Guard with `if (!response.ok) throw new Error(...)`.
Do not wrap the call in try/catch — a rejected request should propagate.

exercise:ex-m42-03-b.solutionExplanation: Every test **clicks the real button** and then inspects what a user would see — the panel's visibility and the button's text. None mentions the listener, an internal flag, or a handler name, so the implementation could be rewritten entirely and these tests would still pass provided the behaviour holds. Deriving the button text from `panel.hidden` **after** toggling keeps the two in sync by construction, rather than tracking a separate variable that could drift.Notice each test builds a **fresh element** rather than reusing a shared one. That is not tidiness — mounting twice on the same element attaches a **second listener**, so one click would toggle twice and land back where it started. Accumulating listeners is a real bug in application code too (Module 32), and it shows up first in tests that share a container.

tests.name: panel starts hidden
tests.body:
const r = document.createElement("div"); r.innerHTML = `
Panel content
`; mountToggle(r); expect(r.querySelector("#panel").hidden).toBe(true);

tests.name: a click reveals the panel
tests.body:
const r = document.createElement("div"); r.innerHTML = `
Panel content
`; mountToggle(r); r.querySelector("#toggle").click(); expect(r.querySelector("#panel").hidden).toBe(false);

tests.name: the button text updates
tests.body:
const r = document.createElement("div"); r.innerHTML = `
Panel content
`; mountToggle(r); r.querySelector("#toggle").click(); expect(r.querySelector("#toggle").textContent).toBe("Hide");

tests.name: a second click hides it again
tests.body:
const r = document.createElement("div"); r.innerHTML = `
Panel content
`; mountToggle(r); const b = r.querySelector("#toggle"); b.click(); b.click(); expect(r.querySelector("#panel").hidden).toBe(true);

tests.name: the text returns to Show
tests.body:
const r = document.createElement("div"); r.innerHTML = `
Panel content
`; mountToggle(r); const b = r.querySelector("#toggle"); b.click(); b.click(); expect(b.textContent).toBe("Show");

tests.name: three clicks leave it visible
tests.body:
const r = document.createElement("div"); r.innerHTML = `
Panel content
`; mountToggle(r); const b = r.querySelector("#toggle"); b.click(); b.click(); b.click(); expect(r.querySelector("#panel").hidden).toBe(false);

Toggle `panel.hidden` on each click.
Set the button text from the new hidden state.

exercise:ex-m42-03-d.solution: Tests written to execute lines rather than check behaviour — often brittle and assertion-light
exercise:ex-m42-03-d.solutionExplanation: The cheapest way to raise coverage is to call code without asserting anything meaningful about it, so a mandatory threshold rewards exactly the tests this lesson warns against. Coverage is genuinely useful as a **signal** — a module at 0%, or an error path never exercised, is real information worth acting on — but it measures which lines **ran**, never whether the assertions mattered. A suite at 60% testing behaviour is more valuable than one at 95% asserting on internals.
hints: What is the cheapest way to raise a coverage number?

exercise:ex-m43-01-c.solutionExplanation: Scheduling the next chunk with `setTimeout` makes it a **separate task**, so the event loop can render and handle input between chunks — a recursive `queueMicrotask` would keep the checkpoint open and block the page exactly as an unbroken loop does (Module 33). The sixth test confirms the work is genuinely deferred rather than done synchronously. Carrying one `index` across chunks preserves order, and passing it to `fn` matches the `map` signature, which the hidden test checks. The empty case resolves on the first `step`.

tests.name: does not complete synchronously
tests.body: let done = false; mapInChunks([1, 2, 3], (n) => n, 1).then(() => { done = true; }); expect(done).toBe(false);

tests.name: passes the index to the callback

hints: Wrap everything in `new Promise((resolve) => { ... })`.
A `step` function processes one chunk then schedules itself.
Track a single index across chunks so order is preserved.

exercise:ex-m43-01-d.solution: Move it to a Web Worker — it is heavy CPU work needing no DOM access
exercise:ex-m43-01-d.solutionExplanation: The premise rules out the usual first answer: the algorithm is already correct, so there is no complexity win available. Parsing and aggregating needs **no DOM**, which makes it exactly what workers are for — it runs on a genuine second thread and the page stays fully responsive rather than merely twitching between chunks. Chunking would work but keeps two seconds of work on the main thread, interleaved with rendering. Memoisation helps only for repeated identical input, and swapping a loop for `reduce` changes nothing about the total work.
hints: Does this work need the DOM?

exercise:ex-m43-02-b.solutionExplanation: Injecting `now` is what makes every test instant and deterministic — no timers, no sleeping, no flakiness (Module 42). Initialising `lastRun` to `-Infinity` guarantees the first call always passes, where `0` would fail if the clock also started at `0`. Using `>=` for the boundary (expressed here as `< interval` returning early) means a call exactly one interval later is **allowed**, which the hidden test pins down. Note the omission from the lesson: this has no trailing call, so the very last event in a burst is dropped.

tests.name: calls on the first invocation
tests.body: const calls = []; let t = 0; const f = throttle((v) => calls.push(v), 100, () => t); f("a"); expect(calls).toEqual(["a"]);

tests.name: suppresses within the interval
tests.body: const calls = []; let t = 0; const f = throttle((v) => calls.push(v), 100, () => t); f("a"); t = 50; f("b"); expect(calls).toEqual(["a"]);

tests.name: allows after the interval
tests.body: const calls = []; let t = 0; const f = throttle((v) => calls.push(v), 100, () => t); f("a"); t = 100; f("b"); expect(calls).toEqual(["a", "b"]);

tests.name: suppresses a whole burst
tests.body: const calls = []; let t = 0; const f = throttle((v) => calls.push(v), 100, () => t); for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) f(i); expect(calls).toEqual([0]);

tests.name: runs steadily across intervals
tests.body: const calls = []; let t = 0; const f = throttle((v) => calls.push(v), 10, () => t); for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { t = i * 10; f(i); } expect(calls).toEqual([0, 1, 2, 3, 4]);

tests.name: passes several arguments
tests.body: const calls = []; let t = 0; const f = throttle((a, b) => calls.push(a + b), 10, () => t); f(2, 3); expect(calls).toEqual([5]);

tests.name: the boundary counts as allowed
tests.body: const calls = []; let t = 0; const f = throttle((v) => calls.push(v), 10, () => t); f("a"); t = 10; f("b"); expect(calls.length).toBe(2);

hints: Track the timestamp of the last allowed call.
Initialise it so the first call always passes.
`now() - lastRun >= interval` decides.

exercise:ex-m43-02-c.solutionExplanation: A `Map` iterates in **insertion order**, so deleting and re-inserting a key moves it to the end — which is what makes recency tracking possible without a second data structure. Doing that inside `get` is what makes the sixth test pass: reading `"a"` refreshes it, so `"b"` becomes the eviction candidate instead. Deleting before setting in `touch` also handles the seventh test, since re-setting an existing key must not grow the size. Bounding the cache is the fix for the unbounded-growth leak; a `WeakMap` is the alternative when the key is an object whose lifetime already governs the entry.

tests.name: reports size
tests.body: const c = createCache(3); c.set("a", 1); c.set("b", 2); expect(c.size).toBe(2);

tests.name: never exceeds the limit
tests.body: const c = createCache(2); c.set("a", 1); c.set("b", 2); c.set("c", 3); expect(c.size).toBe(2);

tests.name: evicts the oldest
tests.body: const c = createCache(2); c.set("a", 1); c.set("b", 2); c.set("c", 3); expect(c.get("a")).toBe(undefined);

tests.name: keeps the newest
tests.body: const c = createCache(2); c.set("a", 1); c.set("b", 2); c.set("c", 3); expect(c.keys()).toEqual(["b", "c"]);

tests.name: reading refreshes recency
tests.body: const c = createCache(2); c.set("a", 1); c.set("b", 2); c.get("a"); c.set("c", 3); expect(c.get("a")).toBe(1);

tests.name: re-setting a key does not grow the size
tests.body: const c = createCache(2); c.set("a", 1); c.set("a", 2); expect(c.size).toBe(1);

hints: Delete then re-set a key to move it to the end of the Map.
`cache.keys().next().value` is the oldest key.
`get` should also refresh the key's position.

exercise:ex-m43-03-b.solutionExplanation: Storing the **promise** rather than the result is what lets simultaneous callers join a request already in flight — the second and third tests confirm one underlying call and one shared promise. Using `finally` rather than `then` is what makes the hidden test pass: clearing only on success would leave a **rejected** promise cached, so every later caller would receive the same stale failure and a retry would be impossible. Note this is deduplication rather than caching: it deliberately clears on settle, so it carries no staleness risk.

tests.name: returns the value
tests.body: const load = createLoader(async (id) => ({ id })); expect(await load(1)).toEqual({ id: 1 });

tests.name: collapses simultaneous calls
tests.body: let calls = 0; const load = createLoader(async (id) => { calls += 1; return id; }); await Promise.all([load(1), load(1), load(1)]); expect(calls).toBe(1);

tests.name: shares the same promise
tests.body: const load = createLoader(async (id) => ({ id })); const [a, b] = await Promise.all([load(1), load(1)]); expect(a).toBe(b);

tests.name: different ids are separate
tests.body: let calls = 0; const load = createLoader(async (id) => { calls += 1; return id; }); await Promise.all([load(1), load(2)]); expect(calls).toBe(2);

tests.name: refetches after settling
tests.body: let calls = 0; const load = createLoader(async (id) => { calls += 1; return id; }); await load(1); await load(1); expect(calls).toBe(2);

tests.name: propagates a rejection
tests.body: const load = createLoader(async () => { throw new Error("nope"); }); let msg = ""; try { await load(1); } catch (e) { msg = e.message; } expect(msg).toBe("nope");

tests.name: clears after a rejection so a retry is possible
tests.body: let calls = 0; const load = createLoader(async () => { calls += 1; throw new Error("x"); }); try { await load(1); } catch {} try { await load(1); } catch {} expect(calls).toBe(2);

hints: A `Map` from id to the pending promise.
Return the existing promise when one is present.
`finally` clears on both success and failure.

exercise:ex-m43-03-c.solutionExplanation: One request replaces one-per-post, which is the whole point of removing an N+1 — with fifty posts the naive version makes fifty round trips and this still makes one. The `Set` deduplicates before the request is sent (third test), so a repeated author is not fetched twice. Building a `Map` makes the mapping-back step O(n) rather than a `find` per post, which would reintroduce a quadratic (Module 39). Spreading into new objects leaves the input untouched, which the hidden test confirms.

tests.name: attaches an author
tests.body: const f = async (ids) => ids.map((id) => ({ id, name: `a${id}` })); expect((await attachAuthors([{ id: 1, authorId: 7 }], f))[0].author.name).toBe("a7");

tests.name: makes exactly one request
tests.body: let calls = 0; const f = async (ids) => { calls += 1; return ids.map((id) => ({ id })); }; await attachAuthors([{ authorId: 1 }, { authorId: 2 }], f); expect(calls).toBe(1);

tests.name: deduplicates ids
tests.body: let seen = null; const f = async (ids) => { seen = ids; return ids.map((id) => ({ id })); }; await attachAuthors([{ authorId: 7 }, { authorId: 7 }], f); expect(seen).toEqual([7]);

tests.name: preserves post order
tests.body: const f = async (ids) => ids.map((id) => ({ id })); const out = await attachAuthors([{ id: 1, authorId: 8 }, { id: 2, authorId: 7 }], f); expect(out.map((p) => p.id)).toEqual([1, 2]);

tests.name: preserves post fields
tests.body: const f = async (ids) => ids.map((id) => ({ id })); const out = await attachAuthors([{ id: 1, authorId: 7, title: "t" }], f); expect(out[0].title).toBe("t");

tests.name: handles an empty list
tests.body: let calls = 0; const f = async (ids) => { calls += 1; return []; }; expect(await attachAuthors([], f)).toEqual([]);

tests.name: does not mutate the input
tests.body: const posts = [{ id: 1, authorId: 7 }]; const f = async (ids) => ids.map((id) => ({ id })); await attachAuthors(posts, f); expect("author" in posts[0]).toBe(false);

Build a `Map` from id to author for O(1) lookup.
Spread each post into a new object with the author added.

exercise:ex-m44-01-c.solutionExplanation: Using `new URL` to **parse** rather than pattern-matching the string is what makes the hidden test pass: the parser normalises the scheme, so `JaVaScRiPt:` is recognised as `javascript:` and rejected, where a naive `startsWith("javascript:")` check would let it through. Allowlisting is the essential choice — a blocklist must anticipate every dangerous scheme, while an allowlist rejects anything unanticipated by default. The `try`/`catch` turns genuinely unparseable input such as `"http://["` into a safe `"#"` rather than an exception. Note what `":::"` does, though: because a **base** is supplied, it resolves as a *relative path* on your own origin rather than throwing — safe, but a reminder that the `catch` fires rarely and the **allowlist** is what actually does the work. An unlisted scheme like `ftp:` parses perfectly and is rejected by the allowlist alone.

tests.name: resolves odd input as a relative path
