interview:iv-async-await-ordering-output.shortAnswer: `1`, `2`, `3`, `4`. An `async` function body runs synchronously up to its first `await`. The `await` then suspends the function and schedules the remainder as a microtask, so `3` prints before the continuation resumes with `4`.
deepAnswer: `console.log(1)` runs. Then `run()` is called — and this is the key point — **the body starts executing immediately and synchronously**, so `console.log(2)` runs before `run()` returns anything.
At `await Promise.resolve()`, the function suspends. Everything after the `await` is packaged as a continuation and scheduled as a **microtask**. `run()` returns a pending promise at this moment.
Control returns to the caller, so `console.log(3)` runs, completing the synchronous phase.
The stack empties, the microtask queue drains, the continuation resumes, and `4` prints.

The mental model that makes every question of this shape tractable: **an `async` function is synchronous until its first `await`, and everything after each `await` is a microtask.** Awaiting an already-resolved promise still yields — it does not continue inline.

A precise detail worth knowing for harder variants: `await somePromise` on a native promise costs one microtask tick, but `await` on a **thenable** (an object with a `.then`) costs extra ticks because the promise machinery has to adopt it. That is why cross-chain ordering puzzles sometimes have surprising answers, and why relying on exact interleaving between independent chains is fragile.

interview:iv-async-loop-ordering-output.shortAnswer: `sync`, then both promises, then both timeouts. The loop only **schedules**; nothing async runs during it. Then the whole microtask queue drains (both promise callbacks) before the event loop takes any timer.
deepAnswer: The loop body runs twice synchronously, scheduling two macrotasks and two microtasks. Neither callback executes during the loop.
`console.log("sync")` completes the synchronous phase.
The stack empties. The event loop drains the **entire** microtask queue: `promise 1`, then `promise 2` in the order they were queued.
Only then does it take macrotasks, one per cycle: `timeout 1`, then `timeout 2`.

The tempting wrong answer is the interleaved one — `promise 1, timeout 1, promise 2, timeout 2` — which assumes the two queues alternate. They do not: microtasks are drained **exhaustively** before a single macrotask runs.

`let i` also matters here: each iteration gets a fresh binding, so the callbacks capture 1 and 2. With `var` all four callbacks would print 3, which is a natural follow-up combining this with the closure question.

interview:iv-async-promise-states.shortAnswer: Pending, fulfilled or rejected. "Settled" means fulfilled **or** rejected — no longer pending. A promise settles exactly once and is immutable thereafter; later `resolve` or `reject` calls are ignored.
deepAnswer: A promise starts **pending**. It transitions once, to either **fulfilled** (with a value) or **rejected** (with a reason). **Settled** is the umbrella term for "fulfilled or rejected" — it is not a fourth state, and using it precisely is a small signal of care.

The transition is **one-way and single-shot**. Once settled, the state and value are fixed. Calling `resolve()` twice, or `reject()` after `resolve()`, has no effect — which is exactly what makes promise-based race conditions safe: whichever settles first wins and the rest are silently ignored.
That immutability is why `Promise.race` works, why a timeout wrapper is safe, and why a late-arriving response cannot overwrite an earlier settlement.

**Resolved is not the same as fulfilled**, and this catches people. A promise can be **resolved to another promise**, meaning it has locked onto that promise's eventual outcome but is still pending until the inner one settles. So "resolved" describes the resolution mechanism; "fulfilled" describes the successful outcome.

Attaching a `.then` to an already-settled promise still schedules the callback as a microtask — it never runs synchronously. That guarantee of asynchrony is deliberate: it means callback timing does not depend on whether the promise happened to settle before you attached the handler.

"Settled" = fulfilled or rejected, not a separate state
Transitions once and is then immutable — later calls are ignored
That immutability makes `race` and timeout wrappers safe
"Resolved" ≠ "fulfilled" — a promise can be resolved to another pending promise
`.then` on a settled promise still defers to a microtask

interview:iv-async-promise-combinators.shortAnswer: `all`: all succeed or reject on the first failure. `allSettled`: never rejects, reports every outcome. `race`: settles as the first promise settles, success **or** failure. `any`: first **success**, rejecting with an `AggregateError` only if all fail.
deepAnswer: **`Promise.all`** — fulfils with an array of results in input order, or rejects immediately with the first rejection. Use it when you need everything and any failure makes the whole operation pointless. The trap: a single failure discards the successful results too.

**`Promise.allSettled`** — never rejects. Fulfils with one descriptor per input: `{ status: "fulfilled", value }` or `{ status: "rejected", reason }`. Use it when partial success is useful and you want to report exactly what failed. This is usually the right choice for a dashboard of independent widgets.

**`Promise.race`** — settles as soon as **any** input settles, whether that is a fulfilment or a rejection. The classic use is a timeout: race the real work against a promise that rejects after N milliseconds. The subtlety is that a fast **rejection** wins too, which is sometimes not what people expect.

**`Promise.any`** — fulfils with the first **fulfilment**, ignoring rejections. It rejects only if every input rejects, and then with an `AggregateError` whose `errors` array holds all the reasons. Use it for redundant sources where you want whichever responds successfully first.

The two axes that organise all four: **all versus first**, and **does a rejection count**. `all`/`allSettled` wait for everything; `race`/`any` settle early. `all` and `race` treat rejection as a settlement; `allSettled` and `any` are tolerant of failure.

A shared caveat worth raising: none of them **cancels** the other operations. `race` losing does not stop the slower request — it keeps running and consuming a connection. Real cancellation needs `AbortController` threaded through.
keyPoints: `all`: everything, fails fast, discards successes on failure
`allSettled`: never rejects, one descriptor per input
`race`: first to settle, success or failure
`any`: first success; `AggregateError` only if all fail
Axes: all-vs-first, and whether rejection counts as settling
None of them cancels the losing operations

Assuming a lost `race` cancels the slower request.

interview:iv-async-fetch-404.shortAnswer: `fetch` rejects only when the request itself could not be made — network failure, DNS, CORS block. A 404 or 500 is a **successful HTTP exchange** that returned an error status, so the promise fulfils. You must check `response.ok` explicitly.
deepAnswer: This is the most commonly misunderstood part of `fetch`, and it is deliberate design: `fetch` models "did the HTTP transaction complete", not "was the server happy".

`fetch` **rejects** for: network unreachable, DNS failure, connection refused, a CORS preflight failure, or an aborted request. It **fulfils** for every response that arrives, including 404, 401 and 500.

So on a 404 the `await fetch(url)` succeeds. Execution proceeds to `response.json()`, which typically throws a `SyntaxError` because the error page is HTML rather than JSON — meaning you **do** end up in the `catch`, but with a misleading "Unexpected token < in JSON" message instead of "not found". That misdirection is what makes this bug expensive to debug.
**The fix** is an explicit status check before parsing:

A production client should distinguish three failure kinds — network, HTTP status, and parse — because callers respond differently to each: retry a network blip, show "not found" for a 404, and report a bug for malformed JSON. Attaching the original as `cause` preserves the detail while keeping the classification useful.
Worth noting `response.ok` is simply `status >= 200 && status < 300`, and that a redirect is followed transparently by default so you rarely see a 3xx.
keyPoints: `fetch` rejects only on network/CORS/abort failures, not HTTP error statuses
A 404 fulfils; `response.ok` must be checked explicitly
Parsing an HTML error page produces a misleading `SyntaxError`
`response.ok` is `status >= 200 && status < 300`
Distinguish network, HTTP and parse failures — callers handle them differently
commonMistakes: Believing `fetch` rejects on 4xx/5xx.
Catching the resulting JSON `SyntaxError` and reporting it as a parse bug rather than a 404.

interview:iv-async-foreach-debug.shortAnswer: `forEach` ignores the promise each async callback returns, so it starts them all and returns immediately. Nothing awaits them. Use `for...of` with `await` for sequential, or `Promise.all(users.map(...))` for concurrent.
deepAnswer: An `async` callback returns a promise. `forEach` has no concept of promises — it calls the callback and discards the return value. So `saveAll` fires every `save` and reaches `console.log("done")` while all of them are still pending.

Two further consequences worth naming. First, **errors are unhandled**: a rejection inside one of those discarded promises becomes an unhandled rejection rather than something `saveAll`'s caller can catch. Second, the function's own returned promise resolves before the work finishes, so any caller awaiting `saveAll` is misled.
**Sequential fix** — when order matters or you must not overwhelm the target:
**Concurrent fix** — when the operations are independent:

The choice is a real trade-off. `Promise.all` is much faster for independent work but fires every request at once, which can rate-limit you or exhaust connections. For a large list, a bounded-concurrency helper — running at most N at a time — is the production answer.

`await` inside `for...of` is one of the few places awaiting in a loop is correct rather than a mistake, because serialising is the explicit intent. Linters that flag `no-await-in-loop` are worth overriding here with a comment saying why.

Nothing awaits the work; `done` logs immediately
Rejections become unhandled rather than catchable
Sequential: `for...of` + `await`. Concurrent: `Promise.all(map(...))`
For large lists, bound the concurrency rather than firing everything

interview:iv-async-missing-return-debug.shortAnswer: The inner `fetchPosts` promise is never returned, so the outer chain does not wait for it. `user` is returned with `posts` still undefined, and any error from `fetchPosts` is unhandled. Return the inner promise from the `.then`.
deepAnswer: A `.then` callback links the next step to whatever it **returns**. Returning a promise makes the chain adopt it and wait; returning a plain value settles immediately with that value.

Here the inner `fetchPosts(...).then(...)` is created and left dangling. The callback returns `user` right away, so the outer promise resolves before the posts arrive. The assignment `user.posts = posts` does eventually happen — but after the caller already received the object, so it is a race the caller cannot see.

That also makes the bug **intermittent**, which is the worst kind: on a fast connection the assignment may land before the caller reads it, so it appears to work in development and fails in production.
**Two independent problems** follow from the same missing `return`: the ordering bug, and the fact that a rejection from `fetchPosts` has no handler and becomes an unhandled rejection.
**Fixes.** Return the inner chain: `return fetchPosts(user.id).then((posts) => ({ ...user, posts }));`. Or rewrite with `async`/`await`, where the mistake is much harder to make:
Note the version above also avoids mutating `user` in place, which was a second smell in the original.
**The general rule**: in a `.then` callback, either return the promise or explicitly handle it. A promise you neither return nor `catch` is almost always a bug.

The dangling inner promise makes the resolution order a race
Fails intermittently — often works locally, breaks under latency
A rejection from the inner promise is also unhandled
`async`/`await` makes this class of mistake much harder to write

interview:iv-async-sequential-vs-paralle.shortAnswer: The two requests are independent but run sequentially — the total time is the sum rather than the maximum. Start both before awaiting either, or use `Promise.all`, and the page loads in the time of the slower one.
deepAnswer: `await fetchUser()` suspends until it completes, and only then is `fetchStats()` even **called**. Since neither depends on the other, that serialisation is pure waste: 300ms plus 400ms is 700ms where 400ms was achievable.
**Fix with `Promise.all`:**
This works because `fetchUser()` and `fetchStats()` are both **invoked** before `Promise.all` awaits anything — the requests are already in flight.

The equivalent explicit form makes that clearer: `const userPromise = fetchUser(); const statsPromise = fetchStats(); const user = await userPromise; const stats = await statsPromise;`. Starting both, then awaiting, is the actual technique; `Promise.all` is the tidy expression of it.

**When sequential is correct**: if the second call genuinely needs the first result — `fetchPosts(user.id)` — you have no choice. The question to ask of any `await` chain is "does this line need the previous line's value?" If not, it should not be waiting.

**The trade-off with `Promise.all`**: one failure rejects the whole thing and discards the successful result. For a dashboard where each panel can render independently, `Promise.allSettled` is often the better fit — you show the user what loaded and an error only in the panel that failed.

The requests are in flight because the functions are **called** first
Sequential is correct only when the second depends on the first
`allSettled` is often better than `all` for independent UI panels

interview:iv-async-error-handling.shortAnswer: `async`/`await` uses ordinary `try`/`catch`; chains use `.catch()`. The differences that matter: a `.catch()` placed before a `.then` will not catch that `.then`'s error, and a synchronous throw inside a promise executor is caught by the chain while one before the chain starts is not.
deepAnswer: **With `await`**, a rejected promise throws at the `await`, so a normal `try`/`catch` works and the code reads like synchronous error handling. That readability is the main argument for `await` over chains.

**With chains**, `.catch(fn)` handles a rejection from anything **earlier** in the chain. Position matters: `.catch().then()` will not catch a rejection produced by that trailing `.then`. Putting the `.catch` last is the usual correct placement.

**`.then(onFulfilled, onRejected)`** takes a second argument that handles rejection from **preceding** steps only — it will not catch an error thrown by its own `onFulfilled`. `.catch()` after it will. That distinction is a genuine interview differentiator.
**`finally`** runs on both paths and passes the value or reason through untouched — useful for hiding a spinner. It does not swallow the rejection.

**Common failure modes**: an over-broad `try` block that wraps rendering logic as well as the request, so a rendering bug is reported as a network failure; catching and logging without rethrowing, which hides the failure from the caller; and forgetting that `catch (error)` may receive a non-`Error` value, since anything can be thrown or rejected with.

**Unhandled rejections** are worth mentioning: a promise that rejects with no handler triggers `unhandledrejection` in browsers and can crash a Node process. Wiring a global handler for reporting is standard practice, but it is a safety net, not a substitute for handling.

`.catch()` only catches rejections from earlier in the chain
`.then(onFulfilled, onRejected)` does not catch its own `onFulfilled` errors
`finally` runs either way and passes the outcome through
Do not wrap unrelated logic in the same `try`
A caught value is not guaranteed to be an `Error`

interview:iv-async-timeout-coding.shortAnswer: Race the real promise against one that rejects after `ms`. Clear the timer in a `finally` so a fast success does not leave it pending. The key limitation: this **ignores** the slow operation, it does not cancel it — the request keeps running.
deepAnswer: **Approach.** Build a promise that rejects on a timer, race it against the real one. Because a promise settles only once, whichever finishes first wins and the loser is silently ignored — that immutability is what makes the race safe.

**Clearing the timer matters.** Without `clearTimeout`, a fast success still leaves a pending timer; in Node that can keep the process alive, and in a browser it is a small leak repeated on every call. `finally` is the right place because it runs on both the success and failure paths.

**The real limitation**, and the thing to volunteer unprompted: this does not cancel anything. The underlying `fetch` or database query keeps running, holding its connection, and its result is simply discarded. For a slow endpoint under load, timing out and retrying can make the problem **worse** by multiplying in-flight work.

**Actual cancellation** requires `AbortController`: create one, pass `controller.signal` into `fetch`, and call `controller.abort()` when the timer fires. That genuinely terminates the request. `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` now provides this directly for fetch.

**Edge cases** to mention: a rejection from the real promise should propagate as itself, not be masked by the timeout error; and the error type should be distinguishable so callers can retry a timeout differently from a 500.

**Testing**: inject the scheduler rather than calling `setTimeout` directly, so tests drive the clock instead of sleeping — otherwise every timeout test costs real seconds and becomes flaky under CI load.

Clear the timer in `finally` to avoid a pending timer on fast success
It ignores the slow work — it does not cancel it
`AbortController` / `AbortSignal.timeout` gives real cancellation
Inject the scheduler so tests do not sleep

Forgetting to clear the timer.

interview:iv-async-retry-coding.shortAnswer: Loop over attempts with `try`/`catch`, waiting between tries with increasing backoff. Crucially, do **not** retry non-transient failures — a 400, a validation error or a 401 will fail identically every time, so retrying wastes time and hides the real problem.
deepAnswer: **Approach.** A counted loop, returning on success and catching to decide whether to try again. `return await task()` inside the `try` is deliberate — writing `return task()` would return the promise without awaiting it there, so a rejection would escape the `try` and never be retried.

**What not to retry** is the part that separates a thoughtful answer. Retry **transient** failures: network errors, timeouts, 429, 502/503/504. Do **not** retry deterministic ones: 400 (bad request), 401/403 (auth), 404, or a validation error — the same request will fail the same way, so retrying just delays the error report by several seconds.

**Backoff.** Retrying immediately hammers a struggling service. Exponential backoff — 100ms, 200ms, 400ms — gives it room to recover. Add **jitter** (randomising the delay) so that many clients failing simultaneously do not retry in lockstep and create a thundering herd. Mentioning jitter is a strong signal.

**Idempotency.** Only retry operations that are safe to repeat. Retrying a GET is fine; retrying a POST that creates an order may create two. Either restrict retries to idempotent methods or use an idempotency key so the server can deduplicate.

**Injection for testing.** `wait` is a parameter rather than a hardcoded `setTimeout`, so tests can pass an instant fake and still assert that the delays **increase** — verifying the backoff policy without waiting seconds.
**Edge cases**: `attempts` counts the initial call, so `attempts: 3` means one try plus two retries; no wait happens after the final failure; and the last error is what propagates.
keyPoints: `return await task()` inside the `try`, or rejections escape it
Retry transient failures only: network, timeout, 429, 5xx
Never retry 400/401/403/404 or validation errors
Exponential backoff plus jitter to avoid a thundering herd
Only retry idempotent operations, or use an idempotency key
Inject `wait` so backoff is testable without sleeping
commonMistakes: Retrying every error indiscriminately.
Omitting jitter and creating synchronised retry storms.
Retrying a non-idempotent POST.

interview:iv-async-race-condition-scenar.shortAnswer: An earlier, slower request resolves after a later, faster one and overwrites the fresher results. Fix by tagging each request and ignoring any response that is not the most recent — or by aborting the previous request with `AbortController`.
deepAnswer: **The mechanism.** The user types "a", firing request A. They type "ab", firing request B. If A is slower — different server load, a cold cache, an unlucky route — it resolves **after** B, and the naive `setResults(response)` overwrites B's correct results with A's stale ones. The UI then shows results for a query that is no longer in the box.
It is invisible locally, where every request takes 5ms, and constant on real networks. That asymmetry is why it survives into production.
**Fix 1 — sequence tagging.** Keep an incrementing counter; capture its value per request; before applying a response, check it is still the latest:
Simple, robust, and it does not require the request layer to support cancellation.
**Fix 2 — `AbortController`.** Abort the previous request before starting a new one and pass the signal to `fetch`. This also stops wasted network work, which sequence tagging does not.

**Related but different concerns** worth separating clearly, because interviewers probe whether you conflate them: **debounce** reduces how many requests are fired but does not order them; **caching** avoids repeating an identical query; **deduplication** shares one in-flight request between concurrent identical callers. A production search box wants debounce **and** race protection — they solve different problems.

**Testing it**: give the mock client an artificial variable delay so the earlier request resolves last, then assert the displayed results match the final query. Without a variable delay the test cannot reproduce the bug at all.
keyPoints: An older slow response overwrites a newer fast one
Invisible in local development, common on real networks
Fix: tag requests and ignore non-latest responses
Or `AbortController`, which also stops the wasted work
Debounce, caching and dedup solve different problems — not this one
Test with variable mock latency so the race is reproducible

interview:iv-async-microtask-starvation.shortAnswer: The event loop drains the microtask queue **completely** before doing anything else — including rendering and taking the next task. A microtask that queues another microtask never lets the queue empty, so the loop never proceeds. A `setTimeout` chain yields between every callback.
deepAnswer: The loop's contract is: drain microtasks **exhaustively**, then take **one** macrotask, then drain microtasks again. Rendering happens between macrotasks, not during a microtask drain.

So `function loop() { Promise.resolve().then(loop); }` produces a queue that is never empty. The loop cannot move on to a macrotask, cannot render, and cannot process input. The tab freezes even though no individual callback is slow.

By contrast `function loop() { setTimeout(loop, 0); }` queues one **macrotask** per iteration. The loop takes one, drains microtasks, renders if needed, and takes the next. The page stays responsive — it burns CPU, but it does not block.

The practical lesson is about **chunking long work**. Splitting a long computation across `await Promise.resolve()` boundaries does **not** let the browser render, because those are microtasks. To actually yield to the browser you need a macrotask (`setTimeout`, `MessageChannel`) or `scheduler.yield()` where available.

This is exactly the mechanism behind cooperative time-slicing schedulers: run work until a time budget is exhausted, then yield via a macrotask so the browser can paint and handle input, then continue.
It also explains why `queueMicrotask` is the right tool for "run right after this synchronous block, before anything else" and the wrong tool for "let the UI breathe".

A self-queueing microtask never lets the queue empty — the loop stalls
A `setTimeout` chain yields between callbacks, so the page stays responsive
Awaiting a resolved promise does **not** yield to the renderer
To yield for painting, use a macrotask or `scheduler.yield()`

interview:iv-async-generators-async-iter.shortAnswer: They let you consume an asynchronous sequence — paginated API results, a stream — with ordinary loop syntax, pulling the next chunk only when the consumer asks for it. That laziness is the point: nothing is fetched ahead of demand.
deepAnswer: An `async function*` can both `await` inside and `yield` out. `for await...of` drives it, awaiting each value before running the loop body.

The canonical use is **pagination**. Without it, callers deal with cursors and page loops themselves. With it, the generator hides the paging entirely and the caller writes an ordinary loop over **items** — the abstraction the caller actually wants.

**Laziness is the real benefit.** The generator suspends at each `yield`, so the next page is requested only when the consumer has exhausted the current one and asks for more. A consumer that `break`s after three items never triggers a second page fetch. An eager "fetch all pages then return an array" implementation cannot do that, and on a large dataset the difference is between a fast partial read and downloading everything.
It also gives natural **backpressure**: production is driven by consumption, so a slow consumer does not cause unbounded buffering.
Errors need no special handling — a rejected `await` inside the generator propagates out to the consumer's `for await` loop, where a normal `try`/`catch` works.

**Caveat worth raising**: `for await...of` processes items strictly one at a time. If the per-item work is independent and slow, that serialisation may be exactly what you do **not** want, and a bounded-concurrency approach fits better. Async iteration is about ordered, lazy consumption, not throughput.

Hides pagination behind an ordinary item-level loop
Lazy: the next page is fetched only when demanded
Provides natural backpressure
Errors propagate to the consumer's `try`/`catch`
Processes serially — not a throughput tool

interview:iv-async-callback-hell.shortAnswer: Beyond flattening nesting: guaranteed single settlement, guaranteed asynchronous callback timing, composable error propagation through a chain, a first-class value you can pass around and combine, and combinators like `all` and `race` that callbacks have no equivalent for.
deepAnswer: "Callback hell" is the visible symptom people cite, but the deeper problems are about **guarantees**.

**Single settlement.** A callback API can invoke your callback twice, or zero times, and nothing prevents it. A promise settles exactly once and is then immutable — so double-callback bugs, which are genuinely hard to diagnose, cannot happen.

**Consistent timing.** A callback might fire synchronously on a cache hit and asynchronously on a miss, meaning the caller's code runs in a different order depending on data. That "releasing Zalgo" inconsistency causes subtle bugs. Promise callbacks are **always** asynchronous, even on an already-settled promise.

**Error propagation.** With callbacks, every level must check `err` and forward it manually; one missed check swallows the failure. A promise rejection propagates down the chain automatically to the nearest handler, and a `throw` inside any `.then` becomes a rejection.

**First-class value.** A promise can be stored, returned, passed, and awaited by several consumers. A callback is a one-shot arrangement between exactly two parties. That is what makes deduplication — several callers sharing one in-flight request — trivially expressible with promises and awkward with callbacks.

**Composition.** `Promise.all`, `race`, `any` and `allSettled` express multi-operation coordination declaratively. Doing that with callbacks means hand-written counters and flags, which is where the real bugs live.

The honest caveat: promises are single-value and not cancellable by design. For streams of values you want async iterators or an event/observable model, and for cancellation you need `AbortController` — promises alone do not provide it.
keyPoints: Guaranteed single settlement — no double-callback bugs
Callbacks always async, so timing does not vary with cache state
Automatic error propagation down the chain
A first-class value: storable, shareable, awaitable by many
Combinators (`all`, `race`, `any`) have no clean callback equivalent
Not a solution for streams or cancellation

Claiming promises are cancellable.

interview:iv-async-await-in-loop-output.shortAnswer: `start 1 | start 2 | end 1 | end 2`, then `1,2`. `map` calls `work` for every element synchronously, so both functions run to their first `await` before either resumes. The continuations then run in the order they were queued.
deepAnswer: `map(work)` invokes `work(1)` and `work(2)` synchronously, one after the other. Each runs its body until the first `await`, so `start 1` and `start 2` are pushed before anything resumes.
Each `await Promise.resolve()` queues its continuation as a microtask. They were queued in call order, so the drain runs them in that order: `end 1`, then `end 2`.
Hence the interleaving `start 1 | start 2 | end 1 | end 2` — which demonstrates the operations genuinely overlap rather than running one after the other.

`Promise.all` preserves **input order** in its results regardless of completion order, so `results` is `[1, 2]`. That guarantee is worth stating explicitly — it is a common point of confusion, and it holds even when the promises settle out of order.

The contrast to draw: `for (const n of [1,2]) { await work(n); }` would give `start 1 | end 1 | start 2 | end 2` — genuinely sequential. `map` plus `Promise.all` is concurrent; `for...of` with `await` is sequential. Knowing which you want, and being able to show the difference in output, is the substance of this question.
keyPoints: `map` invokes every async callback synchronously up to its first `await`
Continuations resume in the order they were queued
The interleaving proves the work overlaps
`Promise.all` returns results in **input** order, not completion order
`for...of` + `await` would serialise instead
commonMistakes: Expecting `map` with async callbacks to serialise.
Assuming `Promise.all` returns results in completion order.

interview:iv-bp-target-vs-currenttarget.shortAnswer: `target` is the deepest element where the event originated. `currentTarget` is the element whose listener is currently running. They are the same for a direct listener and differ whenever the event has bubbled — which is exactly the case delegation relies on.
deepAnswer: Click an icon inside a button inside a list item, with the listener on the list. `event.target` is the icon — the deepest element under the pointer. `event.currentTarget` is the list, because that is where this listener is attached.

The distinction matters most for delegated handlers. Using `currentTarget` there always gives you the container, which tells you nothing about which row was clicked. Using raw `target` gives you whatever inner element happened to be hit, which may be an icon or a text node's parent rather than the control you care about.

A practical detail: `currentTarget` is only valid **during** dispatch. Reading it later — inside a `setTimeout`, or after an `await` in an async handler — gives `null`, because the browser clears it once dispatch finishes. Capture what you need synchronously.

`this` inside a non-arrow listener equals `currentTarget`, which is a small argument for `function` handlers. An arrow handler has no such binding, so `currentTarget` is the explicit way to get it either way.

Related properties worth knowing: `relatedTarget` (the element being left or entered on `mouseover`/`focusin`), and `composedPath()`, which gives the full path including nodes inside a shadow root that `target` deliberately hides.
keyPoints: `target` = where it originated; `currentTarget` = where the listener is attached
They differ only when the event has propagated
Delegation should use `target.closest(selector)`, not either one raw
`currentTarget` is `null` after dispatch ends — capture it synchronously
`this` in a non-arrow listener equals `currentTarget`
`composedPath()` reveals the path through shadow DOM

interview:iv-bp-prevent-vs-stop.shortAnswer: `preventDefault` cancels the browser's built-in action but lets the event keep travelling. `stopPropagation` stops the event reaching further elements but lets the default action happen. `stopImmediatePropagation` additionally stops other listeners on the **same** element. They are independent — neither implies the other.
deepAnswer: **`preventDefault()`** cancels the default behaviour: navigating a link, submitting a form, checking a checkbox, showing the context menu. The event continues to propagate normally, so other listeners still run and can still see that it was cancelled via `event.defaultPrevented`.
**`stopPropagation()`** halts travel through the tree. Ancestor listeners never fire. The default action still happens — a link with only `stopPropagation` still navigates, which surprises people.

**`stopImmediatePropagation()`** does that and also prevents any remaining listeners on the same element from running, in registration order. Useful when one handler must be authoritative; also a good way to create bugs that are very hard to find, since another team's listener simply stops firing with no error.

The default-action nuance: `preventDefault` only works if the event is cancelable (`event.cancelable`). `scroll` is not cancelable, and a `touchstart` listener registered as `{ passive: true }` cannot cancel — the browser assumes it will not, which is what lets scrolling start without waiting for JavaScript. Chrome makes wheel and touch listeners on the document passive by default for that reason.

`stopPropagation` is overused. It is a local fix with global consequences: any delegated handler higher up — analytics, a click-outside-to-close dropdown, a framework's root listener — silently stops receiving events. Prefer a condition in the outer handler over stopping the event at the source.

Two more details: returning `false` from a jQuery handler did both `preventDefault` and `stopPropagation`, which is a common source of confusion when people carry the habit into plain DOM code, where returning `false` only cancels the default in inline `on*` attributes. And a form's submit handler must `preventDefault` **before** any `await`, because the default action is decided synchronously during dispatch.
keyPoints: `preventDefault`: cancel the built-in action, keep propagating
`stopPropagation`: stop travelling, keep the default action
`stopImmediatePropagation`: also stop other listeners on the same element
Only cancelable events can be prevented; passive listeners cannot cancel
`stopPropagation` silently breaks delegated handlers higher up
Call `preventDefault` before any `await` in the handler

Reaching for `stopPropagation` instead of a condition in the outer handler.

interview:iv-bp-live-collections.shortAnswer: `getElementsByClassName` and `getElementsByTagName` return **live** `HTMLCollection`s that update as the DOM changes. Removing elements while iterating forwards shrinks the collection underneath the loop, so elements get skipped. `querySelectorAll` returns a static `NodeList` and does not have this problem.
deepAnswer: A live collection is a query, not a snapshot. It re-reflects the document whenever it is read, so adding or removing matching elements changes its `length` immediately.

The fixes: take a snapshot with `[...items]` or `Array.from(items)` before looping; iterate backwards; or use `querySelectorAll`, which returns a static `NodeList` that is unaffected by later DOM changes.

`NodeList` from `querySelectorAll` has `forEach` but not `map`, `filter` or `reduce` — it is array-**like**, not an array. Spread it when you want array methods. `HTMLCollection` has no iteration methods at all, only indexing and `length`, though it is iterable with `for...of`.

Liveness is occasionally useful — `document.forms`, `document.images` and `element.children` are live, and a live collection is genuinely convenient when you want a continuously accurate count. But as a default it surprises people, which is why `querySelectorAll` is the modern choice.

Performance is the other side: `getElementById` and `getElementsByClassName` are highly optimised, while `querySelectorAll` parses a selector and builds a snapshot. In a hot loop that is measurable — but the correct move is to hoist the query out of the loop rather than to choose the API by micro-benchmark.
keyPoints: `getElementsBy*` return live `HTMLCollection`s; `querySelectorAll` returns a static `NodeList`
Removing while iterating a live collection skips elements
Snapshot with `[...items]`, iterate backwards, or use `querySelectorAll`
`NodeList` has `forEach` only; `HTMLCollection` has no array methods
`document.forms`, `element.children` are live too

interview:iv-bp-attributes-vs-properties.shortAnswer: Attributes are the values written in the markup and are always strings; properties live on the DOM object and have real types. They are initialised from attributes, but for form controls the property tracks the **current** state while the attribute keeps the original — which is why `value` and `checked` behave the way they do.
deepAnswer: At parse time the browser creates a property for each recognised attribute. `<input value="ada">` gives `input.getAttribute("value") === "ada"` and `input.value === "ada"`.

Once the user types, they diverge: `input.value` becomes what is in the field now, while `getAttribute("value")` still returns `"ada"` — it is the **default** value, which is exactly what a form reset restores. The same holds for `checked` (property = current state, attribute = default) and `selected`.
So for reading what the user actually entered, always use the **property**. Reading `getAttribute("value")` is the classic bug behind "my form always submits the initial value".

Types differ too. Properties are properly typed: `input.checked` is a boolean, `a.href` is the resolved absolute URL, `input.valueAsNumber` is a number. Attributes are strings, so `getAttribute("checked")` returns `""` for a present boolean attribute and `null` when absent — never `false`.

Names occasionally differ where the attribute collides with a reserved word: the `class` attribute is the `className` property, and `for` on a label is `htmlFor`. `classList` is the better API for classes in either case.

Custom attributes have no matching property, which is why `data-*` exists: `<li data-id="7">` is readable as `li.dataset.id`, with the kebab-case name converted to camelCase. That is the right channel for attaching your own data to an element.

A useful consequence: because `href` resolves relatively, `link.href` gives an absolute URL while `link.getAttribute("href")` gives exactly the string in the markup. Which one you want depends on whether you are comparing or reproducing.
keyPoints: Attributes are markup strings; properties are typed values on the DOM object
For form controls the property is current state, the attribute is the default
Read user input from the property, never from `getAttribute`
`getAttribute("checked")` returns `""` or `null`, never a boolean
`class` → `className`, `for` → `htmlFor`; prefer `classList`
Custom data belongs in `data-*`, read via `dataset`

interview:iv-bp-observers.shortAnswer: They are push-based replacements for polling. `IntersectionObserver` reports when an element enters or leaves the viewport, `ResizeObserver` reports element size changes, and `MutationObserver` reports DOM changes. All three run off the main thread's hot path and avoid the forced layout that manual polling causes.
deepAnswer: **`ResizeObserver`** — an element changing size for any reason, not just a window resize. A `window.resize` listener misses size changes caused by content, a sibling collapsing, or a CSS container query, which is exactly why this API exists. It is the correct tool for responsive components that must react to their own box rather than the viewport.

**`MutationObserver`** — reacting to DOM changes you do not control: a third-party widget injecting content, or an integration with code you cannot modify. In your own application it is usually a smell, because you already know when you changed the DOM. It is also the API that replaced the deprecated and catastrophically slow mutation events.

All three batch their callbacks and deliver them asynchronously, so a burst of changes produces one callback with many entries rather than one callback each. That batching is most of the performance benefit.
All three need cleanup: `disconnect()` when the component goes away, or `unobserve(el)` for a single target. An observer holding element references is the same leak shape as an unremoved listener.

A detail people miss: `IntersectionObserver` fires once on observe with the current state, so you get an initial reading without a scroll. And `ResizeObserver` callbacks that resize the observed element can loop — the browser detects this and logs "loop limit exceeded" rather than hanging, but the design is still wrong.
keyPoints: Push-based replacements for polling; no forced synchronous layout
`IntersectionObserver`: visibility, lazy loading, infinite scroll — use `rootMargin`
`ResizeObserver`: element size from any cause, which `window.resize` misses
`MutationObserver`: DOM you do not control; a smell inside your own app
Callbacks are batched and asynchronous
Always `disconnect()`/`unobserve` — observers retain their targets

interview:iv-bp-custom-events.shortAnswer: Dispatch a `CustomEvent` that carries data in `detail` and let interested parties listen. The DOM already provides a pub/sub system with bubbling, so a shared element — or a plain `EventTarget` used as a bus — avoids importing one component into the other.
deepAnswer: `detail` is the only place data belongs — it is the property the constructor is designed to carry, and it can hold any value including objects.
Namespacing the event type (`cart:add`, not `add`) prevents collisions with built-in events and with other features, and makes the source obvious when reading a listener.

For components with no common ancestor, a standalone bus works and needs no library: `const bus = new EventTarget()` supports `addEventListener` and `dispatchEvent` exactly like a DOM node, without being attached to the document.

The tradeoff to state honestly: events decouple the publisher from the subscriber, which is the point — but they also make control flow implicit. With more than a handful, "what happens when I click this?" becomes a search across the codebase. That is the same critique as a global event bus in any architecture.

When to prefer something else: parent-to-child is a direct method call or a property; child-to-parent is a callback passed in; genuinely shared application state belongs in a store, not in a stream of events. Custom events fit best for genuinely broadcast notifications with unknown or variable subscribers.

Two platform details: `dispatchEvent` is **synchronous** — every listener runs before the call returns, so a slow listener blocks the publisher. And for a custom event to escape a shadow root it needs `composed: true` as well as `bubbles: true`.
keyPoints: `CustomEvent` with data in `detail`; `bubbles: true` is not the default
Namespace the type to avoid collisions
`new EventTarget()` is a dependency-free bus for unrelated components
Events decouple but make control flow implicit — use them sparingly
Prefer props/callbacks for parent-child, a store for shared state
`dispatchEvent` is synchronous; `composed: true` to cross a shadow boundary
commonMistakes: Omitting `bubbles: true` and wondering why nothing listens.

interview:iv-bp-classlist.shortAnswer: Toggle a class with `classList` and keep the styling in CSS. Inline styles via `element.style` are for values that are genuinely dynamic and computed — a position, a percentage width — not for appearance that could be expressed as a state.
deepAnswer: `classList` gives `add`, `remove`, `toggle`, `contains` and `replace`, each operating on one class without disturbing the others. `element.className = "active"` replaces the entire attribute and silently destroys classes other code relies on.

`classList.toggle("open", isOpen)` with the second argument is worth knowing: it forces the class on or off rather than flipping it, which removes a whole category of state-drift bugs where the DOM and your variable disagree.

Keeping appearance in CSS means media queries, `prefers-reduced-motion`, `prefers-color-scheme`, hover and focus states, and the design system's tokens all keep working. Inline styles bypass all of it and are difficult to override because of their specificity.

Inline styles are right when the value cannot be known in advance: `el.style.transform = "translateX(" + x + "px)"` for a drag, or a computed bar width. Even then, a CSS custom property is often cleaner — `el.style.setProperty("--progress", pct)` — because the styling stays in the stylesheet and JavaScript only supplies a number.

For state, prefer semantic attributes over presentational classes where one exists: `aria-expanded`, `aria-selected`, `disabled`, `hidden`, or a `data-state`. CSS can select on them (`[aria-expanded="true"]`), and assistive technology gets the state for free instead of it being encoded only in a class name.
The performance footnote: batch class changes and avoid interleaving them with geometry reads, since each write invalidates layout and the next read forces a recalculation.
keyPoints: `classList` for state; keep the appearance in CSS
`className =` replaces every class — avoid it
`classList.toggle(name, force)` sets rather than flips
Inline styles for genuinely computed values; prefer CSS custom properties
Drive styling from `aria-*`/`data-*` state where one exists

interview:iv-bp-critical-path.shortAnswer: Parse HTML into the DOM, parse CSS into the CSSOM, combine them into a render tree, compute layout (geometry), paint (pixels), and composite layers. Scripts can block parsing and stylesheets block rendering, which is why script and style placement dominates first-paint time.
deepAnswer: **Parse** — the HTML is tokenised into the DOM incrementally, so the browser can start rendering before the document has fully arrived. A preload scanner runs ahead of the parser to start fetching subresources early.

**CSSOM** — stylesheets are parsed into a second tree. CSS is **render-blocking** by design: painting with incomplete styles would cause a flash of unstyled content, so the browser waits. This is why a stylesheet in `<head>` delays first paint and why inlining the critical subset helps.
**Render tree** — DOM plus CSSOM, containing only what will be displayed. `display: none` nodes are excluded entirely; `visibility: hidden` nodes are included, because they still occupy space.
**Layout (reflow)** — computing the geometry of every box. Cost scales with the number of elements, which is why very large DOMs are slow independently of any JavaScript.

**Paint** — filling in pixels, potentially onto several layers. **Composite** — assembling the layers, which the GPU can do. This is why animating `transform` and `opacity` is cheap: they skip layout and paint and only require a recomposite.

Where JavaScript intervenes: a synchronous `<script>` blocks parsing, and because a script might query styles, it also waits for any pending stylesheet — so a stylesheet above a script blocks that script too. `defer` and `type="module"` avoid the parser block entirely.

The practical levers follow directly from the sequence: inline critical CSS and defer the rest, `defer` your scripts, preload the LCP image, set explicit dimensions on images to avoid layout shift, and keep the DOM small. Each maps to a stage above rather than being a folk remedy.
keyPoints: DOM + CSSOM → render tree → layout → paint → composite
HTML parsing is incremental; a preload scanner fetches ahead
CSS is render-blocking by design to prevent unstyled flashes
A synchronous script blocks parsing and waits on pending stylesheets
`transform`/`opacity` changes skip layout and paint

interview:iv-as-timer-accuracy.shortAnswer: The delay is a **minimum**, not a guarantee. After it elapses the callback is queued, and it only runs when the call stack is empty and the event loop reaches it — so any long-running synchronous work delays it further. Browsers also clamp nested timers and throttle background tabs.
deepAnswer: `setTimeout` schedules; it does not preempt. Once the timer expires the callback becomes a macrotask, and it waits behind whatever is already running or queued. A 200ms synchronous loop means a 100ms timer fires at roughly 200ms.
The microtask queue drains completely before any macrotask, so a burst of promise reactions also delays a timer.

**Clamping**: after about five levels of nesting, browsers enforce a minimum of roughly 4ms, so `setTimeout(fn, 0)` in a recursive chain is not zero. Background tabs are throttled much harder — often to once per second, and in some cases far less — which is why a timer-based counter drifts badly if the user switches away.

Because of all that, never accumulate time by counting timer fires. Store a target timestamp and compute the remaining time from `Date.now()` on each tick; the display then stays correct regardless of how much drift occurred.

For animation, `requestAnimationFrame` is the right tool — it runs before the next paint, aligns with the display refresh rate, and pauses entirely in a background tab. Using a timer for animation produces uneven motion because timer fires and frames are not synchronised.
For precise elapsed-time measurement, use `performance.now()`: it is monotonic, sub-millisecond, and unaffected by the system clock being adjusted mid-measurement, which `Date.now()` is not.

The general point worth making in an interview: timing in a single-threaded environment is cooperative. A timer is a request to be run soon after a deadline, not an interrupt — nothing preempts running JavaScript.

Long synchronous work and microtask bursts both delay timers
Nested timers are clamped to ~4ms; background tabs are throttled hard
Derive elapsed time from a timestamp instead of counting fires
`requestAnimationFrame` for animation; `performance.now()` for measurement
Nothing preempts running JavaScript — timers are cooperative

interview:iv-as-unhandled-rejection.shortAnswer: A promise that rejects with no rejection handler attached by the time the microtask queue drains. The browser fires `unhandledrejection` and logs it; Node terminates the process by default. The fix is that every promise needs an owner that awaits it, catches it, or returns it to someone who will.
deepAnswer: The runtime tracks whether a rejected promise has a handler. If none is attached by the end of the current microtask checkpoint, it reports the rejection. Attaching a handler later still works functionally, but the warning has already fired.

The usual sources: calling an `async` function without awaiting or catching it ("floating promise"); a `.then` chain with no terminal `.catch`; a `forEach` with an `async` callback, which discards every promise it creates; and a promise created inside a `try`/`catch` but not awaited there, so the `catch` never sees it.

Node exits on an unhandled rejection by default, which is deliberate: an unknown failed operation means the process is in an undefined state. Browsers keep going but surface it in the console and on `window.onunhandledrejection`.

Deliberate fire-and-forget should be explicit. If you truly do not care about the result, write `void doThing().catch(reportOnly)` so the intent is visible and the rejection is still observed. Silence is what makes these bugs invisible.
`@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` catches the majority of these statically, and it is one of the highest-value lint rules for async-heavy code.
The counterpart worth knowing: `rejectionhandled` fires when a handler is attached to an already-reported rejection, which lets monitoring retract a false positive.
keyPoints: A rejection with no handler by the end of the microtask checkpoint
Node exits by default; browsers report on `unhandledrejection`
Sources: floating async calls, chains with no `.catch`, `forEach` with `async`
A global handler is for reporting, never for silently handling
Make fire-and-forget explicit with `void ...catch(report)`
Lint for floating promises

interview:iv-as-thenable.shortAnswer: It still works, and it still defers. `await` wraps the value with `Promise.resolve` semantics, so `await 42` yields `42` — but only after suspending the function and scheduling the continuation as a microtask. Anything with a callable `then` is treated as a promise.
deepAnswer: `await x` where `x` is a plain value resolves to `x`. The important part is that it is **not** a no-op: the function suspends and the rest of the body runs as a microtask, so code after the call site executes first.
This makes `await` safe in generic code — a function that may or may not return a promise can be awaited unconditionally, without a `typeof x.then === "function"` check.

A **thenable** is any object with a callable `then` method. The promise machinery duck-types: it calls `then(resolve, reject)` and adopts whatever that does. That is how promises from different libraries, or from another realm such as an iframe, interoperate with native ones. It is also why `instanceof Promise` is the wrong check — `typeof x?.then === "function"` is what the specification itself uses.

The sharp edge: an object that happens to have a `then` property becomes accidentally awaitable. Returning `{ then: "later" }` is fine because it is not callable, but a data object with a callable `then` will be treated as a promise and will hang or misbehave. It is rare, and memorable when it happens.
`await` on a rejected promise throws at that line, which is what makes `try`/`catch` work around asynchronous code — the mechanism is the same as a synchronous throw from the resumed continuation.

One micro-detail sometimes asked: awaiting a native promise takes fewer microtask ticks than awaiting a thenable, because a thenable must be assimilated through an extra job. It affects ordering puzzles, essentially never real code.

Safe to await anything, which helps generic code

interview:iv-as-setinterval-vs-recursive.shortAnswer: `setInterval` schedules by wall clock regardless of how long the work takes, so slow callbacks can queue up back to back. A recursive `setTimeout` schedules the next run only after the current one finishes, which guarantees a real gap between executions. For anything asynchronous, the recursive version is almost always correct.
deepAnswer: `setInterval(fn, 1000)` asks for a callback every second. If `fn` takes 1.5 seconds, the runtime does not skip — the callbacks queue, and once the stack clears they can run one immediately after another with no gap. The intent ("do this every second") becomes "do this constantly".

This is much worse when the callback is asynchronous. `setInterval(() => fetch(url), 1000)` starts a request every second regardless of whether the previous one has returned. On a slow connection you accumulate overlapping requests, and responses can arrive out of order.
`setInterval` remains fine for cheap synchronous work — updating a clock display, a progress animation — where the callback cannot outrun its period.
Neither is accurate over time: both drift, and both are throttled in background tabs. Derive displayed times from a timestamp rather than counting iterations.

For polling specifically, the production answer adds more: back off when the tab is hidden (`document.visibilityState`), back off after repeated failures, and stop entirely when the component unmounts. And consider whether polling is the right mechanism at all — server-sent events or a WebSocket push the data instead of asking repeatedly.
Whichever you use, keep the handle and clear it. An interval that outlives its component is one of the most common leaks in single-page applications.
keyPoints: `setInterval` schedules by clock and can queue callbacks back to back
With async work it starts overlapping operations
Recursive `setTimeout` schedules after completion — a guaranteed gap, one in flight
Use `finally` so a failure does not stop the loop
`setInterval` is fine for cheap synchronous updates
Back off when hidden or failing; consider SSE/WebSocket instead of polling
Always keep the handle and clear it on teardown
commonMistakes: Polling an API with `setInterval` and creating overlapping requests.

interview:iv-as-ui-states.shortAnswer: At minimum idle, loading, success, empty and error — and "empty" is the one most often forgotten, because a successful response with zero results is not the same as a failure. Beyond that: refetching while showing stale data, and partial failure.
deepAnswer: **Idle** — nothing requested yet. **Loading** — a request is in flight, with a skeleton or spinner. **Success with data** — render it. **Success with no data** — an explicit empty state explaining what would appear here and, ideally, how to get some. **Error** — what failed and a way to retry.

Conflating empty with error is the classic bug: a user with no orders sees "Something went wrong" and files a support ticket. Conflating empty with loading is the other half — a spinner that never resolves because the list is simply empty.

Modelling matters. Independent booleans (`isLoading`, `hasError`, `isEmpty`) permit impossible combinations — loading and error at once — and every render has to defend against them. A single discriminated status (`"idle" | "loading" | "success" | "error"`) makes the impossible states unrepresentable, which is the point.

Refetching is a separate state from initial loading. Replacing a populated list with a spinner on every refresh makes the UI flicker and feel slower than it is; keeping the stale data visible with a subtle indicator is what SWR-style caching does and why it feels fast.

Errors should distinguish what the user can act on. Offline and a 500 are both "try again"; a 403 is "you do not have access"; a 404 is a not-found state; a validation error belongs next to the field. One generic message for all of them wastes the information the server sent.

Two practical details: guard against showing a spinner for a 50ms response by delaying it slightly, which avoids a distracting flash; and make sure the states are announced to assistive technology with a live region, since a visual-only spinner tells a screen-reader user nothing.
Finally, the race: after any `await`, check the result is still the one wanted before rendering. A component that unmounted, or a newer request that superseded this one, must not write to the DOM.
keyPoints: Idle, loading, success-with-data, success-empty, error — empty is not error
Model one status value, not independent booleans
Refetching is distinct from initial load — keep stale data visible
Differentiate errors by what the user can do about them
Delay the spinner slightly; announce state changes to assistive technology
Re-check relevance after `await` before rendering

Using independent booleans that allow impossible combinations.

interview:iv-as-top-level-await.shortAnswer: Only in an ES module. Modules have an asynchronous evaluation model, so top-level `await` is legal there and makes the module's importers wait for it. In a classic script or a CommonJS module it is a syntax error, and the workaround is an immediately-invoked async function.
deepAnswer: ES modules are evaluated asynchronously by design — the loader already has to fetch and link dependencies before running them. Top-level `await` extends that: the module's evaluation simply does not complete until the awaited promise settles.

The consequence is that the wait propagates. Every module that imports it waits too, transitively up to the entry point. That is a real cost: a slow top-level fetch delays the entire dependency subtree, so it is appropriate for genuine initialisation — loading configuration, initialising a WASM module, choosing an implementation dynamically — and not for ordinary data fetching.

CommonJS cannot support it at all, because `require` is synchronous by definition — the module must be fully evaluated before `require` returns. This is one of the concrete, unbridgeable differences between the two systems.
A caveat worth raising: a cycle involving top-level `await` can deadlock, since two modules can each be waiting for the other to finish evaluating. It is another reason to avoid circular imports.
keyPoints: Legal only in ES modules; a `SyntaxError` in classic scripts
Module evaluation is already asynchronous, so it fits the model
Importers wait transitively — use it for initialisation, not data fetching
Pairs well with dynamic `import()` for choosing an implementation
CommonJS cannot support it because `require` is synchronous
A cycle plus top-level `await` can deadlock

Using it for per-request data fetching and delaying the whole app.

interview:iv-as-raf-ordering.shortAnswer: `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks run as part of the browser's rendering step, just before layout and paint, and at most once per frame. Microtasks still drain before them. Timers are ordinary macrotasks and are not tied to frames at all, which is why they are wrong for animation.
deepAnswer: A rough iteration of the loop: take one macrotask, drain the microtask queue completely, then — if the browser has decided to render this turn — run `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks, then style, layout, paint and composite.

The consequences follow from the position. `rAF` callbacks run immediately before layout, so DOM changes made there are painted in the same frame with no intermediate visual state. A timer, by contrast, may fire twice between paints or not at all before one, producing uneven motion.

`rAF` is throttled to the display refresh rate — usually 60Hz, but 120Hz on many modern displays, which is why animation should be driven by the elapsed time passed to the callback rather than by a fixed per-frame increment. It also stops entirely in a background tab, saving battery, whereas a timer keeps firing at a throttled rate.

Microtasks still take priority: a `Promise.resolve().then()` queued inside a `rAF` callback runs before the browser proceeds to layout. And a microtask that enqueues another microtask can starve rendering entirely, because the loop cannot reach the rendering step until the queue is empty.

The practical use beyond animation is batching DOM reads and writes. Doing all writes inside a single `rAF` callback groups them into one layout pass, which is why libraries schedule DOM updates there.

A related detail: reading a geometry property inside a `rAF` callback still forces layout at that moment, so the read/write separation matters there too — `rAF` schedules the work well, it does not make thrashing free.

`requestIdleCallback` sits at the opposite end: it runs only when the browser has spare time after rendering, making it right for genuinely deferrable work like prefetching or analytics flushing, and wrong for anything the user is waiting on.
keyPoints: Order: macrotask → all microtasks → `rAF` callbacks → style/layout/paint
`rAF` runs at most once per frame, before layout — no intermediate paint
Throttled to the refresh rate and paused in background tabs
Drive animation by elapsed time, not a fixed per-frame step
Microtask recursion can starve the rendering step entirely
Batch DOM writes in `rAF`; reads there still force layout
`requestIdleCallback` is for work the user is not waiting on
commonMistakes: Animating with `setInterval` and assuming frames align.
Assuming `rAF` outranks microtasks.
followUps: Why does a 120Hz display break fixed per-frame increments?

interview:iv-rt-browser-vs-node.shortAnswer: The language is the same; the host is different. The browser supplies the DOM, `window`, `fetch`, storage and a security sandbox tied to an origin. Node supplies the filesystem, processes, networking and `process`, with no DOM and no origin-based sandbox.
deepAnswer: The ECMAScript specification defines syntax, types, objects like `Array`, `Promise` and `Math`, and the job queue. Everything else is host-provided.

**Browser**: `document`, `window`, `localStorage`, `fetch`, `history`, `navigator`, the event loop with a rendering step, and a security model built on origins — same-origin policy, CORS, cookie rules. Code runs on someone else's machine and is fully visible to them.

**Node**: `fs`, `path`, `process`, `Buffer`, `http`, `child_process`, and access to the whole machine within the user's permissions. It also has extra event-loop phases and `process.nextTick`, which runs before promise microtasks — a Node-specific ordering that does not exist in browsers.
The **global object** differs: `window` in a browser, `global` in Node. `globalThis` works in both and is the portable way to reach it.

**Modules** are the practical friction. Browsers speak ESM natively; Node supports both ESM and CommonJS, decided by file extension and by `"type"` in `package.json`. `require` is synchronous and cannot load ESM directly, which is why the two systems interoperate awkwardly.

The consequences that matter day to day: environment variables and secrets are safe in Node and impossible to keep in a browser; the filesystem is available in Node and deliberately unavailable in the browser; and browser code must survive many different engines and versions while server code runs on the one you chose.

Other hosts exist and use the same split — Deno and Bun, Cloudflare Workers and other edge runtimes (a browser-like subset, no filesystem), Electron (both at once). WinterCG is the effort to standardise a common subset like `fetch` and `URL` across them, which is why modern Node has `fetch` built in.
keyPoints: Same language, different host-provided APIs
Browser: DOM, storage, origin-based security, a rendering step in the loop
Node: filesystem, processes, `Buffer`, extra loop phases, `process.nextTick`
`globalThis` is the portable global reference
ESM everywhere in browsers; ESM and CommonJS in Node, awkwardly
Secrets are safe server-side and impossible client-side

Assuming Node's microtask ordering matches the browser's.

interview:iv-rt-single-threaded.shortAnswer: One call stack, so exactly one piece of your code executes at a time and it runs to completion before anything else starts. That gives you freedom from data races, and the corresponding cost that any slow synchronous work freezes everything — including rendering and input.
deepAnswer: There is one call stack per execution context. A function runs, calls others, and returns; nothing else — no timer, no event handler, no promise reaction — can interleave into the middle of it. This is called run-to-completion.

The upside is substantial and worth naming: no locks, no mutexes, no deadlocks, and no torn reads. `count++` cannot be interrupted between the read and the write, which in a threaded language is a genuine hazard requiring synchronisation.

The cost is that everything shares that one thread — including rendering. A 500ms synchronous loop means 500ms with no paint, no scroll response and no click handling. The tab appears frozen because it is.

This is exactly why the asynchronous model exists. I/O is handed to the host, which does the waiting elsewhere, and only the **response handling** comes back to your thread. Without that, one slow request would block the page.

What is single-threaded is precisely **your JavaScript**. The browser is heavily multi-threaded — networking, parsing, compositing, and often a separate process per tab. `rAF` callbacks, layout and paint are coordinated with your thread but much of the work is not on it.
Web Workers add threads that run their own code with their own stack and loop, isolated by message passing. Because they share no mutable state by default, the no-data-races property survives.

The practical rule that falls out: keep every task short. Anything above roughly 50ms is a "long task" and is perceptible as unresponsiveness, so heavy work must be chunked with explicit yields or moved to a worker.
keyPoints: One call stack; run-to-completion, no interleaving
No locks, no deadlocks, no torn reads
Rendering shares the thread — slow synchronous code freezes the page
Asynchrony exists so waiting happens off-thread
The browser itself is multi-threaded; your JavaScript is not
Workers add threads, isolated by message passing
Keep tasks under ~50ms or the page feels unresponsive
commonMistakes: Thinking `async` functions run on another thread.
Assuming the browser as a whole is single-threaded.

interview:iv-rt-polyfill-transpile.shortAnswer: A transpiler rewrites **syntax** the target engine cannot parse — arrow functions into `function`, optional chaining into conditionals. A polyfill supplies a missing **API** at runtime — `Array.prototype.at`, `Promise`, `fetch`. Syntax has to be handled at build time; missing functions can be added when the page loads.
deepAnswer: The split follows from when the failure happens. Unsupported syntax is a parse error — the file fails to load at all, before any of your code runs, so nothing at runtime can rescue it. A missing method is a runtime `TypeError` at the moment it is called, which means a script that runs earlier can define it.
**Transpiling** (Babel, TypeScript, esbuild, SWC) rewrites source to an older syntax level. `const`, arrows, classes, `async`/`await`, optional chaining, private fields — all syntax, all build-time.

**Polyfilling** adds the missing API: `Object.hasOwn`, `Array.prototype.flat`, `structuredClone`, `IntersectionObserver`. A polyfill should feature-detect and only install when absent (`if (!Object.hasOwn) { ... }`), and should behave like the specification — a partial implementation that differs in edge cases is worse than none, because code will branch on its presence.

A **shim** is the looser term for a compatibility layer that may normalise behaviour rather than only fill a gap; a **ponyfill** exports the function instead of patching the global, which avoids modifying built-ins that other code shares.

Both cost bytes, and the modern approach is to ship less of them. A browserslist target driven by real usage data, plus `core-js` with `useBuiltIns: "usage"`, includes only what the targeted browsers actually lack. Module/nomodule or differential builds go further: modern browsers get untranspiled code and legacy ones get the heavy build.

Some things cannot be polyfilled — `Proxy`, `WeakRef`, and anything requiring engine-level behaviour. Those are genuine capability boundaries, not gaps to fill, and the answer there is a different design rather than a shim.

The trend worth noting: as evergreen browsers became the norm, the amount of transpilation and polyfilling needed collapsed. Shipping ES2020 untranspiled is reasonable for most audiences now, and checking rather than assuming is the professional move.
keyPoints: Transpiler rewrites syntax at build time; a polyfill adds an API at runtime
Unsupported syntax is a parse error — nothing at runtime can fix it
Polyfills must feature-detect and match the specification
A ponyfill exports rather than patching a global
Target with browserslist and `useBuiltIns: "usage"` to ship less
Some features cannot be polyfilled at all

Shipping a broad polyfill bundle to browsers that need none of it.

interview:iv-rt-url-to-page.shortAnswer: URL parsing, DNS resolution, TCP and TLS handshakes, the HTTP request, the response streaming back, HTML parsing into the DOM while subresources are fetched, CSS into the CSSOM, script execution, then layout, paint and composite — with interactivity arriving once the main thread stops being busy.
deepAnswer: **Resolution and connection.** The URL is parsed, the browser checks its caches, then DNS resolves the hostname (often cached at several levels). A TCP connection is established, and for HTTPS a TLS handshake negotiates encryption. Each of these is a round trip, which is why connection setup dominates on high-latency links and why HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 focus on reducing them.

**Request and response.** The browser sends the request with its headers and cookies; the server responds with a status, headers and a body. Caching headers on that response decide whether the next visit repeats any of this.

**Parsing.** HTML is parsed incrementally into the DOM as bytes arrive, so rendering can begin before the document is complete. A preload scanner runs ahead to start fetching images, stylesheets and scripts early.

**Blocking.** Stylesheets block rendering by design. A synchronous script blocks parsing, and also waits on any pending stylesheet before it can run. `defer` and `type="module"` avoid the parse block.

**Render.** DOM and CSSOM combine into the render tree; layout computes geometry; paint produces pixels; compositing assembles layers. First Contentful Paint is the first of these to show anything, and Largest Contentful Paint marks the main content.

**Interactivity.** The page can look finished while still being unresponsive, because event handling shares the main thread with script execution. Hydration in a server-rendered application is the usual culprit — the markup is visible but the JavaScript that makes it work has not finished running. That gap is what INP measures.

A good answer names where the levers are rather than reciting the list: CDN and connection reuse for the network phase, critical CSS and `defer` for the parse phase, code splitting and smaller bundles for the execution phase, and image dimensions for layout stability.

HTML parses incrementally; a preload scanner fetches ahead
CSS blocks rendering; a synchronous script blocks parsing and waits on CSS
Render tree → layout → paint → composite
Looking finished is not being interactive — the main thread may still be busy
The levers map to phases: CDN, critical CSS, `defer`, code splitting, image sizing

interview:iv-code-delegate-helper.shortAnswer: Attach one listener to the container, use `event.target.closest(selector)` to find the matching element, verify it is actually inside the container, then call the handler with both the event and the matched element. Return an unsubscribe function.
deepAnswer: `closest` walks up from the deepest element the event hit, so a click on an icon inside the button still resolves to the button. Comparing `event.target` directly against the selector would fail for any nested markup.

The `container.contains(match)` check matters more than it looks: `closest` can walk past the container to an ancestor that also matches, and with portals or moved nodes the match may not be a descendant at all. Without the check the handler fires for the wrong element.
Returning the unsubscribe function removes the need for callers to keep both the type and the exact listener reference — the usual reason delegated listeners are never cleaned up.

The event-type caveat: `focus`, `blur`, `mouseenter` and `mouseleave` do not bubble, so they never reach the container. Use `focusin`/`focusout`, which do, or register with `{ capture: true }` to catch them on the way down.

The payoff is one listener regardless of how many rows exist, working for rows added after registration, with no per-row cleanup. For a 500-row table that is 500 fewer listener registrations and 500 fewer references to release.

A refinement worth mentioning: for high-frequency types such as `mousemove` or `scroll`, add `{ passive: true }` where you will not call `preventDefault`, so the browser need not wait for the handler before scrolling.
keyPoints: One listener on the container; `target.closest(selector)` to match
Verify the match is inside the container — `closest` can escape it
Pass both the event and the matched element to the handler
Return an unsubscribe function
`focus`/`blur`/`mouseenter` do not bubble — use `focusin` or capture

interview:iv-code-focus-trap.shortAnswer: Intercept Tab on the container, compute the focusable elements at that moment, and wrap from last to first (and first to last on Shift+Tab). Store the previously focused element on entry and restore it on release, and register everything through one `AbortController` so teardown is a single call.
deepAnswer: Recomputing the focusable list **on each Tab** rather than caching it at setup is the detail that makes it survive dynamic content — a dialog that reveals a field, disables a button, or renders a list asynchronously.

Filtering out hidden elements matters: `querySelectorAll` happily returns controls inside a collapsed section, and focusing one moves focus somewhere invisible. `offsetParent !== null` is a cheap visibility approximation; it is not perfect (it misfires for `position: fixed`), and a production implementation would also check `getClientRects().length` and `visibility`.

Restoring focus on release is the step most implementations forget, and its absence is the most disorienting part for a keyboard user — focus falls back to `<body>` and they restart from the top of the page.
The `AbortController` makes teardown one call and keeps the listener from outliving the dialog. That is both correctness and leak prevention.

What this does not cover: a trap should usually also handle Escape to close, prevent background scrolling, and set `aria-modal="true"` with a label. And it does not restrict the browser's own UI — the user can still Tab out to the address bar, which is correct behaviour and not something to fight.

The professional conclusion: use `<dialog>` with `showModal()`, which implements all of this natively including inertness of the rest of the page. Write this only when a native dialog genuinely cannot be used — the exercise is worth knowing because plenty of codebases contain a hand-rolled one.

Recompute the focusable list on each Tab, not once at setup
Filter hidden elements or focus lands somewhere invisible
Store and restore the previously focused element
Register through an `AbortController` for one-call teardown
Also needs Escape, scroll lock and `aria-modal`
`<dialog>` + `showModal()` does all of this natively
