The JavaScript-specific caveat: indexing a string gives UTF-16 code units, so an emoji is two "characters" and a surrogate pair could be split. For text that may contain astral characters, iterate `[...s]` — which yields code points — and be aware that even that does not handle combining marks, where `Intl.Segmenter` is the correct tool. Raising this shows you think about real input rather than ASCII test cases.
Edge cases: empty string returns `0`, a single character returns `1`, and an all-unique string returns its own length.
keyPoints: Sliding window with last-seen indices; O(n) time
Only advance `start` when the duplicate is inside the current window
Space is O(min(n, alphabet)), not O(n)
`start` never moves backwards — that is what keeps it linear
String indexing is UTF-16; `[...s]` iterates code points
commonMistakes: Moving `start` backwards for a duplicate outside the window.
Claiming O(n²) because there appear to be two moving pointers.
followUps: Why is this linear despite two pointers?
How would you handle emoji correctly?

interview:iv-algo-group-anagrams.shortAnswer: Map each word to a canonical key that all its anagrams share — its sorted letters — and group by that key. O(n · k log k) for n words of length k; a character-count key brings it to O(n · k).
deepAnswer: The whole problem is choosing a **canonical form**: a representation that is identical for every member of a group and different for every non-member. Sorted letters satisfy both. Recognising the problem as "canonical key plus group" rather than "compare every pair" is the insight — pairwise comparison would be O(n²·k).

That version assumes lowercase ASCII. Say the assumption out loud, and note the general fallback: a `Map` of character to count, serialised with sorted keys, works for any alphabet at the cost of the constant factor.

For realistic input, decide whether the comparison is case-insensitive and whether Unicode should be normalised — `NFC` normalisation matters if accented characters can arrive either precomposed or as combining sequences.
Returning `[...groups.values()]` preserves first-appearance order of the groups, which is usually what a caller expects even when the problem does not require it.
keyPoints: Group by a canonical key rather than comparing pairs
Sorted letters: O(n · k log k); character counts: O(n · k)
A count key needs a separator or counts collide
State the alphabet assumption; case and Unicode normalisation are real concerns
Pairwise comparison would be O(n²·k)
commonMistakes: Comparing every pair of words instead of building a key.
Joining counts without a separator.
followUps: When is the counting key actually faster?
How would you handle Unicode input?

interview:iv-algo-binary-search-first.shortAnswer: A standard binary search, but on a match do not return — record the index and keep searching the left half. Compute the midpoint as `low + ((high - low) >> 1)` and use `low <= high` consistently so the loop always terminates.
deepAnswer: The only change from a plain binary search is `high = mid - 1` after a match instead of returning immediately. That continues narrowing towards the leftmost equal element while `found` holds the best answer so far. Mirroring it — `low = mid + 1` on a match — gives the last occurrence.

The three ways binary search goes wrong, all worth naming: an off-by-one in the loop condition (`low < high` skips the final element when the target is there); failing to move `low` or `high` past `mid`, which loops forever; and overflow in `(low + high) / 2`. The overflow is a genuine hazard in fixed-width languages; in JavaScript, numbers are doubles so it only matters above 2^53 — but `low + ((high - low) >> 1)` is the habit, and note `>>` itself coerces to 32 bits, so an array longer than 2^31 would break it. Saying that precisely, rather than parroting the C advice, is the strong answer.
Complexity is O(log n) time, O(1) space. The recursive formulation is O(log n) stack space and offers nothing extra here.
Preconditions matter: the array must be sorted by the same ordering the comparison uses. A binary search over an array sorted with a custom comparator must use that comparator, not `<`.

The natural extension is `lowerBound`/`upperBound` — the first index at which the target could be inserted while keeping the array sorted. Those are strictly more useful than a plain search, since together they give the full range of equal elements in O(log n) and therefore the count as well.
keyPoints: On a match, record the index and continue left rather than returning
Mirror it (`low = mid + 1`) for the last occurrence
`low + ((high - low) >> 1)` for the midpoint; `>>` is a 32-bit operation
Always move `low` or `high` past `mid` or the loop never terminates
O(log n) time, O(1) space; the array must be sorted by the same ordering
`lowerBound`/`upperBound` give the whole equal range
commonMistakes: Returning on the first match and getting an arbitrary occurrence.
Using `low < high`, which misses the final element.
followUps: How do you find the last occurrence?
How would you count occurrences in O(log n)?

interview:iv-algo-merge-intervals.shortAnswer: Sort by start, then sweep once: if the current interval starts at or before the end of the last merged one, extend that end to the maximum of the two; otherwise start a new interval. O(n log n), dominated by the sort.
deepAnswer: Sorting by start is what makes a single pass sufficient: once ordered, any interval that overlaps the running one must overlap at its start, so only the most recent merged interval ever needs checking.

`Math.max(last[1], end)` rather than `end` handles a fully-contained interval such as `[1, 10]` followed by `[2, 3]`. Assigning `end` directly would shrink the merged interval — a bug that passes many test cases and fails on containment.

`[...intervals].sort(...)` copies first, because `sort` mutates. Returning a result that has silently reordered the caller's array is a side effect nobody asked for. The `[...sorted[0]]` copy likewise avoids mutating the caller's inner arrays when `last[1]` is written.

The clarifying question to ask: are touching intervals — `[1, 2]` and `[2, 3]` — merged? `start <= last[1]` says yes. For half-open intervals, or for calendar bookings where an event ending at 10:00 does not conflict with one starting at 10:00, it should be `<`. This genuinely changes the answer, so ask before coding.
Complexity: O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the sweep, O(n) space for the output. If the input is already sorted, the whole thing is O(n).

The family of related problems all use the same sweep: inserting one interval into a sorted list, finding the intersection of two lists, and "minimum meeting rooms", which sorts start and end times separately and tracks a running count.
keyPoints: Sort by start, then one linear sweep
`Math.max` when extending, or contained intervals shrink the result
Copy before sorting — `sort` mutates the caller's array
Ask whether touching intervals count as overlapping
O(n log n) time, O(n) space; O(n) if already sorted
commonMistakes: Assigning `end` instead of taking the maximum.
Sorting the caller's array in place.
followUps: How would you find the minimum number of meeting rooms?
What changes for half-open intervals?

interview:iv-algo-balanced-brackets.shortAnswer: Push opening brackets onto a stack; on a closing bracket, pop and check it matches. Balanced means every pop matches and the stack is empty at the end. O(n) time, O(n) space.
deepAnswer: The final `stack.length === 0` check is the half people forget. Without it, `"((("` returns `true` — every closing bracket that appeared matched, there just were not any.

`stack.pop()` on an empty array returns `undefined`, which cannot equal any opener, so an unmatched closing bracket is rejected without a separate emptiness check. That is a small elegance worth pointing out rather than adding a redundant guard.

A stack is the right structure because nesting is inherently last-in-first-out: the most recently opened bracket must be the next one closed. Counting occurrences instead of stacking fails on `"([)]"` — equal counts, wrong order — and that counter-example is the standard way to demonstrate you understand **why** a stack is required.
Non-bracket characters are ignored here, which is the usual requirement for validating code or expressions. Whether they should be is a clarifying question.
Complexity: O(n) time; O(n) space in the worst case of all opening brackets. There is no way to do better than O(n) time — every character must be examined at least once.

The realistic extension is what makes this more than a toy: real parsing has to handle brackets inside string literals and comments, which must be skipped. That turns the problem into a small tokeniser, and mentioning it shows awareness of why editors get this subtly wrong.
keyPoints: A stack, because nesting is last-in-first-out
Check the stack is empty at the end, not just that pops matched
`pop()` on an empty array gives `undefined`, which safely fails the match
Counting brackets fails on `"([)]"` — order matters
O(n) time and space; real parsing must skip strings and comments
commonMistakes: Omitting the final emptiness check.
Counting openers and closers instead of tracking order.
followUps: Why is counting insufficient?
How would you handle brackets inside string literals?

interview:iv-algo-top-k-frequent.shortAnswer: Count with a `Map`, then select the top k. Sorting all counts is O(m log m) and perfectly acceptable; bucket sort by frequency gives O(n) because frequencies are bounded by the array length, which is the answer an interviewer is usually fishing for.
deepAnswer: The third approach, a min-heap of size k, gives O(m log k). It wins specifically when k is much smaller than m, and it is the only one of the three that works on a stream where you cannot hold all the data. JavaScript has no built-in heap, so you would be writing one — say that, and say it is not worth it unless the constraints demand it.
The judgment being tested is choosing among these, not memorising the fastest. Naming the sort version, then offering the bucket version with its reasoning, is a complete answer.

Clarifying questions: how are ties broken (arbitrarily, or by first appearance); is k guaranteed to be at most the number of distinct values; are the elements primitives, since object elements would need a key function because `Map` compares them by reference.
keyPoints: Count with a `Map`, then select — the counting step is O(n) regardless
Sorting counts is O(m log m) and usually the right code to write
Frequencies are bounded by n, so bucket sort gives O(n)
A size-k min-heap is O(m log k) and the only streaming-capable option
Clarify tie-breaking and whether elements are primitives
commonMistakes: Sorting the original array rather than the counts.
Presenting the heap as always optimal without noting JavaScript has no built-in one.
followUps: When does the heap approach actually win?
How would you handle a stream you cannot buffer?

interview:iv-algo-fibonacci-approaches.shortAnswer: Naive recursion is O(2^n) and unusable past about n = 40. Memoization makes it O(n) time and O(n) space. Iteration with two rolling variables is O(n) time and O(1) space, and is the answer to give. Above n = 78 the result exceeds `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, so `BigInt` is required.
deepAnswer: The naive recursion is exponential because it recomputes the same subproblems: `fib(5)` calls `fib(3)` twice, `fib(2)` three times, and the call tree has roughly 2^n nodes. Being able to explain **why** it is exponential — overlapping subproblems, not "recursion is slow" — is the point of asking.
Memoization fixes exactly that: each `fib(k)` is computed once and reused, collapsing the tree to a chain. O(n) time and O(n) space, plus O(n) stack depth — which still overflows around n = 10,000.

This is the classic illustration of dynamic programming. Memoization is top-down DP; the iterative loop is bottom-up DP with the table reduced to two variables, since only the last two values are ever needed. That "keep only what you need" reduction is the transferable technique.

The precision limit is the detail most candidates miss and interviewers like: `fib(79)` is 14,472,334,024,676,221, which is already above `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 − 1). The result stays a **finite number** but is silently wrong. `BigInt` — `let prev = 0n; let curr = 1n;` — gives exact results at any size, at the cost of slower arithmetic and no mixing with regular numbers.

For completeness: there is an O(log n) matrix-exponentiation solution, and Binet's closed-form formula — which is O(1) but loses accuracy above about n = 70 due to floating-point error, so it is not actually a correct answer for large n.
Validate the input. `fib(-1)` and `fib(2.5)` should be rejected rather than silently looping or returning nonsense.
keyPoints: Naive recursion is O(2^n) from overlapping subproblems, not from recursion itself
Memoization: O(n) time and space, top-down DP
Iteration with two variables: O(n) time, O(1) space — the answer to give
Above n = 78 the result silently exceeds `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`; use `BigInt`
Matrix exponentiation is O(log n); Binet's formula is inaccurate for large n
Validate that n is a non-negative integer
commonMistakes: Saying recursion is slow rather than identifying overlapping subproblems.
Ignoring the safe-integer limit and returning a silently wrong result.
followUps: Why is the closed-form formula not a correct O(1) answer?
What does the memoized version cost in stack depth?

interview:iv-algo-tree-traversal.shortAnswer: DFS uses a stack (or the call stack) and goes deep first — natural for rendering nested threads and for anything needing the full path to a node. BFS uses a queue and visits level by level — the right choice for shortest-path-in-hops and for rendering only the top N levels.
deepAnswer: The only structural difference is stack versus queue. That is the sentence to lead with — everything else follows from it.

Two implementation details worth pointing out. DFS pushes children in **reverse** so they pop in original order. BFS advances a `head` index rather than calling `queue.shift()`, because `shift` is O(n) and turns the whole traversal into O(n²) on a wide tree — a real performance bug that hides in a lot of interview code.

Choosing between them: BFS finds the shallowest match first, so "the nearest node satisfying X" and "shortest path in unweighted hops" are BFS problems. DFS is natural when you need the path from the root — it is already on the stack — and for post-order work like computing a subtree size or total reply count.
Memory is the practical differentiator: DFS holds O(depth), BFS holds O(width). For a wide, shallow comment tree DFS is much cheaper; for a deep, narrow one BFS is.

The recursive DFS is shorter and usually clearer for tree rendering, but it is bounded by the engine's stack — around 10,000 frames. For user-supplied or arbitrarily deep data, the explicit stack is the safe choice.

For a general **graph** rather than a tree, both need a visited `Set` or they loop forever on a cycle. A comment tree should not have cycles, but data that arrived over a network has whatever shape it actually has — validating that assumption rather than trusting it is the mature answer.
keyPoints: DFS is a stack, BFS is a queue — everything else follows
Push DFS children in reverse to preserve order
Use an index instead of `queue.shift()`; `shift` is O(n)
BFS for shallowest-match and level-limited rendering; DFS for paths and post-order
DFS costs O(depth) memory, BFS costs O(width)
Any graph traversal needs a visited `Set` to survive cycles
commonMistakes: Using `queue.shift()` and making BFS quadratic.
Assuming recursive DFS is always safe regardless of depth.
followUps: Which uses less memory for a wide, shallow tree?
What breaks if the data contains a cycle?

interview:iv-algo-move-zeroes.shortAnswer: Two pointers: a write index that only advances when a non-zero is copied into it, then fill the remainder with zeroes. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) extra space — and stability falls out for free.
deepAnswer: The read/write two-pointer pattern is the transferable part. The same shape solves "remove duplicates from a sorted array", "remove all instances of a value", and any in-place compaction: read scans everything, write marks where the next kept element goes.

Stability is automatic because elements are copied in the order they are read. A swap-based variant also works and does fewer writes when zeroes are rare, but it is easier to get wrong and the difference rarely matters.

"In place" is the constraint that makes it interesting. `nums.filter(x => x !== 0)` plus padding is one line and O(n) time, but it allocates a new array — which is exactly what the question rules out. Say that you know the easy version exists and why it does not satisfy the constraint.

A common wrong approach is repeatedly calling `splice` to remove a zero and `push` it to the end. Each `splice` is O(n), so the whole thing becomes O(n²), and mutating the array while iterating forwards also skips elements.

Edge cases: an empty array, an array with no zeroes (the loop copies each element onto itself, which is correct but does n redundant writes — a `if (read !== write)` guard avoids them), and an all-zeroes array.
Note that `0 !== -0` is `false`, so `-0` is treated as a zero here. If that distinction mattered you would need `Object.is`, but for this problem treating them alike is correct.
keyPoints: Read/write two pointers; one pass, O(n) time, O(1) space
The same pattern solves any in-place compaction problem
Stability comes free from copying in read order
`filter` + pad is simpler but allocates, violating the constraint
Repeated `splice` is O(n²) and skips elements
commonMistakes: Using `splice` in a loop.
Producing a new array when the requirement is in place.
followUps: What other problems use the same two-pointer shape?
When is the swap variant preferable?

interview:iv-dbg-settimeout-this.shortAnswer: The callback is a plain `function`, so its `this` is decided by how the timer calls it — not by the enclosing method. It is `undefined` in strict mode (or the global/timer object in sloppy mode), so `this.remaining` throws. Use an arrow function, which has no `this` of its own and inherits the instance.
deepAnswer: `this` is set at the call site. `setInterval` invokes the callback with no receiver, so a `function` expression gets `undefined` as `this` under strict mode — and class bodies are always strict. Reading `.remaining` off `undefined` throws `TypeError`.
The older equivalents are worth naming: `.bind(this)` on the function expression, or capturing `const self = this` before the callback. Both work; the arrow is simply the modern spelling.

A third point that shows production experience: an uncleared interval holding `this.el` keeps the element and its whole subtree reachable, so this is also a memory leak in a single-page app that creates and destroys timers.

Finally, `setInterval` drifts — it does not guarantee exactly 1000ms between callbacks, and browsers throttle timers in background tabs. For a visible countdown, compute the remaining time from a stored `Date.now()` deadline rather than by decrementing a counter.
keyPoints: A `function` callback gets its `this` from the call site — `undefined` in strict mode
Arrow functions inherit `this` lexically; `bind` is the older fix
The interval id is never stored, so it can never be cleared
An uncleared interval holding a DOM node is a memory leak
Do not accumulate time by decrementing — derive it from a deadline
commonMistakes: Fixing `this` and stopping there, missing the uncleared interval.
Claiming `setInterval` guarantees the stated period.
followUps: How would you make the countdown accurate in a background tab?
Where should `clearInterval` be called in a component?

interview:iv-dbg-map-parseint.shortAnswer: `map` passes three arguments — value, index, array — and `parseInt` takes two: string and **radix**. So the calls are `parseInt("10", 0)`, `parseInt("10", 1)` and `parseInt("10", 2)`. Fix it with `raw.map((s) => parseInt(s, 10))` or `raw.map(Number)`.
deepAnswer: `parseInt("10", 0)` — radix `0` is falsy and treated as "unspecified", so it defaults to base 10 and gives `10`.
`parseInt("10", 1)` — base 1 is not a valid radix (valid range is 2–36), so the result is `NaN`.
`parseInt("10", 2)` — binary, so `"10"` is `2`.

The general lesson is about **arity mismatch when passing a function reference directly**. Point-free style is only safe when the callee ignores the extra arguments. The same trap bites `map(Number)` — safe, because `Number` takes one argument — versus `map(parseFloat)` — also safe — versus anything with an optional second parameter.
The safe fix is an explicit arrow that passes exactly what you mean: `raw.map((s) => parseInt(s, 10))`. Always pass the radix anyway; it is a habit worth keeping even outside `map`.

`Number(s)` is the better choice for whole strings, because it rejects trailing junk: `parseInt("12abc", 10)` is `12`, while `Number("12abc")` is `NaN`. Which you want depends on whether partial parsing is a feature or a silent data corruption — for user input it is almost always the latter.
A caveat worth adding: `Number("")` is `0` and `Number(" ")` is `0`, so validate for emptiness before converting form input.
keyPoints: `map` passes (value, index, array) — the index becomes `parseInt`'s radix
Radix `0` means default, `1` is invalid, `2` is binary
Passing a function reference is unsafe when it has optional extra parameters
Use `(s) => parseInt(s, 10)` or `Number`
`parseInt` stops at junk; `Number` rejects it — and `Number("")` is `0`
commonMistakes: Blaming `map` rather than the arity mismatch.
Recommending `Number` without mentioning that it treats `""` as `0`.
followUps: Which other built-ins are unsafe to pass directly to `map`?
When is `parseInt` preferable to `Number`?

interview:iv-dbg-innerhtml-listeners.shortAnswer: `innerHTML +=` re-parses the entire list and replaces every existing node with a new one, so all previously attached listeners are destroyed. Re-attaching to everything also stacks duplicate listeners on the survivors. Use event delegation: one listener on the container.
deepAnswer: `list.innerHTML += html` is read-modify-write: it serialises the current DOM to a string, appends, and re-parses the whole thing. The original elements are discarded, and listeners live on element objects, not on markup — so they go with them. It also resets any DOM state that has no HTML representation: focus, scroll position, form values, `<video>` playback.
The re-attach loop makes it worse. Every call binds a listener to every button, so after three rows the first button has three identical handlers and `remove` runs three times per click.

There is a security bug here too, and it is the one that matters most: `item.name` is interpolated straight into HTML. If a name can contain markup — and any user-supplied field can — this is a stored cross-site scripting hole. `textContent` assigns text and never parses it, which is why the rewritten version is safe by construction.
For batch inserts, build into a `DocumentFragment` and append once, so layout is recalculated a single time.
keyPoints: `innerHTML +=` re-parses and replaces every node, destroying listeners and DOM state
Re-attaching to all buttons stacks duplicate handlers
Delegate: one listener on the stable container, with `closest`
Build nodes with `createElement` and `textContent`
Interpolating user text into HTML is an XSS hole — `textContent` avoids it
commonMistakes: Fixing only the listener duplication and keeping `innerHTML +=`.
Missing that the interpolated name is an injection point.
followUps: Why does `closest` matter in the delegated handler?
What DOM state besides listeners is lost?

interview:iv-dbg-missing-await.shortAnswer: The `await` is missing. `fetchUser(id)` returns a pending promise, so `user.name` is `undefined` on a promise object, and any rejection happens after `try` has already exited — making the `catch` unreachable and producing an unhandled rejection instead.
deepAnswer: Without `await`, `user` is a `Promise`, not the resolved value. Reading `.name` on it gives `undefined` rather than throwing, which is what makes this bug quiet: nothing crashes at the point of the mistake.

The `catch` problem is more subtle and more important. `try`/`catch` catches synchronous throws in its block. `fetchUser(id)` returns successfully — it just returns a promise that will reject later. By the time the rejection happens the `try` block has long finished, so nothing catches it, and it surfaces as an unhandled rejection far from the code that caused it.

The fix is one word:

```js
const user = await fetchUser(id);
```

`await` on a rejected promise throws inside the `async` function, at that line, which is exactly what makes the surrounding `try`/`catch` work.
The habit worth stating: a `try`/`catch` around asynchronous code is only meaningful if there is an `await` inside the `try`. If there is not, the block is decorative.

The catching mechanism: `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` flags a promise that is neither awaited, returned, nor `.catch`ed. In plain JavaScript, treat "this function is `async` but nothing in the body awaits" as a smell.

A related trap in the same family: `return await x` inside a `try` is not redundant — it makes the rejection catchable there. A bare `return x` hands the promise back to the caller and skips your `catch` entirely, which matters if the `catch` does cleanup or logging.
keyPoints: Missing `await` gives you a promise, so property reads are `undefined`
A rejection after `try` exits cannot be caught by it
The result is an unhandled rejection reported far from the cause
`try`/`catch` around async code needs an `await` inside to mean anything
`return await x` inside `try` differs from `return x`
commonMistakes: Explaining the `undefined` but missing why the `catch` is dead.
Calling `return await` inside `try` a pointless extra `await`.
followUps: When is `return await` meaningfully different from `return`?
How do you catch unhandled rejections globally?

interview:iv-dbg-sort-boolean.shortAnswer: A comparator must return a **number**: negative, zero, or positive. This returns a boolean, which coerces to `1` or `0` — so it never says "a comes before b", only "after" or "equal". The result depends on the engine's sort algorithm and on the input size, which is why it looks browser-dependent.
deepAnswer: `true` coerces to `1` and `false` to `0`. The comparator can therefore express only two of the three required relations. The engine is being told "these are equal" whenever `a.age <= b.age`, including when `a` is genuinely smaller.

Because the comparator is inconsistent, the outcome depends entirely on the sort implementation and the comparison sequence it happens to choose. V8 uses insertion sort for short arrays and TimSort for longer ones, so the same code can appear to work on a 5-element test fixture and fail on 100 elements — an unusually nasty way to lose confidence in a test suite.

The fix for numbers is subtraction:

```js
const byAge = (a, b) => a.age - b.age;
```

For strings, subtraction produces `NaN`, which is also an invalid comparator result. Use `a.name.localeCompare(b.name)`, which handles case and accents according to locale rules rather than raw code-unit order.

For multi-key sorting, chain with `||` — it falls through only on a `0` tie:

```js
const byAgeThenName = (a, b) => a.age - b.age || a.name.localeCompare(b.name);
```

Two properties a correct comparator must have: it must be consistent (`cmp(a, b)` and `cmp(b, a)` must have opposite signs) and transitive. Violating either gives an implementation-defined result — the specification does not promise anything, not even that the elements are preserved in some order you can predict.
And remember `sort` mutates. `people.sort(...)` reorders the original array; use `[...people].sort(...)` or `people.toSorted(...)` when the caller's array must not change.
keyPoints: A comparator must return a negative, zero or positive number
A boolean gives only `1`/`0` — "before" is unrepresentable
Results vary by engine and array length, so small tests can pass
`a - b` for numbers; `localeCompare` for strings; `||` to chain keys
The comparator must be consistent and transitive; `sort` mutates
commonMistakes: Saying it "sometimes works" without explaining that the algorithm choice varies by size.
Using subtraction on strings.
followUps: How would you sort by two keys?
Why can a 5-element test fixture pass?

interview:iv-dbg-localstorage-object.shortAnswer: `localStorage` stores strings only. `setItem` coerces the object with `String()`, producing `"[object Object]"`. Serialise with `JSON.stringify` on the way in and `JSON.parse` on the way out — inside a `try`/`catch`, because stored data can be absent or corrupt.
deepAnswer: The Web Storage API has a string-only value type. Passing an object calls `ToString` on it, and the default `Object.prototype.toString` yields `"[object Object]"` — the data is gone at the moment of writing, not at the moment of reading.
Writes fail too. `setItem` throws `QuotaExceededError` when the ~5MB limit is hit, and it throws in Safari private browsing. A write helper should catch and degrade rather than break the page.
Type fidelity is limited: JSON has no `Date`, no `Map`/`Set`, no `undefined`. A `Date` comes back as an ISO string, so revive it explicitly rather than assuming `saved.createdAt.getTime()` works.

One thing to say unprompted: never store tokens, passwords or personal data here. `localStorage` is readable by any script on the origin, so any XSS becomes a credential theft. Session identifiers belong in `HttpOnly` cookies, which JavaScript cannot read at all.
keyPoints: `localStorage` values are strings — objects become `"[object Object]"`
`JSON.stringify` in, `JSON.parse` out
Guard reads with `try`/`catch`; stored data can be missing or corrupt
`setItem` can throw on quota or in private browsing
JSON loses `Date`, `Map`, `Set` and `undefined`
Never store credentials — any XSS can read the whole origin's storage
commonMistakes: Adding `JSON.parse` without handling `null` or a `SyntaxError`.
Treating storage as a safe place for auth tokens.
followUps: How do you restore a `Date` from JSON?
Where should a session token live instead?

interview:iv-dbg-listener-not-removed.shortAnswer: The scroll listener is added on every open and never removed, so listeners accumulate and every scroll event runs `reposition` N times. It also keeps `panel` reachable forever. Remove the listener on close — which requires a stable reference, or an `AbortController` signal.
deepAnswer: Each `openPanel` call registers a **new** anonymous function. `removeEventListener` could not remove it even if it were called, because it needs the identical function reference — a fresh arrow with the same body is a different object.

The visible symptom is degrading scroll performance: after ten open/close cycles, every scroll event runs `reposition` ten times, on the main thread, during the most latency-sensitive interaction there is.

The invisible symptom is the leak. The listener closes over `panel`, so the element and its subtree stay reachable from the `window` listener list even after the panel is removed from the DOM. In a long-lived single-page app this accumulates.
The classic alternative is a named handler stored somewhere stable, and `removeEventListener("scroll", handler)` in `closePanel`. Both are correct; the signal approach is harder to get wrong.

Two performance points worth adding: register scroll listeners as `{ passive: true }` so the browser need not wait to see whether you will call `preventDefault`, and throttle `reposition` to animation frames with `requestAnimationFrame` rather than running layout work on every scroll event. If the goal is purely to detect visibility, `IntersectionObserver` avoids the scroll listener entirely.
How to confirm it: DevTools has a listener count per element in the Elements panel, and a heap snapshot comparison across open/close cycles shows the retained detached nodes.
keyPoints: A new anonymous function per call cannot be removed and accumulates
Every scroll event then runs the work N times on the main thread
The closure retains the element — a real memory leak
`AbortController` + `{ signal }` removes all listeners in one call
Use `{ passive: true }`, `requestAnimationFrame`, or `IntersectionObserver`
commonMistakes: Calling `removeEventListener` with a new arrow function and believing it worked.
Treating this as only a performance issue and missing the retained DOM.
followUps: Why does `removeEventListener` need the same reference?
How would you confirm the leak in DevTools?

interview:iv-dbg-debounce-broken.shortAnswer: The pending timer is never cancelled, so each call simply schedules another one — every keystroke still fires, just 300ms later. The missing line is `clearTimeout(timer)` before scheduling the new one.
deepAnswer: Debouncing means "run once, after the calls stop". That requires cancelling the previous pending run each time a new call arrives. Without `clearTimeout`, all N timers survive and all N fire, delayed but complete.

Note what the original does get right, and say so: `function` rather than an arrow for the returned wrapper, plus `fn.apply(this, args)`, preserves the caller's `this`. Writing the wrapper as an arrow would break debounced methods.

A production version usually also offers `cancel()` for cleanup on unmount, and sometimes a leading-edge option to fire immediately then suppress:

```js
debounced.cancel = () => clearTimeout(timer);
```

The distinction the interviewer will probe: **debounce** waits for a pause and is right for search-as-you-type, resize handlers and autosave. **Throttle** guarantees at most one call per interval and is right for scroll position, mousemove and analytics — things where you want steady updates rather than only a final one. Debouncing a scroll handler means nothing happens at all while the user keeps scrolling.
One caveat for the search case specifically: debouncing reduces requests but does not order them. The stale-response race still needs a sequence guard or `AbortController`.
keyPoints: Missing `clearTimeout` — every scheduled call still fires
`clearTimeout(undefined)` is safe, so no first-call special case is needed
`function` + `fn.apply(this, args)` correctly preserves `this`
Expose `cancel()` for cleanup
Debounce waits for a pause; throttle rate-limits — they are not interchangeable
commonMistakes: Rewriting the wrapper as an arrow and silently breaking `this`.
Describing debounce and throttle as the same thing.
followUps: When would throttle be correct instead?
How do you cancel a pending debounce on unmount?

interview:iv-dbg-object-includes.shortAnswer: `includes` compares by identity, and `{ id: product.id }` is a brand-new object that is not identical to anything in the cart — so the check is always `false`. Compare by a key instead: `cart.some((item) => item.id === product.id)`.
deepAnswer: Objects are compared by reference. Two object literals with identical contents are two different values, so `{ id: 1 } === { id: 1 }` is `false` and `includes`, which uses SameValueZero, can never match a freshly-built literal.

The fix is to compare on the field that defines identity for your domain:

```js
if (cart.some((item) => item.id === product.id)) return cart;
```

`some` short-circuits on the first match, and the predicate makes the identity rule explicit and reviewable.
`includes` **is** correct when you hold the same reference — `cart.includes(product)` works if `product` came out of the cart. The bug is constructing a lookalike.

For a cart that is checked frequently, a linear `some` per add is O(n) and the whole build is O(n²). A `Map` keyed by id gives O(1) lookups and also solves quantity merging naturally:

```js
const byId = new Map(cart.map((item) => [item.id, item]));
```

The wider point about equality: JavaScript has no built-in structural comparison. `===`, `includes`, `indexOf`, `Set` membership and `Map` keys are all reference-based for objects. Structural equality means either comparing chosen fields, or serialising to a canonical key — and `JSON.stringify` is not canonical, because key order and `undefined` handling make two equivalent objects produce different strings.

A likely follow-up: with `some` fixed, adding the same product twice should probably increment a quantity rather than silently do nothing. Returning the cart unchanged is a design decision the interviewer may want you to notice.
keyPoints: Objects compare by reference — a new literal never matches
`some` with an explicit id predicate is the fix
`includes` is fine when you hold the same reference
A `Map` keyed by id turns O(n) lookups into O(1)
JavaScript has no structural equality; `JSON.stringify` is not canonical
commonMistakes: Suggesting `JSON.stringify` comparison without noting key-order fragility.
Missing that silently ignoring a duplicate may itself be the wrong behaviour.
followUps: How would you handle incrementing quantity instead?
Why is `JSON.stringify` unsafe for equality?

interview:iv-dbg-return-in-foreach.shortAnswer: `return` inside a `forEach` callback returns from the **callback**, not from `validate`. `forEach` discards that value and keeps iterating, so control always reaches `return { ok: true }`. Use `find`, or a `for...of` loop where `return` exits the function.
deepAnswer: The callback is a separate function. Returning from it ends that one invocation; `forEach` ignores the return value entirely and calls the callback for the next element. There is no way to break out of `forEach` — not with `return`, not with `break` (a syntax error there).

Choosing the right array method by the shape of the answer is the underlying skill: `some` for "is there any", `every` for "are they all", `find` for "which one", `filter` for "all of them", `map` for "one output per input", `reduce` for "fold to a single value", `forEach` only for side effects with no early exit.
keyPoints: `return` in a `forEach` callback exits only the callback
`forEach` cannot be broken out of at all
`find` gives first-match-wins semantics directly
`for...of` allows a real `return`, `break` and `continue`
Collecting every error is usually better UX than reporting only the first
commonMistakes: Trying to `break` inside `forEach`.
Fixing the mechanics without questioning first-error-only behaviour.
followUps: How do you choose between `some`, `every`, `find` and `filter`?
Why can you not `break` out of `forEach`?

interview:iv-dbg-nan-check.shortAnswer: `NaN` is the only value not equal to itself, so `value === NaN` is always `false`. Use `Number.isNaN(value)` — and note that a check for valid numeric input needs more than that anyway, since `Number("")` is `0`.
deepAnswer: IEEE-754 defines `NaN` as unordered with respect to everything, itself included. Every comparison involving it — `===`, `<`, `>` — is `false`, and `NaN !== NaN` is the only way to detect it with operators alone.

`Number.isNaN(x)` returns `true` only for the actual `NaN` value. The older global `isNaN(x)` coerces first, so `isNaN("abc")` is `true` and `isNaN(undefined)` is `true` and `isNaN("")` is `false` — a different and usually wrong question. Prefer `Number.isNaN`.
For validating input, `Number.isFinite(value)` is usually the better test: it rejects `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity` in one check, and — unlike the global `isFinite` — does not coerce.

Also worth knowing: `Number(null)` is `0` while `Number(undefined)` is `NaN`, and `Number("0x10")` is `16`. These asymmetries are why explicit trimming and an explicit finite check beat relying on coercion.

Where `NaN` usually comes from in practice is arithmetic on an unparsed value — `undefined * 2`, or adding a form field before converting it. When you see `NaN` propagating through a calculation, trace back to the first operation with a non-numeric operand rather than checking at the end.
keyPoints: `NaN !== NaN` — equality can never detect it
`Number.isNaN` is exact; the global `isNaN` coerces first
`Number.isFinite` rejects `NaN` and both infinities in one test
`Number("")` and `Number(null)` are `0` — check emptiness separately
`NaN` propagates; trace to the first non-numeric operand
commonMistakes: Using the global `isNaN` and inheriting its coercion.
Assuming a finite check also rejects empty input.
followUps: Why is `Number("")` zero?
How would you validate a currency field?

interview:iv-dbg-stale-closure-count.shortAnswer: A stale closure. `count` is read once, at setup time, and the handler closes over that constant binding — not over a live value. Read the current value inside the handler instead: call `getCount()` at click time.
deepAnswer: Closures capture bindings, and `count` is a `const` that is assigned exactly once. The handler faithfully reports the value from setup, however long ago that was. Nothing about closures is broken here — the code asked for a snapshot and got one.

The general shape of the bug: **capturing a value when you meant to capture a source**. Capture the getter, the store, the ref, or the object — anything whose contents can change — rather than the extracted value.

This is the exact mechanism behind the React stale-closure problem: an effect or callback registered with an empty dependency array closes over the first render's state. The framework-level fixes (dependency arrays, functional `setState` updaters, refs) are all ways of saying "capture a source, not a snapshot".

It also explains why the fix for the `var`-in-a-loop bug is different in kind. There, the problem was too **few** bindings — one shared `i`. Here there are enough bindings; the problem is that the value was frozen too early. Both are "closures capture bindings", read from opposite directions.

How to spot it while reviewing: any value read **outside** an asynchronous or event-driven callback but used **inside** it is a candidate. Ask "can this change between registration and invocation?" — if yes, read it inside.
keyPoints: The closure captured a one-time value, not a live source
Nothing is broken — the code asked for a snapshot
Capture the getter/store/object, and read inside the callback
Same mechanism as React stale closures over state
Review heuristic: values read outside a callback but used inside it
commonMistakes: Blaming the closure mechanism rather than where the read happens.
Confusing this with the `var`-in-a-loop bug, which has the opposite cause.
followUps: How is this different from the `var` loop bug?
How does React solve the same problem?

interview:iv-dbg-json-parse-untrusted.shortAnswer: `JSON.parse` throws a `SyntaxError` on anything that is not valid JSON, and stored data can be truncated, written by an older version of the app, or edited by hand. The throw propagates and breaks initialisation. Parse inside `try`/`catch`, validate the shape, and fall back to a safe default.
deepAnswer: Three distinct failure modes hide in these four lines. `raw` can be `null` for a missing key — `JSON.parse(null)` happens to return `null` rather than throwing, so that one is quiet. `raw` can be invalid JSON, which throws. And `data` can be valid JSON of the wrong shape — `"5"` parses fine, and `data.items` is then `undefined`, or `data` is `null` and the property read throws.

The principle: **anything crossing a trust boundary must be validated, not assumed**. `localStorage`, URL parameters, `postMessage` payloads, API responses and file uploads are all input, even when your own code wrote them. Storage in particular is shared across versions of your app, so yesterday's schema is today's malformed data.

The shape check matters as much as the parse. `Array.isArray(data?.items)` is the minimum; for anything larger, a schema validator at the boundary converts a class of runtime `TypeError`s into one clear failure at the point of entry.

On the `catch`: swallowing silently is right here because a cache miss is recoverable, but it should still be observable — log it, or increment a metric. A `catch` that hides a systematic corruption bug forever is its own defect.

What this specifically must **not** become: `eval(raw)`. Parsing untrusted text by executing it turns a data problem into arbitrary code execution. `JSON.parse` exists precisely so that never has to happen.
keyPoints: `JSON.parse` throws `SyntaxError` on malformed input
`getItem` returns `null` for a missing key; `JSON.parse(null)` is `null`
Valid JSON of the wrong shape still breaks the property read
Clear the corrupt entry, or the failure repeats every load
Validate everything crossing a trust boundary; never `eval` stored text
commonMistakes: Adding `try`/`catch` but leaving the corrupt entry in place.
Checking the parse succeeded without checking the shape.
followUps: What else counts as a trust boundary in a browser app?
When is swallowing an error acceptable?

interview:iv-dbg-handler-invoked.shortAnswer: The parentheses **call** `handleClick` immediately and register its return value — `undefined` — as the listener. Pass the function itself: `addEventListener("click", handleClick)`.
deepAnswer: `handleClick()` evaluates during the `addEventListener` call, which is why the log appears at load time. Its return value is `undefined`, and `addEventListener` accepts a non-callable second argument without complaint, so nothing is registered and no error is reported. The silence is what makes this cost more time than it should.
Correct: `button.addEventListener("click", handleClick)` — a reference, not a call.

The variant that is genuinely useful is when you need to pass an argument. Then a wrapper is correct, and the parentheses belong inside it:

```js
button.addEventListener("click", () => handleClick(item.id));
```

But be aware this creates a new function each time it is evaluated, so it cannot later be removed with `removeEventListener` unless you keep the reference.
A related mistake in the same family is `setTimeout(doThing(), 1000)`, which has the identical cause and the identical silent failure.

Worth noting: `handleClick` is a function **declaration**, so hoisting means the code works despite being defined below the registration. Had it been `const handleClick = () => {}`, the same line would throw a `ReferenceError` from the temporal dead zone — a different bug that at least announces itself.
keyPoints: The parentheses call the function and register its return value
`addEventListener` accepts `undefined` silently — no error is raised
Pass the reference; use an arrow wrapper only when passing arguments
A wrapper arrow cannot be removed later without keeping the reference
`setTimeout(fn(), ms)` is the same mistake
commonMistakes: Fixing it with `.bind()` unnecessarily when a plain reference suffices.
Not realising an arrow wrapper makes removal harder.
followUps: How do you pass an argument to a listener?
Why does hoisting matter in this snippet?

interview:iv-dbg-arrow-prototype-method.shortAnswer: An arrow function has no `this` of its own — it captures the `this` of the scope where it was **defined**, which here is module or global scope, not the instance. A prototype method must be a regular function so the call site can supply the receiver.
deepAnswer: Arrows resolve `this` lexically. At the point `greet` is defined, the enclosing `this` is whatever the module or script has — `undefined` in a module, the global object in a classic script. Calling `u.greet()` does not change that, because arrows ignore the receiver entirely.

The rule to state: use an arrow when you **want** to inherit the surrounding `this` — a callback inside a method, a `setTimeout`, an array-method callback that needs the instance. Use a regular function when the caller is supposed to supply `this` — object methods, prototype methods, class methods.

A useful diagnostic detail: in a module (or under strict mode) the outer `this` is `undefined`, so this same code throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` instead of returning `"Hi, undefined"`. Which symptom you see tells you which mode the file is running in.

The related failure worth mentioning: arrows also have no `arguments`, no `prototype`, and cannot be called with `new`. `new (() => {})` throws `TypeError`, so an arrow can never serve as a constructor.
`call`, `apply` and `bind` are equally powerless against an arrow — they cannot override a lexical `this`. If a function seems to ignore `bind`, that is the giveaway.
keyPoints: Arrows capture `this` lexically from the definition site
Prototype and object methods need a regular function
Arrows are right for callbacks that should inherit the surrounding `this`
In a module the outer `this` is `undefined`, so it throws instead
Arrows have no `arguments`, no `prototype`, and cannot be `new`ed or rebound
commonMistakes: Trying to fix it with `.bind(u)` — `bind` cannot override a lexical `this`.
Treating arrows as always-safer shorthand for function expressions.
followUps: Why does `bind` not help here?
When is an arrow the right choice for a method?

interview:iv-dbg-key-collision-numeric.shortAnswer: Numeric-looking keys are integer indices, so `Object.entries` returns them in ascending numeric order regardless of insertion order — the newest-first ordering is silently reversed. A `Map` preserves insertion order and keeps the key type; that is the right structure here.
deepAnswer: `r.year` is a number, and object property names are always strings — `2024` becomes `"2024"`. Because `"2024"` is a valid array index, it is ordered as an integer key, ahead of any non-integer string key and sorted ascending. The insertion order the code relied on is discarded.

If a plain object is required — because the result is serialised to JSON, which has no `Map` — then sort explicitly at the end rather than relying on any order at all: `Object.entries(out).sort((a, b) => b[0] - a[0])`. Relying on implicit ordering is the underlying mistake; making the ordering explicit is the durable fix.

The "missing key" half of the question is the second hazard: `out[r.year] || []` treats any falsy existing value as absent, and a plain object also inherits keys from `Object.prototype`. A record with `year` of `"constructor"` or `"toString"` would find an inherited function instead of `undefined` and take the wrong branch. `Object.create(null)`, `Object.hasOwn`, or a `Map` all avoid this — `Map` most simply.

This is the general case for `Map` over an object: non-string keys, keys that come from data rather than from code, guaranteed insertion order, a real `size`, and direct iterability. Use a plain object for fixed, code-authored shapes; use a `Map` for dynamic collections.
ES2024 adds `Object.groupBy` and `Map.groupBy` for exactly this, and `Map.groupBy` is the one that keeps insertion order and non-string keys.
keyPoints: Integer-like keys are ordered numerically, ignoring insertion order
Object keys are always strings — the number type is lost
`Map` preserves insertion order and key type
Data-derived keys on a plain object can collide with `Object.prototype`
If ordering matters, make it explicit with `sort` rather than implicit
commonMistakes: Assuming object key order always follows insertion.
Missing the prototype-key hazard of a data-keyed plain object.
followUps: When is a plain object still the better choice?
What does `Object.create(null)` give you here?

interview:iv-dbg-form-numeric-concat.shortAnswer: `input.value` is always a string, even for `<input type="number">`. `+` with two strings concatenates, so `"1" + "2"` is `"12"`. Convert explicitly before doing arithmetic, and validate the conversion.
deepAnswer: The DOM `value` property is defined as a string. `type="number"` constrains what the user can type and enables the spinner, but it does not change the property type — the same is true of `type="date"` and `type="range"`.

Because `+` is overloaded, string operands make it concatenate rather than add. Notice that `-`, `*` and `/` would have coerced to number and appeared to work, which is why this bug often shows up only in the one place that uses `+`.

`valueAsNumber` is the purpose-built alternative for numeric and date inputs: `quantityInput.valueAsNumber` returns a number directly, and `NaN` when the field is empty or invalid — which is a cleaner signal than `Number("")` returning `0`.

The general principle: convert once, at the edge where data enters, and keep the interior of your code working in real types. Scattering `Number(...)` through business logic is a sign the boundary is in the wrong place.
For money specifically, do not sum floats. Parse to integer minor units — cents — do the arithmetic there, and format only when writing back to the DOM.
keyPoints: `input.value` is always a string, including for `type="number"`
`+` concatenates when either operand is a string
`-`, `*`, `/` coerce, which is why only `+` misbehaves
`valueAsNumber` gives a number and `NaN` for empty, unlike `Number("")`
Convert and validate once at the boundary; use integer cents for money
commonMistakes: Assuming `type="number"` makes `value` a number.
Using `parseInt` without a radix, or without checking the result.
followUps: Why does subtraction appear to work?
What does `valueAsNumber` return for an empty field?

interview:iv-dbg-recursion-no-base.shortAnswer: Two problems: `node.children` is assumed always to exist, and nothing handles a cycle. A leaf with no `children` throws `TypeError`; a graph where a node reaches itself recurses forever until the stack overflows. Guard the missing field, and track visited nodes.
deepAnswer: The missing base case is the simpler half. `node.children.flatMap` throws immediately if `children` is `undefined` — which is the natural representation for a leaf. `const children = node.children ?? []` handles it, and recursion terminates naturally when a node has no children.
Note the wrapper arrow in `flatMap`: passing `flatten` directly would hand `flatMap`'s index as the `seen` argument — the same arity trap as `map(parseInt)`.

JavaScript engines do not implement tail-call optimisation in practice, despite it being specified — Safari is the only engine that shipped it. So "make it tail recursive" is not a portable answer; converting to iteration is.

Something to say about the debugging process rather than the fix: a stack-overflow trace shows the same few frames repeating, which immediately distinguishes "missing base case" from "legitimately deep data". If the repeating cycle spans several distinct functions, suspect mutual recursion or a cycle in the data.
keyPoints: Missing base case: `children` may be `undefined` on a leaf
A cycle recurses forever — track visited nodes in a `Set`
Passing `flatten` directly to `flatMap` reintroduces the arity trap
Deep-but-acyclic data still overflows; convert to an explicit stack
Tail-call optimisation is specified but not implemented in practice
commonMistakes: Adding a depth limit instead of detecting cycles.
Claiming tail recursion solves stack depth in browsers.
followUps: How would you detect a cycle without a `Set`?
What does a stack-overflow trace tell you?

interview:iv-dbg-optional-chain-swallow.shortAnswer: It converts a missing or malformed order into a confident display of `$0.00`. Optional chaining is right at genuine optional boundaries, but here it hides a data bug behind a plausible-looking number — which is worse than an error, because nobody investigates a total that renders fine.
deepAnswer: The question to ask of every `?.` is: **is absence expected here?** If `summary` is legitimately optional — a draft order that has not been priced yet — the chain is correct and `0` may be the right display. If `summary` should always be present by the time this renders, the chain is silently absorbing a broken invariant.

The failure mode is specifically bad because it is plausible. A thrown error produces a stack trace pointing at the exact property; a rendered `$0.00` produces a support ticket six weeks later saying "the totals are sometimes wrong", with nothing to trace.

The same critique applies to a blanket `try`/`catch` that returns a default, and to `||` defaulting on a value that should never be falsy. The shared anti-pattern is treating "make the error go away" as equivalent to "handle the error".

Where optional chaining genuinely earns its place: reading from a response whose schema legitimately varies, an event target that may be `null`, an optional callback (`options.onDone?.()`), or DOM lookups that may not match. In those cases absence is part of the contract, not a symptom.

A pragmatic middle ground for a case like this is to default **and** report: render `0`, but log or increment a metric so the invariant violation is visible. Resilient for the user, still observable for you — which is usually the right shape for anything user-facing.

The reviewer's deeper point is about where validation belongs. If orders are validated once at the boundary where they enter the app, the interior can read `order.summary.total` directly and any violation surfaces at the edge with full context. Scattered `?.` throughout the interior is a sign the boundary check is missing.
keyPoints: Ask whether absence is expected — if not, `?.` hides a broken invariant
A plausible wrong value is worse than a loud error
Give "legitimately absent" its own explicit state
Same critique applies to blanket `try`/`catch` and `||` defaults
Default **and** report when the UI must stay resilient
Scattered `?.` in the interior usually means the boundary check is missing
commonMistakes: Treating optional chaining as universally good defensive practice.
Equating "no error is thrown" with "the error is handled".
followUps: Where is optional chaining clearly correct?
Where should the validation for this live instead?

interview:iv-dbg-test-time-dependent.shortAnswer: The test depends on the real clock. `getMonth() + 1` is wrong whenever the 30-day window lands in the same month or wraps past December, and it also breaks across daylight-saving transitions. Inject a fixed clock and assert the actual instant, not a derived calendar field.
deepAnswer: Three separate sources of nondeterminism are in play. Real "now" varies, so the arithmetic lands differently depending on the date CI happens to run. `getMonth() + 1` overflows: run it in December and `created.getMonth() + 1` is `12`, which is not a valid month index — the assertion compares against a number `getMonth()` can never return. And in a timezone with daylight saving, 30 days is not always 720 hours, so a naive day-count can be off by an hour and cross a date boundary.

Note the test now also checks the **boundary on both sides**. The original only asserted "not expired", which would still pass if `isExpired` always returned `false`. Testing one side of a threshold is a common way to write a test that cannot fail.

If the production code calls `Date.now()` internally rather than accepting a date, that is the real defect and the test is only revealing it. Injecting the clock — a `now = () => Date.now()` parameter, or a `Clock` dependency — makes the code testable and is the change worth arguing for. Fake timers (`vi.useFakeTimers`, `jest.useFakeTimers`) are the alternative when you cannot change the signature.
Pin the environment too: run CI with a fixed `TZ` so a machine in a different region does not produce different results from a developer laptop.

The general rule for flaky tests: find the ambient input. Clock, timezone, locale, random numbers, network, filesystem ordering, test execution order and shared state between tests are the usual suspects. "Passes locally, fails weekly in CI" is almost always the clock or a date boundary.
keyPoints: The test reads the real clock — the result depends on the run date
`getMonth() + 1` overflows in December and assumes month-length arithmetic
Daylight saving means 30 days is not always 720 hours
Inject the clock; assert a fixed ISO instant, and test both sides of the boundary
Pin `TZ` in CI; flakiness usually traces to an ambient input

Asserting only the "not expired" side, leaving a test that cannot fail.

interview:iv-bul-virtualisation.shortAnswer: Do not put 50,000 rows in the DOM. Render only the visible window plus a small buffer, absolutely positioned inside a container sized to the full list — virtualisation. Before that, ask whether the user needs 50,000 rows at all, because pagination or server-side search is often the better product answer.
deepAnswer: The reason it fails naively is that every node costs memory, layout and style recalculation. Fifty thousand rows with ten cells each is half a million elements; layout alone takes seconds, scrolling drops frames, and the memory footprint can crash a mobile browser.

Virtualisation renders only what is visible. The mechanics: a scroll container with a spacer sized to `rowCount × rowHeight` so the scrollbar is correct, a computed start index from `scrollTop / rowHeight`, and roughly `viewportHeight / rowHeight` rows rendered plus a few above and below as overscan. On scroll, recompute the window and translate the rendered block into position.

Recycling matters as much as windowing: reusing the same DOM nodes and updating their content avoids creating and destroying elements on every scroll event, which is what causes garbage-collection pauses mid-scroll.

Variable row heights are where it gets hard, and it is worth saying so. Fixed heights make the arithmetic trivial. Variable heights need measurement and an estimate that is corrected as rows are measured, which can cause the scrollbar to jump. That complexity is the main argument for using a maintained library rather than writing it.

The costs to state honestly: Ctrl+F does not find unrendered rows, screen readers only see the rendered window unless `aria-rowcount`/`aria-rowindex` are set correctly, print output is wrong, and deep-linking to a row needs explicit scroll-to-index support. Accessibility in particular is the part hand-rolled implementations usually get wrong.

Cheaper alternatives worth considering first: `content-visibility: auto` lets the browser skip rendering work for off-screen content with a one-line CSS change; pagination avoids the problem entirely and is often what users prefer for tabular data; and server-side filtering means the client never receives 50,000 rows in the first place.
And the data side matters independently of rendering: transferring and parsing a 50,000-row JSON payload is its own cost, so the fix is frequently in the API rather than the view.
keyPoints: Render only the visible window plus overscan; size a spacer for the scrollbar
Recycle nodes rather than recreating them each scroll
Variable row heights require measurement and cause scroll jumps
Costs: Ctrl+F, screen readers, printing, deep links — set `aria-rowcount`/`aria-rowindex`
`content-visibility: auto` and pagination are cheaper first options

commonMistakes: Reaching for virtualisation before asking whether pagination fits the product.
Shipping a virtual list with no accessibility attributes.

interview:iv-bul-offline.shortAnswer: Treat request failure as the source of truth and `navigator.onLine` as a hint. Show a clear offline state, queue or preserve the user's unsaved work, and retry when connectivity returns — driven by the `online` event plus a real request, not by the flag alone.
deepAnswer: `navigator.onLine` and the `online`/`offline` events are unreliable in a specific way worth knowing: `false` means definitively no network, but `true` only means the device has **a** network interface. Connected to a wifi captive portal with no internet, it reports `true`. So it is useful for reacting quickly, never for deciding whether a request will succeed.

The reliable signal is a failed `fetch`. `fetch` rejects on network failure — as opposed to resolving with an error status — so `catch` with a check that it is not an `AbortError` is where offline actually surfaces.

What the UI owes the user: say plainly that the connection was lost rather than showing a generic error; never discard what they typed; disable or clearly mark actions that cannot succeed; and retry automatically when the connection returns rather than making them find the button again.

Preserving unsaved work is the part that matters most and is skipped most often. Persisting a draft to `localStorage` or IndexedDB as the user types means a dropped connection plus a refresh does not lose an hour of writing.

For queued mutations, the pattern is an outbox: store the intended change locally, apply it optimistically to the UI, and flush the queue when connectivity returns. That requires the requests to be idempotent or to carry an idempotency key, or a flush after a partial failure duplicates work.

A service worker is what makes a genuinely offline-capable app possible — cache the shell so the page loads at all, serve cached data with a clear "showing offline data" indicator, and use Background Sync where available to flush the outbox even after the tab is closed. It is also the layer most likely to serve stale content after a deploy, so it needs a deliberate update strategy.
Testing this is straightforward and worth mentioning: DevTools has an offline throttling preset, and Playwright can simulate offline, so the offline path should be covered rather than assumed.
keyPoints: `navigator.onLine === true` only means an interface exists — captive portals report online
A rejected `fetch` is the reliable signal; distinguish it from `AbortError`
Never discard unsaved input; persist drafts locally
An outbox queue needs idempotent requests or idempotency keys
A service worker enables offline loading and Background Sync
Simulate offline in DevTools and in end-to-end tests
commonMistakes: Trusting `navigator.onLine` as a guarantee that requests will succeed.

interview:iv-bul-layout-shift.shortAnswer: Layout shift comes from content whose size is not known until it arrives — images without dimensions, web fonts swapping in, ads and embeds, and content injected above what the user is already reading. The fix is to reserve the space in advance so the arriving content lands in a box that already exists.
deepAnswer: Cumulative Layout Shift measures this, and it is a user-experience problem before it is a metric: the classic damage is tapping a button that moves at the moment of the tap, so the user activates something else.

**Images and video**: always set `width` and `height` attributes (or an `aspect-ratio` in CSS). Modern browsers use them to compute the aspect ratio and reserve the correct box before the file loads, even for a responsive image whose rendered size differs.

**Fonts**: a web font that replaces the fallback at a different metric reflows every line of text. `font-display: swap` avoids invisible text but makes the shift visible; `size-adjust` and `ascent-override` on the fallback face, or a metric-compatible fallback, minimise the difference. Preloading the font shortens the window in which any of it matters.

**Injected content**: anything inserted above the current scroll position — a cookie banner, a promotional bar, an error message — pushes everything down. Reserve the space, or overlay it rather than inserting it into flow.

**Async content**: an ad slot, an embed, or a lazily-loaded component needs a container with a fixed minimum height. A skeleton placeholder that matches the final dimensions solves the problem and improves perceived speed at the same time.

The deliberate exception: a shift within 500ms of a user interaction is excluded from the metric, because expanding an accordion the user clicked is expected. Shifts that are not caused by an interaction are the ones that count.

Measurement: the Performance panel highlights shifted regions and names the culprit, and `PerformanceObserver` with the `layout-shift` entry type reports it from real users — which is where you find the shifts that only happen on slow connections.
keyPoints: Reserve space before content arrives — do not let arrival resize the box
`width`/`height` attributes or `aspect-ratio` on every image and video
Font swaps reflow text; use metric-compatible fallbacks and preload
Overlay injected banners rather than inserting them into flow
Skeletons with the final dimensions fix async content and perceived speed together
Shifts within 500ms of an interaction are excluded; measure the rest with `PerformanceObserver`
commonMistakes: Omitting image dimensions because the CSS sets the size responsively.
Inserting a cookie banner into normal flow above the fold.

interview:iv-bul-cross-tab.shortAnswer: Each tab is a separate JavaScript context with its own memory, so in-memory state diverges immediately while `localStorage`, cookies and IndexedDB are shared. `BroadcastChannel` is the direct way to notify sibling tabs; the `storage` event is the older fallback, and it fires in **other** tabs only.
deepAnswer: What actually breaks: logging out in one tab leaves the others showing an authenticated UI until their next failed request; a stale tab overwrites a newer edit made elsewhere; polling and websockets are duplicated per tab, multiplying server load; and a token refreshed in two tabs at once can invalidate itself if the backend rotates refresh tokens.

**The `storage` event** is the fallback and has one property people trip over: it fires in every **other** tab on the origin but never in the tab that made the write. That makes it usable as a signal, but it means the writing tab must update itself separately.

For the auth case specifically, an `HttpOnly` cookie is shared across tabs automatically, so a logout that clears the cookie affects all of them at the request level — the broadcast is then only about updating the UI promptly rather than about correctness.

To avoid duplicated work, elect one tab as the leader and let it own the websocket or polling loop, broadcasting results to the others. `navigator.locks.request` with a never-released lock is a clean way to do leader election; a `SharedWorker` is the alternative where supported, giving one shared context for all tabs of the origin.

For concurrent edits, the last-write-wins default is what causes silent data loss. A version or `ETag` on the record lets the server reject a stale write with `409 Conflict`, which the client can surface as "this changed elsewhere" rather than overwriting.

Testing this is easy to skip and worth doing: open two tabs and exercise logout, session expiry and a concurrent edit. Most cross-tab bugs are found in about two minutes that way, and never by a single-tab test suite.
keyPoints: Tabs share storage and cookies but not memory — in-memory state diverges
`BroadcastChannel` for direct same-origin messaging; the sender is excluded
The `storage` event fires only in **other** tabs
Elect a leader (Web Locks or `SharedWorker`) so polling is not duplicated
Version records so a stale write gets a `409` instead of overwriting
Test logout, expiry and concurrent edits with two tabs open
commonMistakes: Expecting the `storage` event to fire in the tab that wrote the value.
Letting every tab open its own websocket.

interview:iv-ac-race-conditions.shortAnswer: Single-threaded rules out **data** races — no torn reads, no half-finished writes. It does not rule out **ordering** races: every `await` is a suspension point where other code runs, so state you read before it may have changed by the time you resume.
deepAnswer: The guarantee run-to-completion gives you is that a synchronous block cannot be interrupted. `count += 1` is atomic. What it does not give you is that `const a = state.x; await f(); use(a, state.x)` sees a consistent `state.x` — anything can have run in between.

The recurring shapes:

- **Stale response**: two requests in flight, the slower one returns last and overwrites the newer result.
- **Write after unmount / navigation**: an `await` resolves after the component or view is gone, and the continuation writes to something that should no longer exist.
- **Read-modify-write across an await**: two handlers both read a value, both compute a new one from it, and the second overwrites the first's change.
- **Double submit**: the user clicks twice before the first request settles, creating two records.

The defences, and they are different per shape. For stale responses, a sequence number checked **after** the await, or `AbortController` to cancel the superseded request. For unmount, an abort signal or a liveness flag checked after the await. For read-modify-write, do not carry a read across an await — re-read after it, or use a functional update (`setState(prev => ...)`) so the computation happens against current state.
For double submit, disable the control and deduplicate the in-flight promise by key, so concurrent callers share one request rather than starting several.

The reviewing heuristic worth stating: **treat every `await` as a place where the world may have changed**. Anything read before it and used after it is a candidate bug. That single habit catches most of these before they ship.

Server-side races are a separate problem the client cannot fix. Two tabs updating the same record need optimistic concurrency — a version or `ETag` the server checks — because no amount of client-side sequencing prevents two legitimate clients from conflicting.

And these are exactly the bugs that are hard to reproduce, because they depend on timing. That is why the fix is structural rather than "add a small delay", and why network throttling is the tool that makes them reproducible.
keyPoints: Single-threaded prevents data races, not ordering races
Every `await` is a suspension point where other code runs
Shapes: stale response, write after unmount, read-modify-write, double submit
Check sequence or abort after the await; re-read rather than carrying state across it
Deduplicate in-flight requests and disable the control for double submit
Cross-client conflicts need server-side optimistic concurrency
commonMistakes: Concluding that single-threaded means race-free.
Fixing a timing bug with a delay rather than a sequence or abort check.

interview:iv-ac-forawait-vs-all.shortAnswer: `Promise.all` when the work is independent and you want it concurrent — it starts everything at once and waits. `for await...of` when the items must be processed in order, when each depends on the previous, when the source is a genuine stream, or when you must not overwhelm a service.
deepAnswer: `Promise.all(items.map(fn))` starts every operation immediately. Total time is roughly the slowest one, which is the right default for N independent requests.

`for await (const x of source)` processes one at a time. Total time is the sum. That is the correct choice when the operations are genuinely dependent — each request needs the previous cursor — or when order of side effects matters.

The distinction people miss: `for await...of` also consumes an **async iterable**, which `Promise.all` cannot. Paginated APIs, streamed response bodies, and anything where the number of items is not known upfront can only be driven this way — you cannot build an array of promises for pages whose cursors do not exist yet.

Memory is the other axis. `Promise.all` holds every result until all settle, so a thousand large responses are all resident at once. A `for await` loop can process and discard each item, which is what makes it viable for streams.

Failure semantics differ too. `Promise.all` rejects on the first failure while the rest continue unobserved; a `for await` loop throws at the item that failed and simply stops, leaving later items untouched. Which is correct depends on whether partial progress is acceptable — and `allSettled` is the third option when you want every result regardless.

The practical middle ground is bounded concurrency: neither one-at-a-time nor all-at-once, but N in flight. For a few hundred items against a rate-limited API that is almost always the right answer, and it is worth naming rather than presenting the choice as binary.

The anti-pattern to call out: `items.forEach(async (x) => await fn(x))` looks like sequencing and is neither — `forEach` discards the promises, so everything starts at once and nothing is awaited. If you want concurrency use `Promise.all`; if you want sequence use `for...of`.
keyPoints: `Promise.all` for independent work — time is the slowest item
`for await` for dependent, ordered, or streamed work — time is the sum
Only `for await` can consume an async iterable of unknown length
`Promise.all` holds every result in memory; a loop can discard as it goes
First-failure-aborts versus stop-at-the-failing-item
Bounded concurrency is usually the real answer for large lists
commonMistakes: Using sequential awaits for independent requests and multiplying latency.
Using `forEach` with `async` and getting neither concurrency control nor sequencing.

interview:iv-ac-double-submit.shortAnswer: Disable the control and guard with an in-flight flag on the client, but the actual fix is server-side: send a client-generated idempotency key with the request so a duplicate is recognised and the original result returned. Client guards improve the experience; only the server can guarantee correctness.
deepAnswer: The `finally` is essential: without it, a failed request leaves the button permanently disabled and the user stuck.

Why that is not sufficient: the network can duplicate a request without any second click. A request that times out may have succeeded with the response lost, and a retry — yours, or the browser's, or a proxy's — creates a second order. No amount of client-side guarding prevents that.

The correct mechanism is an **idempotency key**: the client generates a unique id (`crypto.randomUUID()`) once per logical operation, sends it as a header, and the server records it. A second request with the same key returns the stored result rather than performing the work again. This is exactly what payment APIs do, and it is the answer that shows production experience.
The key must be generated when the user starts the operation, not per HTTP attempt — otherwise a retry sends a new key and defeats the purpose.

Also worth covering: after success, navigate away or reset the form so the same submission cannot be repeated; and if the user genuinely might want two identical orders, the deduplication window has to be bounded rather than permanent.
The general principle to state: client-side controls are user-experience improvements, and correctness for anything that creates, charges or deletes has to be enforced where the data lives.
keyPoints: Disable the control and guard with an in-flight flag — reset it in `finally`
A `disabled` attribute alone can lose to a fast second click or an Enter submit
The network can duplicate a request with no second click at all
An idempotency key generated once per operation is the real fix
Do not regenerate the key per retry
Client guards are UX; correctness belongs on the server
