interview:iv-util-relative-time.shortAnswer: Compute the difference, pick the largest unit that fits, and hand the number to `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat` rather than building the string yourself. Pass "now" in as a parameter — a function that reads the clock internally cannot be tested deterministically.
deepAnswer: Keeping the sign on `seconds` is what makes past and future both work — a negative value gives "3 minutes ago", a positive one "in 3 minutes". Taking the absolute value too early is the usual bug, producing "ago" for scheduled events.

`Intl.RelativeTimeFormat` is the reason not to hand-roll this. It handles pluralisation rules that are far more complex than "add an s" — Polish has three plural forms, Arabic six — and `numeric: "auto"` gives "yesterday" and "last week" instead of "1 day ago", which is what users expect.

The testability point is the one interviewers press on. A function calling `new Date()` internally produces a different answer every run, so tests either sleep, mock globals, or assert loosely. Passing `now` as a parameter makes it a pure function of its inputs and the test a one-liner with two fixed dates.

Where hand-rolling goes wrong beyond plurals: a "month" is not 30 days, so long intervals drift; daylight-saving transitions mean a day is not always 86,400 seconds; and rounding at boundaries produces "60 minutes ago" instead of "1 hour ago" if you truncate per unit instead of choosing the unit first.

The design decision to raise: relative time is friendly but imprecise, and it goes stale on screen. The usual pattern is relative text with the absolute timestamp in a `title` or a `<time datetime>` attribute, so hovering or assistive technology gives the exact value. And a list of relative timestamps needs re-rendering on an interval or it silently becomes wrong.
keyPoints: Pick the largest fitting unit, then round within it
Keep the sign so future times read "in 3 minutes"
`Intl.RelativeTimeFormat` handles plural rules and "yesterday"
Inject `now` — a function reading the clock cannot be tested cleanly
Months and days are not fixed lengths; DST breaks naive arithmetic
Pair relative text with an absolute timestamp in `<time datetime>`
commonMistakes: Taking the absolute difference first and losing past/future.
Building plurals by appending "s".
followUps: Why does injecting `now` matter for tests?
What does `numeric: "auto"` change?

interview:iv-refactor-lookup-table.shortAnswer: Replace the chain with a lookup from the value to a handler function. Each case becomes a named entry, adding one is a data change rather than a control-flow change, and the dispatch shrinks to a single lookup with an explicit default.
deepAnswer: What this buys: the rates become **data** that can be read at a glance, unit-tested individually, or eventually loaded from configuration; adding a method touches one line and no branching; and the dispatch logic exists in exactly one place.

A `Map` rather than a plain object is the safer default here because the key comes from outside the function. With a plain object, a `method` of `"constructor"` or `"toString"` finds an inherited function and takes the wrong branch. `Object.create(null)` is the alternative if you want object syntax.

Keep the explicit unknown-value error. Silently returning `undefined` or a zero cost for an unrecognised method is worse than the original chain — the whole point of the `else throw` was to make an unknown case loud, and the refactor must preserve it.

When **not** to do this: if the branches test different things (`if (user.isAdmin) ... else if (weight > 50) ...`) rather than one value, a lookup does not apply and forcing it produces something worse. This pattern fits single-value dispatch specifically.

The next step up, when each case needs several related behaviours rather than one function, is the strategy pattern — a map from key to an object of methods. And when the branching is on the **type** of a thing you own, polymorphism replaces the map entirely.

A `switch` is the middle ground and is perfectly reasonable for a handful of cases; it is clearer than a chain and does not require the indirection of a map. The lookup wins when the set is large, is genuinely data, or is likely to be extended.
keyPoints: Map the value to a handler; dispatch becomes one lookup
Cases become data — readable, testable, extensible without new branches
Use a `Map` (or `Object.create(null)`) for keys that come from outside
Preserve an explicit error for unknown values
Only applies to single-value dispatch, not to unrelated conditions
Strategy objects or polymorphism are the next steps up; `switch` is fine for a few cases
commonMistakes: Using a plain object and taking the wrong branch on an inherited key.
Losing the unknown-value error and returning `undefined` silently.
followUps: When would you keep the `switch` instead?
How does this become the strategy pattern?

interview:iv-out-task-microtask.shortAnswer: `A E C D B`. All synchronous code runs first, then the **entire** microtask queue in FIFO order, and only then the timer callback — which is a macrotask.
deepAnswer: Step one: the script runs to completion. `A` prints. `setTimeout` only **schedules**; it returns immediately. `.then` only **registers** a reaction on an already-resolved promise, which enqueues a microtask. `queueMicrotask` enqueues another. Then `E` prints. The synchronous phase is now over.

Step two: before the event loop is allowed to pick up any task, it drains the microtask queue completely. `C` was enqueued before `D`, so `C` then `D`. Promise reactions and `queueMicrotask` callbacks share one queue — there is no separate "promise queue" that outranks it.
Step three: the loop takes the next macrotask, which is the expired `setTimeout` callback, and `B` prints.
The `0` in `setTimeout(fn, 0)` is a **minimum** delay, not a promise of immediacy. Even with an empty queue, browsers clamp deeply nested timers to roughly 4ms.
The practical consequence: a microtask that enqueues another microtask can starve rendering entirely, because the loop will not move on until the queue is empty.
keyPoints: Synchronous code first, always
The whole microtask queue drains before the next macrotask
`Promise.then` and `queueMicrotask` share one FIFO queue
`setTimeout(fn, 0)` is a minimum delay, not "run now"
Infinite microtask recursion starves rendering
commonMistakes: Assuming `setTimeout(fn, 0)` beats a promise callback.
Thinking promise reactions have their own higher-priority queue.
followUps: What happens if a microtask enqueues another microtask?
Where does `requestAnimationFrame` fit?

interview:iv-out-plus-coercion.shortAnswer: `12`, `2`, `[object Object]`, `true`, `false`, `true`. `+` prefers string concatenation when either side is a string; every other operator here coerces to number, and `null` follows two different rules depending on whether the operator is an equality or a relational one.
deepAnswer: `1 + "2"` — `+` is the only overloaded arithmetic operator. If either operand becomes a string after `ToPrimitive`, it concatenates. Result: the string `"12"`.
`"3" - 1` — `-` has no string meaning, so both sides go through `ToNumber`. `3 - 1` is `2`.
`[] + {}` — both are objects, so `ToPrimitive` runs on each: `[]` becomes `""` and `{}` becomes `"[object Object]"`. Concatenating gives `"[object Object]"`.
`[] == false` — loose equality converts `false` to `0`, then the array to the primitive `""`, then `""` to `0`. `0 == 0` is `true`. This is exactly why `==` is avoided.
`null == 0` is `false`: the specification gives `null` and `undefined` a hard-coded rule for `==` — they equal each other and nothing else. No numeric conversion happens.

`null >= 0` is `true`: relational operators have **no** such special case, so `null` is converted with `ToNumber` to `0`, and `0 >= 0` holds. The pair `null == 0` false but `null >= 0` true is the canonical demonstration that `==` and `<`/`>` do not share a coercion path.
keyPoints: `+` concatenates if either operand is a string after `ToPrimitive`
Other arithmetic operators force `ToNumber`
`null`/`undefined` have a special-cased `==` rule
Relational operators do not — they numeric-convert `null` to `0`
Use `===` and convert explicitly
commonMistakes: Assuming `==` and `>=` coerce the same way.
Expecting `[] + {}` to be an object.
followUps: Why is `null > 0` false but `null >= 0` true?
When is `==` acceptable?

interview:iv-out-array-holes.shortAnswer: `3`, `3`, `false`, `-1`, `undefined`. A hole is not the value `undefined` — it is a **missing index**. `length` counts it, `map` preserves it without calling the callback, `in` reports it absent, and `indexOf` skips it entirely.
deepAnswer: `a.length` is `3` because `length` is one more than the highest index, regardless of which indices actually exist.
`a.map(...)` returns an array of length `3`, but the callback never runs for index `1` — the hole is copied through as a hole. This is why `map` cannot be used to fill a sparse array.

`1 in a` is `false`: the property `"1"` genuinely does not exist on the object. Reading `a[1]` still yields `undefined`, because reading a missing property always does — which is why holes are so easy to mistake for `undefined` values.

`a.indexOf(undefined)` is `-1`. `indexOf` skips holes outright. Note that `a.includes(undefined)` would return `true`, because `includes` does **not** skip them — a genuine inconsistency between two methods that otherwise look interchangeable.
Practical advice: never create sparse arrays deliberately. `new Array(3)` is sparse; `Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => 0)` or `new Array(3).fill(0)` gives you real elements.
keyPoints: A hole is a missing index, not an `undefined` value
`length` counts holes; `map`/`forEach` skip them but preserve position
`in` distinguishes a hole from a stored `undefined`
`indexOf` skips holes; `includes` does not
Use `fill` or `Array.from` instead of `new Array(n)` alone
commonMistakes: Treating a hole as a stored `undefined`.
Expecting `map` to visit holes.
followUps: Why does `includes` behave differently from `indexOf`?
How do you build a dense array of length n?

interview:iv-out-key-order.shortAnswer: `1,2,b,a` then `string`. Integer-like keys come first in ascending numeric order, then string keys in insertion order. And every key is a string — `2` became `"2"` when it was used as a property name.
deepAnswer: Property order is specified, not arbitrary, since ES2015. The rule for own string keys is: integer indices first, ascending, then the remaining string keys in creation order.
`2` and `1` are integer indices, so they lead, sorted numerically: `1`, `2`. `b` and `a` are ordinary string keys, so they follow in insertion order: `b`, then `a`.
`typeof Object.keys(o)[0]` is `"string"` because object property names are always strings (or symbols). Writing `{ 2: 2 }` stores the key `"2"`.

The practical consequence: if you use numeric-looking ids as object keys and expect insertion order — a cache keyed by database id, say — you get them back sorted numerically instead. `Map` preserves true insertion order and allows non-string keys, which is why it is the right structure for that job.
Symbols are excluded from `Object.keys` entirely; retrieve them with `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols`.
keyPoints: Integer-like keys first, ascending; then string keys in insertion order
Property names are always strings or symbols
Numeric-looking ids silently reorder — use `Map` if order matters
`Object.keys` never returns symbol keys
commonMistakes: Claiming object key order is undefined.
Expecting numeric keys to keep insertion order.
followUps: When would you choose `Map` over a plain object?
Where do symbol keys appear?

interview:iv-out-finally-return.shortAnswer: `finally runs`, `try`, `finally`. The `finally` block always runs before the function actually returns, but it only **changes** the result if it performs its own `return` (or `throw`), which overrides the pending one.
deepAnswer: In `a`, the return value `"try"` is computed and held pending, `finally` runs its side effect, and then the pending return completes. The log appears before `console.log(a())` prints, which is why `finally runs` comes first.
In `b`, `finally` executes its own `return`. That abrupt completion replaces the pending one entirely, so `"finally"` is what the caller sees.

The same override applies to exceptions: a `return` in `finally` swallows an in-flight exception, making the function look successful when it failed. That is why linters ship a `no-unsafe-finally` rule — the `b` here is deliberately wrong code shown for its behaviour.
Rule to state: use `finally` for cleanup — closing handles, clearing loading flags, releasing locks — and never for producing a value or controlling flow.

Note also that the returned value is evaluated **before** `finally` runs. If `finally` mutates an object you already returned, the caller sees the mutation, because the reference was captured, not a copy.
keyPoints: `finally` always runs before the function returns
A `return` in `finally` overrides the pending return
It also swallows in-flight exceptions — a real bug source
`finally` is for cleanup, not for values
The return value is evaluated before `finally` runs
commonMistakes: Thinking `finally` cannot change the result.
Using `finally` to normalise the return value.
followUps: What happens if `try` throws and `finally` returns?
Why do linters ban this?

interview:iv-out-default-param-eval.shortAnswer: `1`, `1`, `1`, `2`. A default parameter expression is evaluated **on every call where the argument is missing**, so `[]` produces a brand-new array each time. Defaulting to an outer variable instead shares one array across calls.
deepAnswer: This is the crucial difference from Python, where a mutable default is created once at definition time and becomes a notorious trap. JavaScript evaluates the expression per call, so `list = []` is fresh each time and both `push` calls return `1`.
`list = shared` also evaluates per call, but the expression resolves to the **same** array every time. The mutation therefore accumulates: `1`, then `2`.

Defaults are evaluated left to right, and later parameters can reference earlier ones: `function f(a, b = a * 2)` is legal. The reverse is not — referencing a later parameter hits its temporal dead zone.
A default only applies when the argument is `undefined`. Passing `null` explicitly overrides it, which is a frequent source of "why did my default not apply?".
The practical takeaway: `= []` and `= {}` are safe defaults in JavaScript, but a default that closes over shared state is stateful and should be treated as such.
keyPoints: Default expressions evaluate per call, not once at definition
`= []` gives a fresh array every call
Defaulting to an outer variable shares mutable state
Defaults apply only for `undefined`, not `null`
Later defaults may reference earlier parameters, not later ones
commonMistakes: Importing Python's mutable-default rule into JavaScript.
Expecting `null` to trigger the default.
followUps: Why does passing `null` skip the default?
Can a default reference a later parameter?

interview:iv-out-destructuring-defaults.shortAnswer: `1`, `null`, `0`, `4`. A destructuring default fires only when the value is exactly `undefined`. `null` and `0` are real values and are kept, even though both are falsy.
deepAnswer: `a` is present but `undefined`, which is the one trigger for a default — so `1` is used. There is no difference here between a missing key and a key set to `undefined`.

`b` is `null`. `null` is not `undefined`, so no default applies and `null` survives. This is the case that bites people who use defaults to sanitise API responses, since JSON has `null` but no `undefined`.
`c` is `0` — falsy, but a perfectly valid value — so it is kept. This is the same distinction that separates `??` from `||`.
`d` is absent entirely, so reading it yields `undefined` and the default `4` applies.

If you genuinely need `null` handled too, do it explicitly: `const b = obj.b ?? 2` after destructuring, or normalise the payload at the boundary before destructuring it. Do not reach for `||`, which would also replace `0` and `""`.
keyPoints: Defaults trigger on `undefined` only
`null` and `0` are kept despite being falsy
A missing key and an explicit `undefined` behave identically
JSON gives you `null`, never `undefined`
Use `??` — not `||` — to also cover `null`
commonMistakes: Assuming defaults cover all falsy values.
Relying on defaults to clean up JSON nulls.
followUps: How does this relate to `??` versus `||`?
How would you handle `null` from an API?

interview:iv-out-prototype-shadow.shortAnswer: `woof`, `generic`, `false`, `woof`, `changed`. Assignment creates an **own** property on the instance rather than modifying the prototype. That own property shadows the prototype one permanently, so later prototype changes are invisible to `a1` but visible to `a2`.
deepAnswer: Reads walk the prototype chain; writes do not. `a1.sound = "woof"` installs `sound` directly on `a1` — it does not touch `Animal.prototype`, which is why `a2` still reports `generic`.
`Object.hasOwn(a2, "sound")` is `false`: `a2` has no own `sound` at all. Its reads resolve one level up the chain each time, dynamically.

After `Animal.prototype.sound = "changed"`, `a1` still reads `woof` because its own property is found first and the lookup stops there. `a2` reads `changed`, because it never had its own copy and re-resolves through the chain on every access.
This is why prototype mutation is a live link, not a copy: instances that have not shadowed a property see updates immediately.

The classic bug this causes: a mutable object on the prototype — `Animal.prototype.tags = []` — is shared by every instance, because `a1.tags.push(x)` mutates rather than assigns and therefore never shadows. Per-instance state belongs in the constructor or in a class field.
keyPoints: Reads traverse the prototype chain; writes create own properties
An own property permanently shadows the prototype one
Non-shadowing instances see later prototype changes live
`Object.hasOwn` distinguishes own from inherited
Mutable prototype values are shared by every instance
commonMistakes: Believing assignment updates the prototype.
Putting arrays or objects on the prototype as per-instance state.
followUps: Why does `push` on a prototype array affect all instances?
How does a setter on the prototype change this?

interview:iv-out-generator-break.shortAnswer: `1`, `2`, `cleanup`, `done`. `break` does not just abandon the generator — `for...of` calls the iterator's `return()` method, which resumes the generator at the `yield` and unwinds it, running the `finally` block.
deepAnswer: The loop pulls `1`, prints it, pulls `2`, prints it, and then hits `break`.

The iteration protocol specifies that an early exit from `for...of` — via `break`, `return`, or a thrown exception — calls `iterator.return()` if it exists. A generator implements `return()` as "resume as if a `return` statement appeared at the current `yield`".
That injected return unwinds the generator body, and because the `yield` sits inside `try`, the `finally` block executes. `cleanup` prints before the statement after the loop.

This is exactly what makes generators usable for resource management: open a handle before the loop over `yield`s, close it in `finally`, and consumers get cleanup whether they exhaust the sequence or bail out early.

The important caveat: it only works through the iteration protocol. Calling `it.next()` manually and then simply dropping the reference never runs `finally` — nothing is guaranteed by garbage collection, so the cleanup would just never happen. Call `it.return()` yourself if you drive an iterator by hand.
keyPoints: Early exit from `for...of` calls `iterator.return()`
A generator's `return()` unwinds the body, running `finally`
This makes `try`/`finally` in generators a real cleanup mechanism
Manual `.next()` driving must call `.return()` explicitly
Dropping an iterator does not trigger cleanup — GC guarantees nothing
commonMistakes: Assuming `break` abandons the generator without cleanup.
Relying on garbage collection to run `finally`.
followUps: What runs `finally` if the loop body throws?
How do you clean up when driving `.next()` by hand?

interview:iv-out-all-vs-allsettled.shortAnswer: `all rejected: boom` then `fulfilled,rejected`. `Promise.all` rejects as soon as any input rejects, giving you that one reason. `Promise.allSettled` never rejects — it waits for every input and reports each outcome as a status object.
deepAnswer: `Promise.all` short-circuits on the first rejection. The `.then` is skipped entirely and `.catch` receives the rejection reason directly — not an array, just the single `Error`.
Critically, `Promise.all` does not cancel the other operations. `ok` still settles; you simply lose access to its value. If those operations have side effects, they still happen.
`Promise.allSettled` resolves with one descriptor per input: `{ status: "fulfilled", value }` or `{ status: "rejected", reason }`. It rejects only if given something that is not iterable.

Choosing between them is a design decision. `all` when the results are jointly required — three fragments of one page that is meaningless if any is missing. `allSettled` when partial success is useful — a dashboard of independent widgets, where one failing panel should not blank the page.

The two other combinators complete the set: `race` settles with the first result of any kind, which makes it the natural timeout primitive; `any` resolves with the first **fulfilment** and rejects with an `AggregateError` only if all inputs reject.
keyPoints: `all` rejects on the first rejection with that single reason
`all` does not cancel the remaining operations
`allSettled` always fulfils, with per-input status objects
`all` for jointly-required results; `allSettled` for independent ones
`race` settles first-of-any; `any` settles first-fulfilled
commonMistakes: Expecting `all` to hand `.catch` an array of errors.
Believing a rejection cancels the sibling promises.
followUps: How would you add a timeout to a fetch?
When does `Promise.any` reject?

interview:iv-out-typeof-table.shortAnswer: `object`, `number`, `function`, `object`, `true`, `[object Array]`. `typeof null` is a specification bug preserved for compatibility, `NaN` really is a number, and `typeof` cannot distinguish arrays from other objects — that is what `Array.isArray` is for.
deepAnswer: `typeof null === "object"` dates from the first implementation, where the type tag `000` meant object and the null pointer was all zeros. Fixing it would break too much existing code, so it stays. Check with `value === null`.

`typeof NaN === "number"` is correct, not a quirk: `NaN` is a numeric value in IEEE-754 representing an invalid result. Detect it with `Number.isNaN(x)` — never `x === NaN`, which is always `false` because `NaN` is not equal to itself.
`typeof` returns `"function"` for anything callable, the one non-primitive it singles out. Classes also report `"function"`.

`typeof []` is `"object"` because arrays are objects. `Array.isArray` is the reliable test, and it works correctly across iframe or worker boundaries where `instanceof Array` fails, since each realm has its own `Array` constructor.

`Object.prototype.toString.call(x)` reads the internal brand and returns `"[object Array]"`, `"[object Date]"`, `"[object Null]"` and so on. It was the standard type-tagging trick before `Array.isArray` and friends existed, and still turns up in library code.
keyPoints: `typeof null` is `"object"` — a preserved historical bug
`NaN` is genuinely a number; use `Number.isNaN`
`typeof` reports `"function"` for anything callable, classes included
Arrays are objects — use `Array.isArray`, which is realm-safe
`Object.prototype.toString.call` reveals the internal brand
commonMistakes: Using `typeof x === "object"` as a null check.
Comparing against `NaN` with `===`.
followUps: Why does `instanceof Array` fail across iframes?
How do you reliably check for a plain object?

interview:iv-out-float-precision.shortAnswer: Every JavaScript number is an IEEE-754 double. `0.1` and `0.2` have no exact binary representation, so their sum is slightly off `0.3`; and above 2^53 consecutive integers stop being distinguishable.
deepAnswer: `0.1` and `0.2` are stored as the nearest representable doubles. Adding them accumulates both approximations, producing `0.30000000000000004` — not a JavaScript flaw; the same thing happens in C, Java and Python.

Equality therefore fails. The standard workaround for measurements is a tolerance comparison: `Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON` for values near 1. For larger magnitudes you need a relative tolerance, since `EPSILON` is the gap between 1 and the next double, not a universal error bound.
`toFixed(2)` returns the **string** `"0.30"`, not a number. It also rounds by the stored binary value, which is why `(1.005).toFixed(2)` gives `"1.00"` — the stored value is fractionally below 1.005.

`9007199254740992 === 9007199254740993` is `true` because 2^53 is `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1`; beyond that, odd integers cannot be represented and round to their even neighbours. Use `BigInt` for exact large integers, and `Number.isSafeInteger` to check.

For money, the answer expected in an interview is: do not use floats. Store integer minor units (cents) and divide only for display, or use a decimal library. Accumulating a fraction of a cent over millions of rows is a real accounting defect.
keyPoints: All JS numbers are IEEE-754 doubles
`0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3` — compare with a tolerance
`toFixed` returns a string and rounds the stored binary value
Integers above 2^53 are not distinguishable — use `BigInt`
Represent money as integer cents
commonMistakes: Calling this a JavaScript-specific bug.
Treating `toFixed` as returning a number.
followUps: How would you compare two large floats?
How do you represent money correctly?

interview:iv-out-spread-shallow.shortAnswer: `a`, `x,y`, `true`. Spread is a **shallow** copy: top-level primitives are duplicated, but nested objects are copied by reference, so both objects point at the same array.
deepAnswer: `copy.name = "b"` writes a new string onto `copy` only. The original keeps `"a"`, which is the behaviour people expect and the reason shallow copying feels safe at first.
`copy.tags` and `original.tags` are the same array object — spread copied the reference. `push` mutates that shared array, so `original.tags` becomes `["x", "y"]` and the identity check is `true`.
This is the defect that surfaces as "my state updated even though I copied it" in any framework relying on immutable updates. The top level changed identity; the nested level did not.

Fixes, from cheapest to most general: copy the level you are changing (`{ ...original, tags: [...original.tags, "y"] }`), which is the idiomatic pattern and keeps structural sharing for untouched branches; `structuredClone(original)` for a genuine deep copy of data (it handles `Map`, `Set`, `Date` and cycles, but throws on functions and DOM nodes); or a library like Immer for deeply nested trees.
`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` is the old trick and should be named as flawed: it drops `undefined`, functions and symbols, turns `Date` into a string, and throws on cycles.
keyPoints: Spread and `Object.assign` are shallow
Nested objects are shared, not copied
Copy each level you modify: `{ ...o, tags: [...o.tags] }`
`structuredClone` deep-copies data but not functions
`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))` silently loses data
commonMistakes: Calling spread a deep copy.
Reaching for JSON round-tripping without naming its losses.
followUps: How do you update a deeply nested field immutably?
What does `structuredClone` refuse to copy?

interview:iv-out-nullish-vs-or.shortAnswer: `3`, `0`, `none`, `undefined`, `undefined`. `||` falls back on any falsy value — including the meaningful `0` and `""` — while `??` falls back only on `null` or `undefined`. Optional chaining short-circuits to `undefined` rather than throwing.
deepAnswer: `config.retries || 3` is the bug: `0` is falsy, so a deliberate "retry zero times" silently becomes three retries. The same class of bug turns a valid `""` label or a `false` toggle into its default.
`config.retries ?? 3` checks only for `null`/`undefined`, so `0` survives. This is why `??` exists and why it should be the default choice for configuration and API values.
`config.label || "none"` demonstrates the trap on strings — an intentionally blank label is replaced.

`config.nested?.deep?.value` — `nested` is `null`, so the whole chain short-circuits and evaluates to `undefined`. Note it short-circuits to `undefined`, not to `null`, whatever the nullish value was.
`config.missing?.()` is the optional **call** form: because `config.missing` is `undefined`, the call is skipped and the expression is `undefined` instead of throwing "is not a function".
One syntax point worth knowing: `a ?? b || c` is a `SyntaxError`. Mixing `??` with `&&` or `||` requires explicit parentheses, deliberately, so precedence is never guessed.
keyPoints: `||` falls back on every falsy value; `??` only on `null`/`undefined`
`0`, `""` and `false` are the values `||` destroys
Optional chaining short-circuits to `undefined`
`?.()` skips the call instead of throwing
Mixing `??` with `||`/`&&` unparenthesised is a `SyntaxError`
commonMistakes: Using `||` for numeric or boolean defaults.
Expecting `?.` to yield `null` when the base was `null`.
followUps: When is `||` still the right operator?
What does `??=` do?

interview:iv-out-hoisting-kinds.shortAnswer: `function`, `undefined`, `undefined`, `number`, `function`. Function **declarations** are hoisted complete with their body. `var` declarations are hoisted but initialised to `undefined`, so a function **expression** assigned to a `var` is not callable before its line.
deepAnswer: Before any statement runs, the engine creates the bindings for the scope. `fn` is a function declaration, so its entire definition is available from the top — `typeof fn` is `"function"` on line one.
`v` and `expr` are `var` declarations. Both bindings exist immediately but hold `undefined` until their assignment executes, so both report `"undefined"` at the top.

The asymmetry is the point of the question: `expr` **looks** like a function to a reader but behaves like any other `var`. Calling `expr()` before its assignment throws `TypeError: expr is not a function`, not a `ReferenceError`.
After the assignments run, `v` is a number and `expr` is a function.

What to say about practice: none of this should be relied on. `const`/`let` and consistent declare-before-use make hoisting a non-issue, and the temporal dead zone converts these silent `undefined`s into immediate errors. Knowing the rules matters for reading legacy code and for debugging, not for writing new code.
keyPoints: Function declarations hoist with their body
`var` hoists as a binding initialised to `undefined`
A function expression on a `var` is not callable early
An early call gives `TypeError`, not `ReferenceError`
`let`/`const` replace the silent `undefined` with a TDZ error
commonMistakes: Saying function expressions hoist like declarations.
Expecting a `ReferenceError` from an early call.
followUps: What error does calling `expr()` early produce?
How does the TDZ change this?

interview:iv-out-set-samevaluezero.shortAnswer: `4`, `1|1|NaN|0`, `a`, `2`. `Set` and `Map` use SameValueZero: no type coercion (so `1` and `"1"` are distinct), `NaN` **is** equal to itself, `0` and `-0` are the same key, and objects are compared by reference.
deepAnswer: SameValueZero is `===` with one amendment: `NaN` equals `NaN`. That single change is what makes `Set` usable for deduplicating numeric data, where `[NaN].indexOf(NaN)` would return `-1`.
No coercion happens, so `1` and `"1"` are two separate entries — visible in the joined output, where the two look identical as text but are distinct members.
`0` and `-0` are treated as the same key. The set keeps the first inserted, which is why `-0` never appears.
`new Map([[NaN, "a"]]).get(NaN)` returns `"a"` for the same reason — a lookup that `===`-based code could never perform.

`new Set([{}, {}]).size` is `2`: two distinct object literals are two distinct references. `Set` does not deduplicate by structure, so deduplicating objects requires a key function — for example building a `Map` keyed by `item.id`.
Related but distinct: `Object.is` implements SameValue, which differs by treating `0` and `-0` as **different**. `Object.is(0, -0)` is `false` while a `Set` merges them.
keyPoints: `Set`/`Map` use SameValueZero — `===` except `NaN` equals `NaN`
No coercion: `1` and `"1"` are separate entries
`0` and `-0` collapse to one key
Objects compare by reference, not structure
`Object.is` differs: it separates `0` and `-0`
commonMistakes: Expecting a `Set` to deduplicate structurally identical objects.
Assuming `NaN` cannot be a working key.
followUps: How would you deduplicate objects by id?
How does `Object.is` differ?

interview:iv-out-string-immutable.shortAnswer: `a+b-c`, `a+b+c`, `a-b-c`, `3`, `c`. `replace` with a string pattern changes only the **first** match; `replaceAll` changes every match; and strings are immutable, so `s` itself is untouched by either.
deepAnswer: `replace` with a string as the first argument replaces one occurrence. To replace all with `replace` you need a global regex — `s.replace(/-/g, "+")` — which is the older idiom and still the only option when you need a pattern.
`replaceAll` was added precisely because the string form of `replace` surprises people. Note it throws a `TypeError` if given a non-global regex, which prevents the equivalent confusion in reverse.

Printing `s` afterwards shows `a-b-c`: every string method returns a new string and none mutates in place. This is the same reason `s.toUpperCase()` on its own does nothing useful unless you use the result.
`split("-")` produces three pieces from two separators.
`at(-1)` indexes from the end and returns `"c"`. It was added because `s[-1]` is `undefined` and `s.charAt(-1)` is `""` — neither does the intuitive thing.
One caveat to volunteer: all of these operate on UTF-16 code units. For emoji or other astral characters, `[...s]` or `Intl.Segmenter` is what respects real characters.
keyPoints: `replace` with a string replaces only the first match
`replaceAll`, or a `/g` regex, replaces every match
Strings are immutable — methods return new strings
`at(-1)` reads from the end; `[-1]` gives `undefined`
These methods work on UTF-16 units, not user-perceived characters
commonMistakes: Expecting `replace` to be global.
Calling a string method and discarding the return value.
followUps: Why does `replaceAll` reject a non-global regex?
How do you reverse a string containing emoji?

interview:iv-out-class-field-arrow.shortAnswer: `w`, `TypeError`, `true`, `false`. A class field holding an arrow is created **per instance** during construction and captures `this` lexically, so it survives detachment. A normal method lives on the prototype and loses its receiver when detached.
deepAnswer: Class fields are installed on the instance as own properties when the constructor runs. The arrow is created at that moment, inside a scope where `this` is the new instance, and arrows have no `this` of their own — so `arrow()` still resolves `this.label` correctly after destructuring.

`method` is defined on `Widget.prototype`. Destructuring copies the function reference, so calling it bare gives `this === undefined` (class bodies are always strict) and reading `.label` throws `TypeError`.
The `hasOwn` results confirm the mechanism: `arrow` is an own property of `w`, `method` is not.

The tradeoff is real, and stating it is the point of the question. Per-instance arrows cost one function object per instance, cannot be overridden by a subclass through `super`, and do not appear on the prototype for spies or mocks to intercept. Prototype methods are shared and subclassable but need binding when passed as callbacks.

Practical guidance: use a prototype method by default; use a bound field when the function is handed to something that will call it detached — an event listener, a `setTimeout`, a React prop — and you would otherwise write `.bind(this)` in the constructor.
keyPoints: Class fields are own properties, created per instance
An arrow field captures `this` lexically and survives detachment
Prototype methods lose `this` when detached — `TypeError` in strict mode
Fields cost memory per instance and break `super` overriding
Prefer prototype methods; use bound fields for detached callbacks
commonMistakes: Believing class methods are auto-bound.
Using arrow fields everywhere without naming the cost.
followUps: Why can a subclass not `super`-call an arrow field?
How does this affect mocking in tests?

interview:iv-out-reduce-no-initial.shortAnswer: `6`, `5`, `TypeError`, `0`. With no initial value `reduce` uses the first element as the accumulator and starts from index 1 — so a single-element array never calls the callback, and an empty array has nothing to start with and throws.
deepAnswer: `[1, 2, 3].reduce(fn)` starts with `a = 1`, `b = 2`, then `a = 3`, `b = 3`, giving `6`. The callback ran twice for three elements.

`[5].reduce(fn)` never calls the callback at all: the accumulator is `5` and there are no further elements. This matters when the callback has side effects or transforms values — a one-element array silently skips the transformation.

`[].reduce(fn)` throws `TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value`. This is the crash that reaches production when a list happens to be empty, and it is why the initial value should be treated as mandatory.
`[].reduce(fn, 0)` returns the initial value `0` without invoking the callback.

A second reason always to pass an initial value: it fixes the accumulator's type. Building an object with `reduce((acc, x) => ..., {})` is unambiguous, whereas omitting `{}` makes the first element the accumulator and produces something of a different shape.

Style note worth adding: `reduce` earns its place for folds like sums, grouping and index-building. When the same logic reads more clearly as `map` plus `filter`, or as a plain loop, prefer that — a `reduce` that rebuilds an array is usually harder to read than the loop it replaced.
keyPoints: No initial value → first element is the accumulator, iteration starts at index 1
A one-element array never invokes the callback
An empty array without an initial value throws `TypeError`
The initial value also pins the accumulator type
Prefer `map`/`filter` or a loop when they read more clearly
commonMistakes: Omitting the initial value and assuming empty arrays are safe.
Forgetting the callback is skipped for single-element arrays.
followUps: What does `reduce` return for an empty array with an initial value?
When is a plain loop clearer?

interview:iv-out-pass-by-sharing.shortAnswer: `old` then `new`. Arguments are passed by value, but for objects the **value** is a reference. Reassigning the parameter rebinds only the local name; mutating through it reaches the same object the caller holds.
deepAnswer: `reassign` receives a copy of the reference. Assigning to `obj` points that local copy at a new object and leaves the caller's variable untouched — the new object is simply discarded when the function returns.
`mutate` follows the reference it was given and writes a property on the original object, so the caller observes the change.
The accurate name for this is "call by sharing": the reference is copied, the object is shared. It is neither classic pass-by-value of the object nor pass-by-reference of the variable.
Note that `const target` does not prevent any of this. `const` blocks rebinding `target`, not mutation of the object it points at.

The practical consequence: a function that mutates its arguments is doing something invisible at the call site. Prefer returning a new value — `const next = { ...obj, v: "new" }` — and reserve mutation for cases where the caller has explicitly opted in, such as a documented `applyDefaults(target, source)`.
keyPoints: Arguments are copies of the reference — call by sharing
Reassigning a parameter never affects the caller
Mutating through it does
`const` prevents rebinding, not mutation
Prefer returning new values over mutating arguments
commonMistakes: Calling JavaScript "pass by reference".
Expecting `const` to prevent mutation.
followUps: How would you write `reassign` so the caller sees the change?
What does `Object.freeze` add here?

interview:iv-out-async-return-value.shortAnswer: `true`, `function`, `after`, `resolved 1`, `caught x`. An `async` function always returns a promise: a plain `return` fulfils it, and a `throw` rejects it rather than propagating synchronously to the caller.
deepAnswer: `async` wraps the return value in a promise automatically. Returning `1` behaves like `Promise.resolve(1)`; returning a promise does not double-wrap it.

`typeof ok().then === "function"` is the thenable check the specification itself uses — duck typing, not an `instanceof` check, which is why a promise from another realm or a library still interoperates.

The `throw` in `bad` does **not** reach the caller as a synchronous exception. It becomes a rejection, so `try { bad(); } catch {}` around the bare call would catch nothing. Only `await bad()` inside `try`, or `.catch`, handles it.
Ordering: both `.then` and `.catch` reactions are microtasks, so `after` — the last synchronous statement — prints before either. Then the reactions run in registration order.

The everyday consequence: an `async` function whose rejection nobody handles produces an unhandled rejection, which in Node terminates the process by default and in browsers surfaces on `window.onunhandledrejection`. Every promise you start needs an owner that awaits or catches it.
keyPoints: `async` always returns a promise; `return x` fulfils it
`throw` becomes a rejection, not a synchronous exception
A bare call cannot be wrapped in `try`/`catch` usefully — `await` it
Reactions are microtasks, so they run after all synchronous code
Unowned rejections become unhandled rejections
commonMistakes: Wrapping a non-awaited async call in `try`/`catch`.
Expecting the reactions to run before the final synchronous line.
followUps: What happens if you `return` a promise from an `async` function?
How do you handle an unhandled rejection globally?

interview:iv-out-short-circuit-order.shortAnswer: `a,c,e,f` then `false`, `true`, `fallback`. `&&` stops at the first falsy operand, `||` at the first truthy one, and `??` at the first non-nullish one — and each returns the operand itself, not a boolean.
deepAnswer: `t("a", false) && ...` — the left side is falsy, so `&&` returns it immediately and `b` is never evaluated. That is why `b` is missing from the log.
`t("c", true) || ...` — the left side is truthy, so `||` returns it and `d` is skipped.
`t("e", null) ?? ...` — `null` is nullish, so `??` must evaluate the right side, and `f` runs. Had the left side been `0` or `""`, `??` would have stopped there while `||` would have continued.

The results are the operands, not coerced booleans: `r1` is the value `false`, `r2` is `true`, `r3` is the string `"fallback"`. This is what makes `const name = input || "anonymous"` work as a defaulting idiom.

The practical significance of skipping evaluation is guarding: `user && user.profile` avoided a crash long before `?.` existed, and `isEnabled() && expensiveSetup()` avoids work rather than just avoiding an error. Because the right operand may never run, putting a required side effect there is a real bug.
keyPoints: `&&` stops at the first falsy, `||` at the first truthy, `??` at the first non-nullish
They return the operand, not a boolean
Skipped operands are never evaluated — side effects do not happen
`??` differs from `||` exactly on `0`, `""` and `false`
Never place a required side effect on the right of a short-circuit
commonMistakes: Assuming both operands always evaluate.
Expecting a coerced boolean result.
followUps: Why is `const x = a || b` a defaulting idiom?
When is `&&` used for conditional rendering?

interview:iv-out-array-destructuring.shortAnswer: `2`, `1`, `10`, `9`, `h`, `ey`. Destructuring swaps without a temporary, an elision skips a position, a default fills a missing index, and rest collects the remainder — from any iterable, including a string.
deepAnswer: `[a, b] = [b, a]` builds the array `[2, 1]` first, then destructures it. Because the right side is fully evaluated before any assignment, no temporary variable is needed.
The empty slot in `const [x, , z = 9]` is an elision: it consumes index 1 and binds nothing. `x` is `10`, index 1 (`20`) is discarded, and index 2 does not exist so the default `9` applies.
Destructuring works on any iterable, not just arrays. `"hey"` is iterable by code point, so `first` is `"h"` and rest collects `["e", "y"]` into a real array.
Rest must be last, and it always produces an array even when the source was a string or a `Set`.

Two practical notes: a destructuring assignment statement that starts with `[` — as here — needs the previous statement terminated, because ASI will not insert a semicolon before a line beginning with `[`. And destructuring `null` or `undefined` throws `TypeError`, so `const { a } = maybeNull` needs a `?? {}` guard.
keyPoints: Swap works because the right side evaluates fully first
An elision skips a position without binding
Defaults apply to missing indices, i.e. `undefined`
Destructuring consumes any iterable; rest always yields an array
Destructuring `null`/`undefined` throws
commonMistakes: Believing the swap needs a temporary variable.
Destructuring a possibly-null value without a guard.
followUps: Why can a line starting with `[` break under ASI?
How do you safely destructure a possibly-null object?

interview:iv-test-doubles.shortAnswer: A **stub** returns canned values, a **spy** records calls, a **mock** asserts on the interaction, and a **fake** is a working lightweight implementation. Mocking hurts when it asserts on internal collaboration — those tests break on every refactor while still passing when the behaviour is wrong.
deepAnswer: **Stub**: supplies an answer so the code under test can proceed. `getUser` returns a fixed user. It has no opinion about being called.

**Spy**: wraps or replaces a function and records how it was called, so you can assert afterwards. Useful for verifying a genuine side effect — that an analytics event fired, that `onSubmit` was invoked.
**Mock**: a double with expectations built in — "must be called once, with these arguments". The assertion is on the interaction rather than the outcome.

**Fake**: a real, simplified implementation. An in-memory repository, a `Map`-backed cache, a fake clock. Fakes usually give the best tests, because the code under test exercises real behaviour and the test asserts on real results.

The harm comes from **over-mocking**. If a test asserts "the service called the repository with these arguments", any refactor that changes the collaboration — batching two calls into one, caching, renaming a method — breaks the test even though behaviour is unchanged. Worse, the test passes when the repository is broken, because the real one never runs.

The rule of thumb: mock at **boundaries you do not own** — network, clock, randomness, filesystem, third-party SDKs — and use real code inside the boundary. That keeps tests fast and deterministic without making them a mirror of the implementation.

The deterministic doubles worth having by default: an injected clock, an injected random source, and a fetch layer replaced with a fixture map from request to response. Those three remove almost all non-determinism in front-end tests.
keyPoints: Stub returns values; spy records calls; mock asserts interactions; fake is a real simplified implementation
Prefer fakes — the code under test exercises real behaviour
Over-mocking couples tests to implementation and hides real breakage
Mock at boundaries you do not own: network, clock, randomness, filesystem
Inject the clock, the random source and the network layer
commonMistakes: Mocking modules you own and then asserting on internal call patterns.
Using the terms interchangeably without noticing that mocks assert and stubs do not.
followUps: Why is a fake usually better than a mock?
Which boundaries should always be faked?

interview:iv-test-no-network.shortAnswer: Put the network behind a seam you control: inject `fetch` (or a small API module) and supply a fake that maps requests to fixture responses. A test that reaches a real server is not a test — it is slow, non-deterministic, and fails when someone else's service does.
deepAnswer: Test the failures, not just the happy path — that is where the bugs are. A 500, a 404, malformed JSON, an empty `204`, a network rejection, and a request that never resolves so a timeout can be exercised. Each of these is trivial to produce with a fake and impossible to produce reliably against a real service.

The alternative to injection is intercepting at the network layer — MSW (Mock Service Worker) defines handlers per route and works in both the browser and Node. It has the advantage that the application code needs no seam at all and the same handlers can drive local development.
What to avoid: mocking your own `getUser` function and asserting it was called. That tests nothing about request construction, status handling, or parsing — the parts most likely to be wrong.

Contract drift is the remaining risk: a fake stays correct forever even when the real API changes. Contract tests, or schema validation against the provider's published schema, are what close that gap — the fake makes tests deterministic, the contract test makes them truthful.
keyPoints: Inject `fetch` or an API module — never let a unit test reach the network
Drive the fake from fixtures mapping request to response
Test 4xx, 5xx, malformed JSON, empty bodies and network rejection
MSW intercepts at the network layer and needs no code seam
Fakes drift from reality — contract or schema tests close that gap
commonMistakes: Mocking your own wrapper and asserting it was called.
Testing only the success path.
followUps: What does a fake never catch?
How would you test a request timeout?

interview:iv-test-async-pitfalls.shortAnswer: Flakiness comes from waiting on time instead of on a condition. Never assert after a fixed `setTimeout`; await the promise, use fake timers for scheduled work, and poll for the expected state with a deadline. Also make sure a test that should fail actually can.
deepAnswer: The classic broken pattern is `setTimeout(() => expect(...), 100)`. It is a bet that the work finishes in under 100ms — usually true on a developer laptop, sometimes false on a loaded CI runner. It also risks the assertion running after the test has already been reported as passed, so a failure is silently lost.

Return or await the promise so the framework knows when the test is done:

```js
await expect(loadUser(1)).resolves.toMatchObject({ id: 1 });
```

A forgotten `await` on an assertion is the single most common cause of a test that can never fail.

For code that schedules work, use fake timers instead of real ones: `vi.useFakeTimers()`, advance by the exact amount, assert. That makes a debounce test instant and deterministic rather than a real 300ms wait that sometimes is not enough.

When you genuinely cannot know the moment, poll for the condition with a deadline rather than sleeping for a guess. Testing-library's `waitFor` and Playwright's auto-waiting locators do exactly this: retry the assertion until it passes or the timeout expires. The test finishes as soon as the condition holds, so it is both faster and more reliable than a fixed sleep.

Test isolation is the other half. Shared module state, a database not reset between tests, a global `Date` mock left installed, or listeners not removed all create order-dependent failures — the tests pass individually and fail as a suite, or vice versa. Running the suite in a randomised order is how you find these deliberately.
Verify the test can fail. Break the implementation on purpose and confirm the test goes red. An async test with a missing `await` passes unconditionally, and that is not visible from a green run.

When a flaky test appears, the wrong response is a retry setting. Retries hide a real race — often a genuine bug in the code, not in the test — and turn an intermittent product failure into an invisible one.
keyPoints: Never assert after a fixed sleep — wait for a condition with a deadline
Return or await the promise; a missing `await` makes a test that cannot fail
Use fake timers for debounce, throttle, polling and retry logic
Reset shared state between tests; randomise order to expose coupling
Prove the test can fail by breaking the code deliberately
Retrying a flaky test hides a race rather than fixing it
commonMistakes: Adding a longer sleep until CI stops failing.
Enabling automatic retries instead of diagnosing the race.
followUps: How do fake timers change a debounce test?
Why is a randomised test order useful?

interview:iv-test-what-to-test-first.shortAnswer: Start where the cost of being wrong is highest and the code changes most often — usually money, auth and data integrity. Add a characterisation test before changing anything, and write a regression test for every bug as it is fixed.
deepAnswer: Rank by **impact × change frequency**. Code that never changes and never breaks does not need tests written retroactively, however complex it is. Code touched weekly, in a path that costs money or loses data when it fails, is where the first tests belong.
Version-control history is the data source: files with the most commits are the ones most likely to break next, and they are also the ones where tests pay for themselves fastest.

Before changing untested legacy code, write **characterisation tests** — tests that assert what it currently does, correct or not. They are a safety net for refactoring, not a statement that the behaviour is right. Once they pass, you can restructure with confidence and then change behaviour deliberately.

Every bug fix gets a test that fails before the fix and passes after. This is the highest-value test you will ever write: the bug is proof that this path is both reachable and easy to get wrong, and the test is proof the fix works.

Expect to have to make the code testable first. Untested code is usually untestable code — hard-coded `new Date()`, direct `fetch` calls, module-level singletons. Introducing a seam (a parameter, an injected dependency) is often the actual first step, and it is a refactor that needs the characterisation test to be safe.

End-to-end smoke tests over the two or three critical journeys are cheap insurance while the unit-level coverage is still thin. They catch the catastrophic "nothing loads" failures that unit tests never see.
What not to do: declare a coverage target and grind through files alphabetically. That produces the most tests where they matter least, and burns the goodwill you need to keep investing.
keyPoints: Prioritise by impact × change frequency; use commit history as the signal
Money, auth and data integrity first
Characterisation tests before refactoring legacy code
A regression test for every bug — the highest-value test available
Introducing a testing seam is often the real first step
A blanket coverage target produces tests where they matter least
commonMistakes: Chasing a coverage number instead of risk.
Refactoring untested code before pinning its current behaviour.
followUps: What is a characterisation test asserting?
How do you make legacy code testable without changing behaviour?

interview:iv-perf-memory-leaks.shortAnswer: A leak is memory that is still **reachable** but no longer needed. The usual causes are listeners never removed, timers never cleared, closures holding large objects, detached DOM nodes still referenced, and unbounded caches. Find them by comparing heap snapshots across a repeated user action.
deepAnswer: Garbage collection frees what is unreachable. It cannot free something a live reference still points at, so every leak is ultimately "something is still holding this".

The recurring causes: an `addEventListener` on `window` or `document` that is never removed; a `setInterval` that outlives its component; a closure that captures a large array it barely uses; a detached DOM subtree kept alive by a variable or a listener; a `Map` used as a cache with no eviction; and a long-lived event emitter retaining every subscriber.

Finding them: perform the suspect action repeatedly — open and close a modal twenty times — then take heap snapshots before and after and compare. The DevTools Memory panel can filter to **detached DOM nodes**, which is usually the fastest route to a front-end leak. The Performance panel's memory timeline shows the shape: a sawtooth that returns to baseline is healthy; a staircase that never comes down is a leak.

Prevention is structural. Every subscription needs an owner responsible for teardown. `AbortController` with `{ signal }` removes many listeners at once and is much harder to get wrong than matching `removeEventListener` calls. Every cache needs a bound — a size limit or a TTL.

`WeakMap` and `WeakSet` hold keys weakly, so an entry disappears when the key becomes otherwise unreachable. They are the right structure for associating metadata with DOM nodes or objects you do not own, precisely because they cannot keep the key alive.

The honest caveat about testing this: garbage collection is not deterministic or observable. You cannot assert in a test that an object was collected, and `WeakRef`/`FinalizationRegistry` explicitly do not promise timing — the specification permits a collection never to happen. Detect leaks by measuring retained heap growth across many iterations, not by asserting a single object disappeared.
keyPoints: A leak is reachable-but-unneeded memory, not "GC failing"
Listeners, timers, closures, detached DOM nodes and unbounded caches
Compare heap snapshots across a repeated action; filter for detached nodes
A staircase memory graph means a leak; a sawtooth is healthy
`AbortController` for teardown; bound every cache; `WeakMap` for object metadata
Collection timing is not observable — measure growth, never assert collection
commonMistakes: Claiming an object is collected immediately when the last reference is dropped.
Writing a test that asserts garbage collection occurred.
followUps: Why is `WeakMap` the right choice for DOM metadata?
How would you demonstrate a leak in CI?

interview:iv-perf-bundle-size.shortAnswer: Analyse first — a bundle visualiser shows which dependencies dominate. Then: remove or replace oversized dependencies, split routes and heavy features behind dynamic `import()`, ensure tree shaking actually works, and defer anything not needed for the first paint.
deepAnswer: Start with a bundle analyser to see the actual composition. The answer is usually concentrated: a date library, a charting library, an icon set imported wholesale, a polyfill bundle for browsers you no longer support, or the same library included twice at two versions.

**Dependency choices** give the biggest single wins. Replacing a large date library with `Intl.DateTimeFormat` and `Temporal`-style helpers, or a utility library with the handful of functions actually used, can remove hundreds of kilobytes. Check the alternatives on a size-comparison tool before adding anything.

**Import shape** matters as much as the dependency. `import { debounce } from "lodash"` may pull the whole library if the package is not ESM and side-effect-free; `import debounce from "lodash/debounce"` or `lodash-es` does not. Tree shaking only works for static ESM imports, so a CommonJS dependency is effectively unshakeable.

**Code splitting** is the structural fix. Route-level splitting with dynamic `import()` means the first page ships only what it needs. Then split heavy features that are conditionally used — a rich text editor, a chart, a PDF viewer — behind the interaction that opens them.
`"sideEffects": false` in `package.json` tells the bundler that dropping unused modules is safe. Without it, bundlers must conservatively keep modules that might have side effects at import time.

Load strategy is separate from size: `defer` and `type="module"` stop scripts blocking parsing, `preload` prioritises the critical bundle, and modern-only builds avoid shipping transpilation and polyfills to browsers that never needed them.
Track the number over time. A bundle-size budget enforced in CI is what stops the 2MB from coming back — size regressions arrive one small dependency at a time, and nobody notices any single one.
keyPoints: Analyse first — the weight is usually concentrated in a few dependencies
Replace oversized dependencies; check size before adding one
Import shape matters; tree shaking needs static ESM and `sideEffects: false`
Split by route, then by heavy conditional feature, with dynamic `import()`
Use `defer`/modules, preload the critical bundle, ship modern-only builds
Enforce a size budget in CI or the regression returns
commonMistakes: Assuming named imports are always tree-shaken.
Optimising code you wrote while ignoring the dependencies that dominate.
followUps: Why does tree shaking fail for CommonJS?
What does `sideEffects: false` promise?

interview:iv-perf-premature.shortAnswer: Ask for the measurement. For typical array sizes the difference is negligible and invisible next to network and rendering costs. If a profile genuinely shows this loop as a bottleneck, the rewrite is justified — and should carry a comment saying so.
deepAnswer: The factual position: a `for` loop can be measurably faster than a chain of `map`/`filter` for large arrays, mostly because a chain allocates an intermediate array per stage and calls a function per element. For 100,000 elements in a hot path that is real. For the 50 rows a UI usually renders, it is nanoseconds against a 200ms network request.

So the response is not "never optimise" — it is "show me where this ranks". If the profile does not name this function, the rewrite trades readability for nothing measurable, and readability is what determines how many bugs the next person introduces here.

When the array genuinely is large, the better first move is usually algorithmic rather than syntactic: avoid the multiple passes by combining stages, replace a nested `find` with a `Map` lookup to turn O(n²) into O(n), or avoid processing elements nobody will see. Those changes are worth orders of magnitude; loop-versus-`map` is worth a constant factor.

Two more traps to name. Micro-benchmarks are notoriously misleading, because JIT compilers optimise a tight benchmark loop in ways they will not optimise the real call site, and results vary by engine and by data shape. And engines change: advice about which array method was slow in 2015 is not reliable today.

The professional framing is about where effort goes. Bundle size, request waterfalls, long tasks and re-render counts dominate real front-end performance by orders of magnitude. Time spent on array-method micro-optimisation is time not spent on the things the profile actually blames.

How to disagree well: do not block the change on principle. Ask what prompted it, offer to profile together, and agree that if it is measurable it stays with a comment recording the measurement — so the next person does not "clean it up" back to a chain.
keyPoints: Ask for the measurement rather than arguing from principle
The difference is real for large arrays, negligible for typical UI sizes

interview:iv-sec-token-storage.shortAnswer: In an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` cookie set by the server. JavaScript cannot read it, so an XSS cannot exfiltrate it. `localStorage` is readable by any script on the origin, which makes any XSS an immediate credential theft.
deepAnswer: The comparison is between two different failure modes, and the honest answer names both.

**`localStorage`**: readable by every script on the origin, including any third-party script you include and anything an XSS injects. It survives tab closure, is never sent automatically, and is therefore immune to CSRF. Its fatal weakness is that a single XSS reads the token and sends it anywhere.

**`HttpOnly` cookie**: unreadable from JavaScript by design, so an XSS cannot exfiltrate it — though it can still make authenticated requests from the page while the user is there, which is a smaller blast radius but not zero. Because cookies are sent automatically, they need `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` (plus CSRF tokens for cross-site flows) to prevent cross-site request forgery, and `Secure` so they are never sent over plain HTTP.

The standard architecture: a short-lived access token, a long-lived refresh token in an `HttpOnly` cookie, and a refresh endpoint that rotates them. Short expiry limits how long a stolen token is useful; rotation with reuse detection lets the server revoke a whole session when a stolen refresh token is replayed.

What not to do, in any storage: put secrets in a JWT payload. A JWT is signed, not encrypted — the payload is base64url and readable by anyone holding the token. Treat it as public data with a tamper-proof signature.

There is no client-side API key that stays secret. Anything shipped to the browser is visible to the user, so a key that must remain private belongs on a server that proxies the call. Client-visible keys must be restricted by origin, scope and rate limit at the provider.

Do not build your own authentication if you can avoid it. Session management, rotation, revocation and secure password handling are well-solved by established libraries and identity providers, and the failure modes of a bespoke implementation are severe and quiet.
keyPoints: `HttpOnly` + `Secure` + `SameSite` cookie is the default correct answer
`localStorage` is readable by any script — XSS becomes credential theft
Cookies need CSRF protection precisely because they are sent automatically
Short-lived access token plus rotating refresh token limits exposure
A JWT payload is readable — signed, not encrypted
No client-side key is secret; proxy anything that must stay private
commonMistakes: Recommending `localStorage` because "cookies are vulnerable to CSRF" without weighing XSS.
Putting sensitive data in a JWT payload.
followUps: What can an XSS still do against an `HttpOnly` cookie?

interview:iv-sec-dependencies.shortAnswer: Depend on less, pin what you depend on with a committed lockfile, audit and update on a schedule rather than in a panic, and reduce what a compromised package can reach — CI secrets scoped narrowly, install scripts disabled where possible, and builds reproducible.
deepAnswer: The scale of the exposure is the first thing to state: a direct dependency brings its whole transitive tree, and every one of those packages runs with the same privileges as your build. A typical front-end project depends on hundreds of packages maintained by people nobody on the team has met.

**Depend on less.** Every addition is a permanent liability — review size, maintenance activity, the number of transitive dependencies, and whether the standard library or twenty lines of your own code would do. A left-pad-sized dependency is rarely worth its supply-chain surface.

**Pin and verify.** Commit the lockfile, install with `npm ci` in CI so the lockfile is authoritative, and be aware that a caret range means a future `npm install` can pull code nobody reviewed. Consider a delay policy — do not adopt a version on its release day — which blunts the window during which a compromised publish is live.

**Audit continuously.** `npm audit` and automated dependency PRs (Dependabot, Renovate) surface known vulnerabilities. Triage them rather than treating every advisory as urgent: a prototype-pollution advisory in a build-time-only tool has a very different real risk from one in code that processes user input at runtime.

**Limit the blast radius.** `npm ci --ignore-scripts` where the toolchain allows it removes the most common execution vector, since install scripts run automatically with full permissions. CI tokens should be scoped to what a job actually needs, and publish credentials should never be available to a build that only runs tests.
Keep an inventory. Generating an SBOM makes "are we affected by this advisory?" a query rather than an investigation, which is the difference between responding in an hour and responding in a day.
Have a response plan: how a bad version is rolled back, how secrets are rotated, and who decides. Supply-chain incidents are a question of when.
keyPoints: A direct dependency brings its whole transitive tree, running with build privileges
Depend on less; evaluate size, maintenance and transitive count before adding
Commit the lockfile and install with `npm ci`; caret ranges admit unreviewed code
Automate audits and triage by real exposure, not advisory count
Disable install scripts where possible; scope CI credentials narrowly
Keep an SBOM and a rollback/rotation plan
commonMistakes: Treating `npm audit` output as the whole strategy.
Not distinguishing a build-time-only vulnerability from a runtime one.
followUps: Why does a lockfile matter if versions are already ranged?

interview:iv-sec-object-injection-defenc.shortAnswer: Untrusted keys must never be allowed to reach special property names such as `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype`, because a naive recursive merge can end up writing to a shared prototype and affecting unrelated objects. Use an allowlist of expected keys, skip inherited and special names, and prefer `Map` or `Object.create(null)` for data-keyed structures.
deepAnswer: The risk class is **prototype pollution**: a deep merge or deep-set helper that walks keys from untrusted input can be steered into modifying an object that many other objects inherit from. The consequence is not localised — code elsewhere reads a property it never set and behaves differently. Defending against it is a well-understood, purely defensive practice.
The concrete defences, in order of strength:

**Validate against a schema.** Accept only the keys you expect, with the types you expect, and discard everything else. An allowlist is the only defence that does not depend on enumerating dangerous names correctly.

**Use structures without a prototype.** `Object.create(null)` produces an object with no inherited properties at all, and a `Map` has no property semantics to abuse. For anything keyed by data rather than by code, `Map` is the better default anyway.

**Freeze what should not change.** `Object.freeze(Object.prototype)` at startup is a blunt but effective mitigation in some applications; more practically, freeze your own configuration objects so unexpected writes fail loudly in strict mode.
**Do not write the merge yourself** if you can avoid it. Maintained libraries have had these cases reported and fixed; a hand-rolled deep merge in application code has had one reviewer.

The general principle this illustrates: data from outside should never be able to influence **which** property is written, only **what value** goes into a property you chose. Keeping key selection under your program's control is what makes a whole family of injection problems impossible.
keyPoints: A recursive merge over untrusted keys can write to a shared prototype
Schema allowlisting is the strongest defence — accept only expected keys
Explicitly skip `__proto__`, `constructor`, `prototype`; use `Object.hasOwn`
`Object.create(null)` and `Map` remove prototype semantics entirely
Freeze configuration so unexpected writes fail loudly
Data should choose values, never which property is written
commonMistakes: Relying on a denylist of key names as the only defence.
Writing a bespoke deep merge for untrusted input.
followUps: Why is an allowlist stronger than a denylist here?

interview:iv-arch-error-strategy.shortAnswer: Handle an error where you can actually do something about it — usually near the top, where the UI context is known — and let it propagate everywhere else. Add context as it travels, distinguish expected failures from bugs, and never swallow an error just to make code quieter.
deepAnswer: The first distinction is between **expected failures** and **bugs**. A 404, a validation rejection or a network timeout is a normal outcome that the design should account for. A `TypeError` from reading a property of `undefined` is a defect. Handling both with one generic catch guarantees the second class is hidden.

Expected failures are often better modelled as values than as exceptions. A function returning `{ ok: false, error }` makes the failure part of the type, which the caller cannot forget to consider — whereas an exception is invisible in the signature.

Low-level code should generally **not** catch. It lacks the context to decide what to do, and catching there means the caller loses the ability to choose. Where it does catch, it should add context and rethrow: `throw new Error("Loading user " + id + " failed", { cause: err })`. `cause` preserves the original stack, which is what makes a wrapped error debuggable rather than a lie.

The boundaries where handling belongs: a UI error boundary or top-level handler that shows something sensible instead of a blank screen; a per-request boundary that turns a failure into an inline message with a retry; and a global `window.onerror` / `onunhandledrejection` for reporting.

Custom error types make branching honest. A `class HttpError extends Error` carrying `status` lets a caller retry a 503, re-authenticate on a 401, and show "not found" on a 404. String matching on error messages is the alternative, and it breaks on the first wording change.

Distinguish **user-facing** from **diagnostic** messages. Users need what happened and what to do; engineers need the stack, the request id and the inputs. Showing a raw stack to a user is both unhelpful and an information leak.

The one rule with no exceptions: never `catch {}` with an empty body. If an error is genuinely safe to ignore, say so in a comment explaining why — otherwise you have converted a loud failure into a silent one, which is strictly worse.
keyPoints: Separate expected failures from bugs; do not catch both the same way
Model expected failures as return values where it fits
Low-level code rethrows with added context and `cause`, rather than deciding
Handle at boundaries: UI error boundary, per-request, global reporter
Custom error types with a `status` beat string-matching messages
Split user-facing messages from diagnostic detail
Never swallow an error silently
commonMistakes: Wrapping every call in a `try`/`catch` that logs and continues.
Losing the original error by wrapping without `cause`.
followUps: When is a result object better than an exception?
